Distinctive Features of the Poem
Transformation of Defeat: The speaker converts rejection into a spiritual victory
Present-Moment Focus: Emphasis on the value of immediate experience
Philosophical Depth: Reflections on the nature of success, fulfillment, and happiness
Optimistic Tone: Despite rejection, the overall mood is positive and affirming
Comparative Structure: The speaker repeatedly contrasts his situation with others’
Historical Context
Written during the Victorian era when romantic sensibilities were evolving
Composed during Browning’s happy years with Elizabeth Barrett Browning in Italy
Part of his mature work, representing his distinctive dramatic monologue style
Reflects Victorian interest in psychological complexity and moral ambiguity
Demonstrates the period’s fascination with emotional intensity and introspection
Critical Reception
Initially, Browning’s work, including this poem, received mixed reviews
Later critics recognized the psychological depth and innovative form
Praised for its successful combination of emotional intensity and philosophical reflection
Considered one of the finest examples of Browning’s dramatic monologues
Recognized for its complex presentation of love, desire, and acceptance
Robert Browning’s Dramatic Monologue Technique
Speaker is not the poet but a fictional character
Reveals character through speech rather than description
Often features morally ambiguous speakers
Includes an implied listener who doesn’t speak
Captures a crucial moment or psychological turning point
Employs natural speech rhythms with subtle metrical variations

Text of the Poem

It little profits that an idle king,
By this still hearth, among these barren crags,
Match'd with an aged wife, I mete and dole
Unequal laws unto a savage race,
That hoard, and sleep, and feed, and know not me.
I cannot rest from travel; I will drink
Life to the lees.  All times I have enjoy'd
Greatly, have suffer'd greatly, both with those
That loved me, and alone; on shore, and when
Thro' scudding drifts the rainy Hyades
Vext the dim sea.  I am become a name;
For always roaming with a hungry heart
Much have I seen and known,— cities of men
And manners, climates, councils, governments,
Myself not least, but honor'd of them all,—
And drunk delight of battle with my peers,
Far on the ringing plains of windy Troy.
I am a part of all that I have met;
Yet all experience is an arch wherethro'
Gleams that untravell'd world whose margin fades
For ever and for ever when I move.
How dull it is to pause, to make an end,
To rust unburnish'd, not to shine in use!
As tho' to breathe were life!  Life piled on life
Were all too little, and of one to me
Little remains; but every hour is saved
From that eternal silence, something more,
A bringer of new things; and vile it were
For some three suns to store and hoard myself,
And this gray spirit yearning in desire
To follow knowledge like a sinking star,
Beyond the utmost bound of human thought.
This is my son, mine own Telemachus,
To whom I leave the sceptre and the isle,—
Well-loved of me, discerning to fulfill
This labour, by slow prudence to make mild
A rugged people, and thro' soft degrees
Subdue them to the useful and the good.
Most blameless is he, centred in the sphere
Of common duties, decent not to fail
In offices of tenderness, and pay
Meet adoration to my household gods,
When I am gone.  He works his work, I mine.
There lies the port; the vessel puffs her sail;
There gloom the dark, broad seas.  My mariners,
Souls that have toil'd, and wrought, and thought with me,—
That ever with a frolic welcome took
The thunder and the sunshine, and opposed
Free hearts, free foreheads,— you and I are old;
Old age hath yet his honor and his toil.
Death closes all; but something ere the end,
Some work of noble note, may yet be done,
Not unbecoming men that strove with Gods.
The lights begin to twinkle from the rocks;
The long day wanes; the slow moon climbs; the deep
Moans round with many voices.  Come, my friends.
'T is not too late to seek a newer world.
Push off, and sitting well in order smite
The sounding furrows; for my purpose holds
To sail beyond the sunset, and the baths
Of all the western stars, until I die.
It may be that the gulfs will wash us down;
It may be we shall touch the Happy Isles,
And see the great Achilles, whom we knew.
Tho' much is taken, much abides; and tho'
We are not now that strength which in old days
Moved earth and heaven, that which we are, we are,—
One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.

समग्र अर्थ (Overall Meaning in Hindi)

“Ulysses” अल्फ्रेड लॉर्ड टेनिसन की एक प्रसिद्ध कविता है, जिसमें ग्रीक पौराणिक कथा के नायक ओडिसियस (जिसे रोमन में यूलिसीज़ कहा जाता है) का चित्रण किया गया है। कविता यूलिसीज़ के मुख से कही गई है, जो अपने ट्रॉय युद्ध और लंबी यात्रा के बाद घर लौट आया है और अब इथाका का राजा है।

कविता तीन मुख्य भागों में विभाजित है। पहले भाग में यूलिसीज़ अपने वर्तमान जीवन से असंतुष्ट दिखाई देता है, जहाँ वह एक निष्क्रिय राजा है। वह अपने अतीत की यात्राओं, अनुभवों और ज्ञान की खोज का स्मरण करता है, और कहता है कि वह इन सभी अनुभवों का हिस्सा बन गया है, फिर भी हर नए अनुभव से एक नया अनदेखा संसार दिखाई देता है।

दूसरे भाग में यूलिसीज़ कहता है कि केवल जीवित रहना ही काफी नहीं है, जीवन को पूरी तरह से जीना महत्वपूर्ण है। वह अपनी बची हुई उम्र को बेकार बिताने के बजाय नए ज्ञान की खोज में रहना चाहता है, भले ही वह मानवीय सोच की सीमाओं से परे जाना पड़े।

तीसरे भाग में यूलिसीज़ अपने पुत्र टेलीमैकस का उल्लेख करता है, जिसे वह अपना राज्य सौंप रहा है। वह अपने पुत्र को एक योग्य और कर्तव्यनिष्ठ व्यक्ति के रूप में वर्णित करता है। फिर वह अपने पुराने नाविक साथियों को एक अंतिम साहसिक यात्रा पर चलने के लिए आमंत्रित करता है, जिसमें वे सूर्यास्त के पार, पश्चिमी तारों के परे तक जाएंगे। वह स्वीकार करता है कि वे अब उतने शक्तिशाली नहीं हैं जितने पहले थे, लेकिन उनमें अभी भी संघर्ष करने, खोजने और कभी न हार मानने की इच्छाशक्ति है।
कविता आशावाद, साहस और अंतिम साँस तक जीवन को पूरी तरह जीने के संदेश के साथ समाप्त होती है, जो विक्टोरियन युग के आदर्शों को दर्शाती है।

Important Facts for Examination
Classical Source: Based on the character from Homer's Odyssey
Dante's Influence: Also influenced by Dante's portrayal in Inferno
Autobiographical Element: Written after death of Tennyson's friend Arthur Hallam
Victorian Context: Reflects Victorian values of progress and exploration
Monologue Type: Dramatic monologue, speaker is not the poet
Mythological Background: Ulysses (Greek: Odysseus) spent 10 years returning from Troy
Ithaca: Rocky island kingdom of Ulysses in Greece
Telemachus: Name means "far from battle" in Greek
Happy Isles: Elysium, the Greek afterlife for heroes
Achilles: Greek hero of Trojan War, died at Troy
Symbolic Meaning: The voyage represents the pursuit of knowledge and experience
Victorian Reception: Immensely popular, seen as expressing age of exploration

content.value: # Chapter 14: T.S. Eliot - The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
Author Facts
Thomas Stearns Eliot
Birth: September 26, 1888, St. Louis, Missouri, USA
Death: January 4, 1965, London, England
Nationality: American-born, later British citizen (1927)
Education: Harvard University, Sorbonne, Oxford University
Nobel Prize in Literature: 1948
Major Works: "The Waste Land" (1922), "Four Quartets" (1943), "Murder in the Cathedral" (1935)
Literary Movement: Modernism
Occupation: Poet, playwright, literary critic, editor
Spouse: Vivienne Haigh-Wood (1915-1947), Valerie Fletcher (1957-1965)
Notable Position: Editor at Faber and Faber publishing house
Poem Publication Facts
Publication Year: 1915
First Published In: Poetry: A Magazine of Verse (June 1915)
Later Included In: Prufrock and Other Observations (1917)
Form: Dramatic Monologue
Style: Free Verse (no fixed rhyme scheme or meter)
Total Lines: 131 lines
Stanzas: Irregular stanzas of varying lengths
Rhyme Scheme: Irregular, uses scattered rhymes and couplets
Meter: Predominantly iambic pentameter with variations
Text of the Poem

S’io credesse che mia risposta fosse
A persona che mai tornasse al mondo,
Questa fiamma staria senza piu scosse.
Ma perciocche giammai di questo fondo
Non torno vivo alcun, s’i’odo il vero,
Senza tema d’infamia ti rispondo.
 
 
Let us go then, you and I, 
When the evening is spread out against the sky 
Like a patient etherised upon a table; 
Let us go, through certain half-deserted streets, 
The muttering retreats       
Of restless nights in one-night cheap hotels 
And sawdust restaurants with oyster-shells: 
Streets that follow like a tedious argument 
Of insidious intent 
To lead you to an overwhelming question …         
Oh, do not ask, “What is it?” 
Let us go and make our visit. 
 
In the room the women come and go 
Talking of Michelangelo. 
 
The yellow fog that rubs its back upon the window-panes,       
The yellow smoke that rubs its muzzle on the window-panes 
Licked its tongue into the corners of the evening, 
Lingered upon the pools that stand in drains, 
Let fall upon its back the soot that falls from chimneys, 
Slipped by the terrace, made a sudden leap,         
And seeing that it was a soft October night, 
Curled once about the house, and fell asleep. 
 
And indeed there will be time 
For the yellow smoke that slides along the street, 
Rubbing its back upon the window-panes;         
There will be time, there will be time 
To prepare a face to meet the faces that you meet; 
There will be time to murder and create, 
And time for all the works and days of hands 
That lift and drop a question on your plate;         
Time for you and time for me, 
And time yet for a hundred indecisions, 
And for a hundred visions and revisions, 
Before the taking of a toast and tea. 
 
In the room the women come and go         
Talking of Michelangelo. 
 
And indeed there will be time 
To wonder, “Do I dare?” and, “Do I dare?” 
Time to turn back and descend the stair, 
With a bald spot in the middle of my hair—         
They will say: “How his hair is growing thin!” 
My morning coat, my collar mounting firmly to the chin, 
My necktie rich and modest, but asserted by a simple pin— 
They will say: “But how his arms and legs are thin!” 
Do I dare       
Disturb the universe? 
In a minute there is time 
For decisions and revisions which a minute will reverse. 
 
For I have known them all already, known them all:— 
Have known the evenings, mornings, afternoons,         
I have measured out my life with coffee spoons; 
I know the voices dying with a dying fall 
Beneath the music from a farther room. 
  So how should I presume? 
 
And I have known the eyes already, known them all—       
The eyes that fix you in a formulated phrase, 
And when I am formulated, sprawling on a pin, 
When I am pinned and wriggling on the wall, 
Then how should I begin 
To spit out all the butt-ends of my days and ways?       
  And how should I presume? 
 
And I have known the arms already, known them all— 
Arms that are braceleted and white and bare 
But in the lamplight, downed with light brown hair! 
It is perfume from a dress       
That makes me so digress? 
Arms that lie along a table, or wrap about a shawl. 
  And should I then presume? 
  And how should I begin?
       
Shall I say, I have gone at dusk through narrow streets       
And watched the smoke that rises from the pipes 
Of lonely men in shirt-sleeves, leaning out of windows?… 
 
I should have been a pair of ragged claws 
Scuttling across the floors of silent seas.
       
And the afternoon, the evening, sleeps so peacefully!       
Smoothed by long fingers, 
Asleep … tired … or it malingers, 
Stretched on the floor, here beside you and me. 
Should I, after tea and cakes and ices, 
Have the strength to force the moment to its crisis?       
But though I have wept and fasted, wept and prayed, 
Though I have seen my head grown slightly bald brought in upon a platter, 
I am no prophet—and here’s no great matter; 
I have seen the moment of my greatness flicker, 
And I have seen the eternal Footman hold my coat, and snicker,       
And in short, I was afraid. 
 
And would it have been worth it, after all, 
After the cups, the marmalade, the tea, 
Among the porcelain, among some talk of you and me, 
Would it have been worth while,         
To have bitten off the matter with a smile, 
To have squeezed the universe into a ball 
To roll it toward some overwhelming question, 
To say: “I am Lazarus, come from the dead, 
Come back to tell you all, I shall tell you all”—         
If one, settling a pillow by her head, 
  Should say: “That is not what I meant at all. 
  That is not it, at all.” 
 
And would it have been worth it, after all, 
Would it have been worth while,         
After the sunsets and the dooryards and the sprinkled streets, 
After the novels, after the teacups, after the skirts that trail along the floor— 
And this, and so much more?— 
It is impossible to say just what I mean! 
But as if a magic lantern threw the nerves in patterns on a screen:       
Would it have been worth while 
If one, settling a pillow or throwing off a shawl, 
And turning toward the window, should say: 
  “That is not it at all, 
  That is not what I meant, at all.”
         
No! I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be; 
Am an attendant lord, one that will do 
To swell a progress, start a scene or two, 
Advise the prince; no doubt, an easy tool, 
Deferential, glad to be of use,         
Politic, cautious, and meticulous; 
Full of high sentence, but a bit obtuse; 
At times, indeed, almost ridiculous— 
Almost, at times, the Fool. 
 
I grow old … I grow old …       
I shall wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled. 
 
Shall I part my hair behind? Do I dare to eat a peach? 
I shall wear white flannel trousers, and walk upon the beach. 
I have heard the mermaids singing, each to each. 
 
I do not think that they will sing to me.         
 
I have seen them riding seaward on the waves 
Combing the white hair of the waves blown back 
When the wind blows the water white and black. 
 
We have lingered in the chambers of the sea 
By sea-girls wreathed with seaweed red and brown       
Till human voices wake us, and we drown.
Line-by-Line Paraphrase
Opening Epigraph

S'io credesse che mia risposta fosse / A persona che mai tornasse al mondo...
This Italian epigraph from Dante's Inferno translates to: "If I thought my answer were given to someone who might return to the world, this flame would never move again. But since none returns alive from this depth, if what I hear is true, I answer you without fear of infamy." This sets the tone for confession and the idea that Prufrock speaks only because he believes his secrets are safe.
Lines 1-12: The Invitation

"Let us go then, you and I"
Prufrock invites the reader (or perhaps another part of himself) to accompany him on a journey through the city.

"When the evening is spread out against the sky / Like a patient etherised upon a table"
The evening appears lifeless and paralyzed, like a patient under anesthesia, suggesting the numbness and stagnation of modern life.

"Let us go, through certain half-deserted streets"
They will walk through empty, lonely urban streets.

"The muttering retreats / Of restless nights in one-night cheap hotels"
The streets lead to shabby hotels where people spend troubled, sleepless nights.

"And sawdust restaurants with oyster-shells"
They pass cheap restaurants with sawdust floors and oyster shells scattered about.

"Streets that follow like a tedious argument / Of insidious intent"
The winding streets resemble a boring, deceptive argument that seems designed to confuse.

"To lead you to an overwhelming question"
These streets lead to some important, life-changing question.

"Oh, do not ask, 'What is it?' / Let us go and make our visit"
Prufrock refuses to reveal what this question is and insists they continue their journey.
Lines 13-14: The Women

"In the room the women come and go / Talking of Michelangelo"
Inside a social gathering, women move about discussing the famous Renaissance artist, representing cultured conversation that Prufrock feels excluded from.
Lines 15-22: The Yellow Fog

"The yellow fog that rubs its back upon the window-panes"
The fog is personified as a cat-like creature rubbing against windows. The yellow color suggests industrial pollution.

"The yellow smoke that rubs its muzzle on the window-panes"
The smoke continues this animal imagery, nuzzling the glass like a pet.

"Licked its tongue into the corners of the evening"
The fog/smoke extends into all parts of the evening like an animal exploring.

"Lingered upon the pools that stand in drains"
It settles over stagnant water in the gutters.

"Let fall upon its back the soot that falls from chimneys"
Soot from industrial chimneys falls onto the fog.

"Slipped by the terrace, made a sudden leap"
The fog moves past buildings and jumps suddenly.

"And seeing that it was a soft October night / Curled once about the house, and fell asleep"
On this gentle autumn evening, the fog wraps around the house like a sleeping cat.
Lines 23-34: Time and Procrastination

"And indeed there will be time / For the yellow smoke that slides along the street"
Prufrock reassures himself that there is plenty of time for the fog to move through the streets.

"Rubbing its back upon the window-panes / There will be time, there will be time"
He repeats that there is time for the fog's movements.

"To prepare a face to meet the faces that you meet"
There will be time to create a false persona to present to others.

"There will be time to murder and create"
Time exists for both destruction and creation.

"And time for all the works and days of hands / That lift and drop a question on your plate"
Time for all human activities, including the casual way people present questions or problems.

"Time for you and time for me / And time yet for a hundred indecisions"
Time for both speaker and listener, and especially for countless moments of uncertainty.

"And for a hundred visions and revisions"
Time for many dreams and their constant modifications.

"Before the taking of a toast and tea"
All this happens before a simple social ritual like having tea and toast.
Lines 35-36: Repetition

"In the room the women come and go / Talking of Michelangelo"
The same image of cultured women is repeated, emphasizing Prufrock's sense of being an outsider.
Lines 37-48: Self-Consciousness and Fear

"And indeed there will be time / To wonder, 'Do I dare?' and, 'Do I dare?'"
Prufrock will have time to question whether he has the courage to act.

"Time to turn back and descend the stair"
Time to retreat and leave without taking action.

"With a bald spot in the middle of my hair"
He becomes self-conscious about his receding hairline.

"(They will say: 'How his hair is growing thin!')"
He imagines people criticizing his appearance.

"My morning coat, my collar mounting firmly to the chin"
He describes his formal attire - a morning coat with a high collar.

"My necktie rich and modest, but asserted by a simple pin"
His tie is expensive but understated, held with a simple pin.

"(They will say: 'But how his arms and legs are thin!')"
He imagines further criticism of his thin limbs.

"Do I dare / Disturb the universe?"
He questions whether he has the right to make any significant change or impact.

"In a minute there is time / For decisions and revisions which a minute will reverse"
Even in a short time, he can make decisions and change his mind repeatedly.
Lines 49-54: Routine and Emptiness

"For I have known them all already, known them all"
Prufrock claims to have experienced everything before.

"Have known the evenings, mornings, afternoons"
He has lived through countless routine periods of time.

"I have measured out my life with coffee spoons"
His life has been reduced to small, repetitive activities like drinking coffee. This suggests a monotonous, unfulfilling existence.

"I know the voices dying with a dying fall"
He recognizes the fading sounds of conversation (referencing Shakespeare's Twelfth Night).

"Beneath the music from a farther room"
These voices fade under music playing elsewhere.

"So how should I presume?"
Given this mundane existence, how can he dare to act boldly?
Lines 55-61: Being Judged

"And I have known the eyes already, known them all"
He has experienced the judging gazes of others.

"The eyes that fix you in a formulated phrase"
Eyes that categorize and label people with preset judgments.

"And when I am formulated, sprawling on a pin"
When he is classified and displayed like a pinned insect specimen.

"When I am pinned and wriggling on the wall"
Like a butterfly pinned to a display board, struggling helplessly.

"Then how should I begin / To spit out all the butt-ends of my days and ways?"
How can he express the used-up, worthless remnants of his life (comparing them to cigarette butts)?

"And how should I presume?"
Again, he questions his right to act.
Lines 62-69: Physical Attraction and Hesitation

"And I have known the arms already, known them all"
He has observed women's arms before.

"Arms that are braceleted and white and bare"
Arms wearing jewelry, pale and exposed.

"(But in the lamplight, downed with light brown hair!)"
In artificial light, the soft hair on the arms becomes visible.

"Is it perfume from a dress / That makes me so digress?"
He wonders if a woman's perfume is distracting him from his purpose.

"Arms that lie along a table, or wrap about a shawl"
Arms positioned casually on furniture or wrapped in clothing.

"And should I then presume? / And how should I begin?"
He continues questioning whether he should dare approach these women.
Lines 70-74: Observation of Urban Life

"Shall I say, I have gone at dusk through narrow streets"
Should he mention his evening walks through the city?

"And watched the smoke that rises from the pipes / Of lonely men in shirt-sleeves, leaning out of windows?"
He has observed solitary men smoking at their windows in casual clothes.

"I should have been a pair of ragged claws / Scuttling across the floors of silent seas"
He wishes he could be like a crab, moving across the ocean floor without the burden of human consciousness and social anxiety.
Lines 75-83: Peaceful Evening and Hesitation

"And the afternoon, the evening, sleeps so peacefully!"
The time of day seems calm and restful.

"Smoothed by long fingers / Asleep ... tired ... or it malingers"
The evening is described as being gently touched, perhaps pretending to sleep when actually awake.

"Stretched on the floor, here beside you and me"
The evening lies beside both Prufrock and his companion.

"Should I, after tea and cakes and ices"
After polite social refreshments.

"Have the strength to force the moment to its crisis?"
Will he have the courage to bring about a decisive moment?
Lines 84-86: Fear of Death and Insignificance

"But though I have wept and fasted, wept and prayed"
Despite his emotional and spiritual suffering.

"Though I have seen my head grown slightly bald brought in upon a platter"
He imagines his balding head served on a plate like John the Baptist's, but realizes he is no prophet.

"I am no prophet—and here's no great matter"
He acknowledges he is not a religious leader and his concerns are trivial.
Lines 87-110: The Overwhelming Question and Rejection

"I have seen the moment of my greatness flicker"
He has witnessed brief moments when he might have achieved something significant.

"And I have seen the eternal Footman hold my coat, and snicker"
Death (the eternal Footman) has mocked him by preparing for his demise.

"And in short, I was afraid"
Simply put, he was too frightened to act.

"And would it have been worth it, after all"
He questions whether taking action would have been worthwhile.

"After the cups, the marmalade, the tea"
After all the polite social rituals.

"Among the porcelain, among some talk of you and me"
Among fine china and intimate conversation.

"Would it have been worth while / To have bitten off the matter with a smile"
Would it have been worth confronting the issue directly and aggressively?

"To have squeezed the universe into a ball / To roll it toward some overwhelming question"
To have compressed all existence into a single important question.

"To say: 'I am Lazarus, come from the dead / Come back to tell you all, I shall tell you all'"
To proclaim himself like the biblical Lazarus, returned from death with important revelations.

"If one, settling a pillow by her head / Should say: 'That is not what I meant at all. / That is not it, at all.'"
But if the woman he approaches dismisses his profound attempt at communication.
Lines 111-119: Repeated Doubt

"And would it have been worth it, after all / Would it have been worth while"
He continues questioning the value of action.

"After the sunsets and the dooryards and the sprinkled streets"
After all the beautiful moments and ordinary experiences of life.

"After the novels, after the teacups, after the skirts that trail along the floor"
After literature, social rituals, and feminine presence.

"And this, and so much more?"
And everything else besides.

"It is impossible to say just what I mean!"
He cannot express his true feelings or intentions clearly.
Lines 120-125: Final Rejection Continued

"But as if a magic lantern threw the nerves in patterns on a screen"
His anxiety is projected like images from an old-fashioned slide projector.

"Would it have been worth while / If one, settling a pillow or throwing off a shawl"
If a woman, making casual movements.

"And turning toward the window, should say: / 'That is not it at all, / That is not what I meant, at all.'"
Turns away and rejects his attempt at meaningful communication.
Lines 126-131: Self-Comparison to Hamlet

"No! I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be"
He denies being the indecisive tragic hero, though he shares Hamlet's paralysis.

"Am an attendant lord, one that will do / To swell a progress, start a scene or two"
He sees himself as a minor character in someone else's story.

"Advise the prince; no doubt, an easy tool"
He is merely a supporting figure who gives advice.

"Deferential, glad to be of use / Politic, cautious, and meticulous"
He is respectful, helpful, diplomatic, careful, and overly precise.

"Full of high sentence, but a bit obtuse"
He speaks in elevated language but is somewhat dull or unclear.

"At times, indeed, almost ridiculous— / Almost, at times, the Fool"
Sometimes he appears foolish, like a court jester.
Lines 132-133: Aging

"I grow old ... I grow old ..."
He repeats his awareness of advancing age.

"I shall wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled"
He will cuff his pants, perhaps to appear more fashionable or to accommodate his changing body.
Lines 134-139: Final Questions and the Mermaids

"Shall I part my hair behind? Do I dare to eat a peach?"
He contemplates trivial decisions about grooming and eating, showing how paralyzed he is even by minor choices.

"I shall wear white flannel trousers, and walk upon the beach"
He imagines himself in leisurely seaside attire.

"I have heard the mermaids singing, each to each"
He has heard mythical creatures singing to one another, representing beauty and enchantment he observes but cannot join.

"I do not think that they will sing to me"
He believes these magical beings will not sing for him, symbolizing his sense of unworthiness and exclusion from life's beauty.
Lines 140-144: The Ending

"I have seen them riding seaward on the waves"
He has watched the mermaids moving away from shore.

"Combing the white hair of the waves blown back / When the wind blows the water white and black"
The mermaids arrange the foam of the waves as the wind creates patterns of white and dark water.

"We have lingered in the chambers of the sea / By sea-girls wreathed with seaweed red and brown"
Both Prufrock and the reader have remained in underwater fantasy realms with these mythical beings.

"Till human voices wake us, and we drown"
Until reality (human voices) interrupts the dream, and the return to consciousness feels like drowning.
The poem ends with this powerful image of awakening from fantasy being more destructive than the dream itself, capturing Prufrock's tragic relationship with both reality and imagination.

English: S’io credesse che mia risposta fosse / A persona che mai tornasse al mondo, / Questa fiamma staria senza piu scosse. / Ma perciocche giammai di questo fondo / Non torno vivo alcun, s’i’odo il vero, / Senza tema d’infamia ti rispondo.

Line 37-48
English: And indeed there will be time / To wonder, “Do I dare?” and, “Do I dare?” / Time to turn back and descend the stair, / With a bald spot in the middle of my hair— / They will say: “How his hair is growing thin!” / My morning coat, my collar mounting firmly to the chin, / My necktie rich and modest, but asserted by a simple pin— / They will say: “But how his arms and legs are thin!” / Do I dare / Disturb the universe? / In a minute there is time / For decisions and revisions which a minute will reverse.
Hindi Meaning: और वास्तव में समय होगा / सोचने का, “क्या मैं हिम्मत करता हूँ?” और, “क्या मैं हिम्मत करता हूँ?” / वापस मुड़ने और सीढ़ी उतरने का समय, / मेरे बालों के बीच में एक गंजे धब्बे के साथ— / वे कहेंगे: “कैसे उसके बाल पतले हो रहे हैं!” / मेरा सुबह का कोट, मेरा कॉलर ठोड़ी तक मजबूती से चढ़ा हुआ, / मेरी टाई अमीर और विनम्र, लेकिन एक साधारण पिन द्वारा जोर दिया गया— / वे कहेंगे: “लेकिन कैसे उसके बाहु और पैर पतले हैं!” / क्या मैं हिम्मत करता हूँ / ब्रह्मांड को विचलित करने की? / एक मिनट में समय है / निर्णयों और संशोधनों के लिए जिन्हें एक मिनट उलट देगा।
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक सोचता है “क्या मैं हिम्मत करूँ?” वह अपनी उम्र बढ़ने के लक्षणों के बारे में चिंतित है - गंजापन, पतले अंग। वह सोचता है कि क्या वह “ब्रह्मांड को विचलित” करने की हिम्मत रखता है, लेकिन फिर तय करता है कि निर्णय और संशोधन क्षणभंगुर हैं।

Line 49-54
English: For I have known them all already, known them all:— / Have known the evenings, mornings, afternoons, / I have measured out my life with coffee spoons; / I know the voices dying with a dying fall / Beneath the music from a farther room. / So how should I presume?
Hindi Meaning: क्योंकि मैंने उन सभी को पहले ही जान लिया है, सभी को जान लिया है:— / शामों, सुबह, दोपहर को जान लिया है, / मैंने अपने जीवन को कॉफी के चम्मचों से नाप लिया है; / मैं आवाज़ों को एक मरती गिरावट के साथ मरते हुए जानता हूँ / दूर के कमरे से आती संगीत के नीचे। / तो मैं कैसे अनुमान लगाऊँ?
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक कहता है कि उसने जीवन के सभी क्षणों को जान लिया है, और अपने दिनों को छोटे-छोटे “कॉफी के चम्मचों” जैसी नगण्य इकाइयों में माप लिया है। वह सोचता है कि वह कैसे कुछ बड़ा करने का अनुमान लगा सकता है।

Line 55-61
English: And I have known the eyes already, known them all— / The eyes that fix you in a formulated phrase, / And when I am formulated, sprawling on a pin, / When I am pinned and wriggling on the wall, / Then how should I begin / To spit out all the butt-ends of my days and ways? / And how should I presume?
Hindi Meaning: और मैंने आँखों को पहले ही जान लिया है, सब को जान लिया है— / वे आँखें जो तुम्हें एक सूत्रबद्ध वाक्य में स्थिर करती हैं, / और जब मैं सूत्रबद्ध होता हूँ, एक पिन पर फैला हुआ, / जब मैं पिन किया हुआ और दीवार पर तड़पता हूँ, / तब मैं कैसे शुरू करूँ / अपने दिनों और तरीकों के सिगरेट के टुकड़े थूकने को? / और मैं कैसे अनुमान लगाऊँ?
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक महसूस करता है कि दूसरों की आँखें उसका निरीक्षण और न्याय करती हैं, और उसे एक कीड़े की तरह पिन किया हुआ महसूस होता है। वह अपने जीवन के “बचे-खुचे टुकड़ों” को कैसे व्यक्त करे और फिर से पूछता है “मैं कैसे अनुमान लगाऊँ?”

Line 62-69
English: And I have known the arms already, known them all— / Arms that are braceleted and white and bare / But in the lamplight, downed with light brown hair! / It is perfume from a dress / That makes me so digress? / Arms that lie along a table, or wrap about a shawl. / And should I then presume? / And how should I begin?
Hindi Meaning: और मैंने बाहुओं को पहले ही जान लिया है, सब को जान लिया है— / बाहुएँ जो कंगन पहने और सफेद और नंगी हैं / लेकिन लैंप की रोशनी में, हल्के भूरे बालों से ढकी हुई! / क्या यह एक पोशाक से आती खुशबू है / जो मुझे इतना भटकाती है? / बाहुएँ जो एक मेज़ पर लेटी हैं, या एक शॉल के चारों ओर लिपटी हैं। / और क्या मुझे तब अनुमान लगाना चाहिए? / और मैं कैसे शुरू करूँ?
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक महिलाओं की बाहुओं का वर्णन करता है - कंगन पहने हुए, सफेद, हल्के बालों वाली। वह सोचता है कि क्या एक पोशाक की खुशबू ने उसे भटका दिया है। फिर से, वह अनिश्चित है - क्या उसे अनुमान लगाना चाहिए, और कैसे शुरू करे?

Line 70-72
English: Shall I say, I have gone at dusk through narrow streets / And watched the smoke that rises from the pipes / Of lonely men in shirt-sleeves, leaning out of windows?…
Hindi Meaning: क्या मैं कहूँ, मैं गोधूलि में संकरी गलियों से होकर गया हूँ / और धुएँ को देखा है जो पाइप से उठता है / अकेले आदमियों के जो शर्ट की आस्तीन में, खिड़कियों से बाहर झुके हुए हैं?…
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक सोचता है कि क्या उसे अपनी यात्रा के बारे में बताना चाहिए, जहां उसने शाम के समय तंग गलियों में अकेले आदमियों को देखा जो खिड़कियों से बाहर झुके हुए पाइप से धुआँ उड़ा रहे थे।

Line 73-74
English: I should have been a pair of ragged claws / Scuttling across the floors of silent seas.
Hindi Meaning: मुझे एक जोड़ी फटे पंजे होना चाहिए था / मौन समुद्रों के फर्श पर दौड़ते हुए।
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक सोचता है कि उसे एक केकड़े जैसा होना चाहिए था, जो समुद्र के तल पर बिना किसी जिम्मेदारी या सामाजिक दबाव के स्वतंत्र रूप से दौड़ता है।

Line 75-80
English: And the afternoon, the evening, sleeps so peacefully! / Smoothed by long fingers, / Asleep … tired … or it malingers, / Stretched on the floor, here beside you and me. / Should I, after tea and cakes and ices, / Have the strength to force the moment to its crisis?
Hindi Meaning: और दोपहर, शाम, इतनी शांति से सोती है! / लंबी उँगलियों से सुचारु की गई, / सोई हुई … थकी हुई … या बीमारी का बहाना करती है, / फर्श पर फैली हुई, यहाँ तुम्हारे और मेरे पास। / क्या मुझे, चाय और केक और आइस क्रीम के बाद, / क्षण को उसके संकट तक पहुँचाने की शक्ति होनी चाहिए?
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक शाम की शांति का वर्णन करता है, जैसे कि वह एक थकी हुई महिला है जो फर्श पर लेटी हुई है। वह सोचता है कि क्या उसमें चाय और मिठाइयों के सामाजिक अनुष्ठान के बाद एक महत्वपूर्ण पल को लाने की हिम्मत होगी।

Line 81-86
English: But though I have wept and fasted, wept and prayed, / Though I have seen my head grown slightly bald brought in upon a platter, / I am no prophet—and here’s no great matter; / I have seen the moment of my greatness flicker, / And I have seen the eternal Footman hold my coat, and snicker, / And in short, I was afraid.
Hindi Meaning: लेकिन हालांकि मैंने रोया और उपवास किया, रोया और प्रार्थना की, / हालांकि मैंने अपने सिर को थोड़ा गंजा होते हुए एक थाली में लाया हुआ देखा है, / मैं कोई नबी नहीं हूँ—और यहाँ कोई बड़ी बात नहीं है; / मैंने अपनी महानता के क्षण को टिमटिमाते हुए देखा है, / और मैंने अनंत फुटमैन को मेरा कोट पकड़े हुए, और मुस्कुराते हुए देखा है, / और संक्षेप में, मैं डर गया था।
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक कहता है कि उसने रोया, उपवास और प्रार्थना की है, अपने गंजेपन को देखा है (जॉन द बैपटिस्ट के सिर के संदर्भ में), लेकिन वह कोई नबी नहीं है। उसने अपनी महानता के अवसर को गुज़रते देखा है, और मृत्यु (अनंत फुटमैन) को उसका मज़ाक उड़ाते देखा है, और वह डर गया था।

Line 87-93
English: And would it have been worth it, after all, / After the cups, the marmalade, the tea, / Among the porcelain, among some talk of you and me, / Would it have been worth while, / To have bitten off the matter with a smile, / To have squeezed the universe into a ball / To roll it toward some overwhelming question,
Hindi Meaning: और क्या यह योग्य होता, आखिरकार, / कप, मुरब्बा, चाय के बाद, / चीनी मिट्टी के बरतन के बीच, तुम्हारी और मेरी बातचीत के बीच, / क्या यह सार्थक होता, / मामले को मुस्कुरा कर खत्म कर देना, / ब्रह्मांड को एक गेंद में दबा देना / उसे किसी अभिभूत करने वाले सवाल की ओर लुढ़काना,
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक पूछता है कि क्या वह प्रयास सार्थक होगा - चाय पीने और सामान्य बातचीत के बाद, क्या यह योग्य होगा कि वह मुस्कुराकर मामले को सीधे तौर पर संबोधित करे और ब्रह्मांड को एक गेंद में दबाकर उस महत्वपूर्ण प्रश्न की ओर लुढ़का दे।

Line 94-98
English: To say: “I am Lazarus, come from the dead, / Come back to tell you all, I shall tell you all”— / If one, settling a pillow by her head, / Should say: “That is not what I meant at all. / That is not it, at all.”
Hindi Meaning: कहने के लिए: “मैं लाज़रस हूँ, मृत्यु से आया हूँ, / तुम सभी को बताने वापस आया हूँ, मैं तुम्हें सब कुछ बताऊंगा”— / यदि कोई, अपने सिर के पास तकिया व्यवस्थित करते हुए, / कहे: “वह बिलकुल वह नहीं है जो मेरा मतलब था। / यह वह नहीं है, बिल्कुल भी।”
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक कल्पना करता है कि वह लाज़रस (बाइबिल में मृत्यु से जीवित हुआ व्यक्ति) की तरह महत्वपूर्ण संदेश के साथ आया है, लेकिन वह डरता है कि उसकी प्रेमिका अपना तकिया ठीक करते हुए सिर्फ इतना कहेगी: “यह वह नहीं है जो मैं चाहती थी।”

Line 99-110
English: And would it have been worth it, after all, / Would it have been worth while, / After the sunsets and the dooryards and the sprinkled streets, / After the novels, after the teacups, after the skirts that trail along the floor— / And this, and so much more?— / It is impossible to say just what I mean! / But as if a magic lantern threw the nerves in patterns on a screen: / Would it have been worth while / If one, settling a pillow or throwing off a shawl, / And turning toward the window, should say: / “That is not it at all, / That is not what I meant, at all.”
Hindi Meaning: और क्या यह योग्य होता, आखिरकार, / क्या यह सार्थक होता, / सूर्यास्त और आँगनों और छिड़के हुए सड़कों के बाद, / उपन्यासों के बाद, चाय के कप के बाद, फर्श पर घसीटती स्कर्ट के बाद— / और यह, और इतना कुछ अधिक?— / यह कहना असंभव है कि मेरा क्या मतलब है! / लेकिन जैसे कि एक जादुई लालटेन ने नसों को पर्दे पर पैटर्न में फेंक दिया हो: / क्या यह सार्थक होता / यदि कोई, तकिया व्यवस्थित करते हुए या शॉल फेंकते हुए, / और खिड़की की ओर मुड़कर, कहे: / “यह बिलकुल वह नहीं है, / यह बिलकुल वह नहीं है जो मेरा मतलब था।”
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक फिर से सोचता है कि क्या यह सब प्रयास योग्य होगा - सूर्यास्त, उपन्यास, चाय की चर्चाओं के बाद। वह महसूस करता है कि वह अपने विचारों को ठीक से व्यक्त नहीं कर सकता। वह भयभीत है कि अगर वह कुछ कहे, तो भी उसकी प्रेमिका खिड़की की ओर मुड़कर यही कहेगी कि “यह वह नहीं है जो मैं चाहती थी।”

Line 111-119
English: No! I am not Prince Hamlet, nor was meant to be; / Am an attendant lord, one that will do / To swell a progress, start a scene or two, / Advise the prince; no doubt, an easy tool, / Deferential, glad to be of use, / Politic, cautious, and meticulous; / Full of high sentence, but a bit obtuse; / At times, indeed, almost ridiculous— / Almost, at times, the Fool.
Hindi Meaning: नहीं! मैं राजकुमार हैमलेट नहीं हूँ, न ही होने वाला था; / एक परिचारक हूँ, ऐसा जो करेगा / एक प्रगति को बढ़ाने के लिए, एक या दो दृश्य शुरू करने के लिए, / राजकुमार को सलाह देने के लिए; निःसंदेह, एक आसान उपकरण, / विनम्र, उपयोगी होने पर प्रसन्न, / चतुर, सावधान, और सूक्ष्म; / उच्च वाक्य से भरा, लेकिन थोड़ा मंदबुद्धि; / कभी-कभी, वास्तव में, लगभग हास्यास्पद— / लगभग, कभी-कभी, मूर्ख।
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक स्वीकार करता है कि वह हैमलेट जैसा नायक नहीं है, बल्कि एक छोटा परिचारक है जो केवल मदद करता है, दृश्य शुरू करता है, और राजकुमार को सलाह देता है। वह खुद को विनम्र, चतुर और सूक्ष्म मानता है, लेकिन साथ ही मंदबुद्धि और कभी-कभी हास्यास्पद भी।

Line 120-121
English: I grow old … I grow old … / I shall wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled.
Hindi Meaning: मैं बूढ़ा होता जाता हूँ … मैं बूढ़ा होता जाता हूँ … / मैं अपने पैंट के निचले हिस्से को मोड़कर पहनूंगा।
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक अपनी उम्र बढ़ने की चिंता करता है और कहता है कि वह अपने पैंट के निचले हिस्से को मोड़कर पहनेगा, जो उस समय बुजुर्गों की फैशन थी।

Line 122-124
English: Shall I part my hair behind? Do I dare to eat a peach? / I shall wear white flannel trousers, and walk upon the beach. / I have heard the mermaids singing, each to each.
Hindi Meaning: क्या मैं अपने बाल पीछे से बिछाऊँ? क्या मैं एक आड़ू खाने की हिम्मत करता हूँ? / मैं सफेद फलालैन के पैंट पहनूंगा, और समुद्र तट पर चलूंगा। / मैंने जलपरियों को गाते सुना है, एक-दूसरे से।
Simple Explanation: प्रुफ्रॉक अपने बूढ़ापे के बारे में चिंतित है - क्या वह अपने बाल पीछे से बिछाए, एक आड़ू खाने की हिम्मत करे (जो बूढ़े दांतों वालों के लिए मुश्किल हो सकता है)? वह सफेद पैंट पहनकर समुद्र तट पर चलने की योजना बनाता है और कहता है कि उसने जलपरियों को गाते सुना है।

# Chapter 15: Pablo Neruda - Keeping Quiet
Author Facts
Pablo Neruda (Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto)
Birth: July 12, 1904, Parral, Chile
Death: September 23, 1973, Santiago, Chile
Real Name: Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto
Pen Name Origin: Adopted from Czech poet Jan Neruda
Nationality: Chilean
Nobel Prize in Literature: 1971
Occupation: Poet, diplomat, politician
Political Affiliation: Communist Party of Chile
Major Works: "Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair" (1924), "Canto General" (1950), "Residence on Earth" (1933)
Diplomatic Posts: Served as consul in various countries including Burma, Ceylon, Mexico
Awards: Lenin Peace Prize (1953), Nobel Prize (1971)
Notable Position: Senator of the Chilean Republic (1945-1948)
Text of the Poem

It would be an exotic moment
without rush, without engines;
we would all be together
in a sudden strangeness.

Fishermen in the cold sea
would not harm whales
and the man gathering salt
would not look at his hurt hands.

Those who prepare green wars,
wars with gas, wars with fire,
victories with no survivors,
would put on clean clothes
and walk about with their brothers
in the shade, doing nothing.

What I want should not be confused
with total inactivity.
Life is what it is about...

If we were not so single-minded
about keeping our lives moving,
and for once could do nothing,
perhaps a huge silence
might interrupt this sadness
of never understanding ourselves
and of threatening ourselves with
death.

Now I'll count up to twelve
and you keep quiet and I will go.

Alliteration: "single-minded," "sadness of never"
Personification: Earth as a living entity
Paradox: Life through stillness, activity through inactivity
Anaphora: Repeated "let's" and "we will"

| Twelve | Completeness (12 hours, 12 months); also a manageable pause |
| Keeping still/quiet | Introspection, cessation of violence |
| Green wars | Environmental destruction, chemical warfare |
| Wars with gas | Chemical/biological warfare |
| Wars with fire | Traditional warfare, nuclear weapons |
| Fishermen | Those who harm sea life |
| Salt gatherers | Those who exploit natural resources |
| Winter | Death, stillness, dormancy |
| Spring | Renewal, rebirth, hope |
| Earth | Shared home, life-giver |
Stanza-wise Summary
Stanza 1-2: Poet calls for counting to twelve and keeping still; stopping all activity and language
Stanza 3: Describes the strange and exotic feeling of togetherness when all are still
Stanza 4-5: Fishermen would not harm whales; salt gatherers would not hurt their hands
Stanza 6-7: Those preparing wars (green wars, gas wars, fire wars) should put on clean clothes and walk with brothers in the shade
Stanza 8: If we weren't rushing through life, we could understand ourselves better
Stanza 9: A huge silence might interrupt sadness and help those who never understood themselves
Stanza 10: Poet clarifies he doesn't want death but life; stillness is not death
Stanza 11-12: Earth can teach us about life through death (winter to spring); poet counts to twelve and asks everyone to keep quiet as he goes

समग्र अर्थ (Overall Meaning in Hindi)

“Keeping Quiet” पाब्लो नेरूदा की एक प्रसिद्ध कविता है जो मानव जाति के लिए एक सामूहिक मौन का आह्वान करती है। यह कविता शांति, आत्म-चिंतन और प्रकृति के साथ सद्भाव के महत्व पर जोर देती है। नेरूदा हमें आधुनिक जीवन की भागदौड़ और विनाशकारी गतिविधियों से विराम लेने के लिए कहते हैं।

कविता का प्रमुख संदेश है कि हमें अपनी दैनिक गतिविधियों से थोड़ा समय निकालकर शांत होना चाहिए, प्रकृति की रक्षा करनी चाहिए, और युद्ध और हिंसा को रोकना चाहिए। यह पूर्ण निष्क्रियता का आह्वान नहीं है, बल्कि एक जागरूक विराम का आह्वान है जो हमें अपने आप को बेहतर ढंग से समझने और अधिक शांतिपूर्ण दुनिया बनाने में मदद करेगा।
“बारह तक गिनना” समय के एक छोटे से टुकड़े का प्रतीक है - केवल कुछ क्षणों का विराम जो एक बड़ा बदलाव ला सकता है। कविता युद्ध, पर्यावरणीय विनाश और मानवीय पीड़ा के विरुद्ध एक शक्तिशाली आवाज़ है।

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Nissim Ezekiel - Night of the Scorpion

content.value: # Chapter 16: Nissim Ezekiel - Night of the Scorpion
Author Facts
Nissim Ezekiel
Birth: December 16, 1924, Mumbai (then Bombay), India
Death: January 9, 2004, Mumbai, India
Religion: Bene Israel Jewish community
Nationality: Indian
Education: Wilson College, Mumbai; Birkbeck College, University of London
Occupation: Poet, playwright, art critic, editor
Father: Professor Moses Ezekiel (Botany professor)
Mother: English teacher
Awards: Sahitya Akademi Award (1983), Padma Shri (1988)
Known As: Father of Post-Independence Indian English Poetry
Academic Position: Professor of English at University of Mumbai
Editorial Work: Editor of Poetry India and Quest magazine
Major Works by Nissim Ezekiel
A Time to Change (1952) - First poetry collection
Sixty Poems (1953)
The Third (1959)
The Unfinished Man (1960)
The Exact Name (1965)
Hymns in Darkness (1976)
Latter-Day Psalms (1982)
Collected Poems 1952-1988 (1989)
Text of the Poem

I remember the night my mother
was stung by a scorpion. Ten hours
of steady rain had driven him
to crawl beneath a sack of rice.

Parting with his poison - flash
of diabolic tail in the dark room -
he risked the rain again.

The peasants came like swarms of flies
and buzzed the name of God a hundred times
to paralyse the Evil One.

With candles and with lanterns
throwing giant scorpion shadows
on the mud-baked walls
they searched for him: he was not found.
They clicked their tongues.
With every movement that the scorpion made his poison moved in Mother's blood, they said.

May he sit still, they said
May the sins of your previous birth
be burned away tonight, they said.
May your suffering decrease
the misfortunes of your next birth, they said.
May the sum of all evil
balanced in this unreal world

against the sum of good
become diminished by your pain.
May the poison purify your flesh

of desire, and your spirit of ambition,
they said, and they sat around
on the floor with my mother in the centre,
the peace of understanding on each face.
More candles, more lanterns, more neighbours,
more insects, and the endless rain.
My mother twisted through and through,
groaning on a mat.
My father, sceptic, rationalist,
trying every curse and blessing,
powder, mixture, herb and hybrid.
He even poured a little paraffin
upon the bitten toe and put a match to it.
I watched the flame feeding on my mother.
I watched the holy man perform his rites to tame the poison with an incantation.
After twenty hours
it lost its sting.

My mother only said
Thank God the scorpion picked on me
And spared my children.
Poem Publication Facts
Publication Year: 1965
Collection: "The Exact Name" (1965)
Form: Free Verse Narrative
Type: Narrative Poem
Total Lines: 48 lines
Stanzas: One continuous stanza (no breaks)
Rhyme Scheme: No fixed rhyme scheme
Meter: No regular meter
Narrative Voice: First-person narrator (the poet as a child)
Setting: Rural Indian village during monsoon
Poem Structure Details
Form: Narrative poem in free verse
Point of View: First-person retrospective (adult remembering childhood)
Tense: Past tense
Structure: Single unbroken stanza creating continuous narrative flow
Line Length: Varying line lengths
Style: Realistic, descriptive, observational
Tone: Detached yet empathetic observer
Language: Simple, conversational English with Indian context
Plot Summary

The poem narrates an incident from the poet's childhood when his mother was stung by a scorpion on a rainy night. The scorpion had crawled beneath a sack of rice for shelter from ten hours of rain. After stinging the mother, it escaped into the darkness. Peasants from the village came with lanterns and searched for the scorpion but could not find it. They sat around the suffering mother, chanting prayers and offering superstitious explanations about karma, sins, and the afterlife. They believed the scorpion's movement would increase the poison in the mother's blood. The poet's father, usually rational and skeptical, tried every possible remedy including holy water and incantations. For twenty hours, the mother twisted in pain on the floor. When the poison finally subsided, her first words were thanking God that the scorpion had stung her and not her children.
Main Characters

| Character | Description |
| --- | --- |
| The Mother | Central figure who suffers the scorpion sting; selfless and maternal |
| The Scorpion | Catalyst of the incident; seeks shelter from rain |
| The Peasants/Villagers | Superstitious neighbors who come to help; represent traditional beliefs |
| The Father | Rationalist who becomes desperate, trying every remedy |
| The Narrator (Poet) | Observer recounting childhood memory; detached perspective |
| Holy Man | Mentioned as performing incantations and rites |
Themes
Motherly Love and Sacrifice: Mother's selfless concern for children despite her pain
Superstition vs. Rationalism: Conflict between traditional beliefs and rational thinking
Rural Indian Life: Depiction of village customs and community response
Suffering and Pain: Physical and mental anguish
Helplessness: Inability to relieve suffering despite efforts
Community Bonding: Village unity in crisis
Faith and Belief: Religious and superstitious responses to tragedy
Irony: Rationalist father resorting to superstitious practices
Karma and Fate: Peasants' explanations about past-life consequences
Nature's Indifference: Scorpion acts instinctively without malice
Literary Devices Used
Imagery: "Rain... ten hours of steady rain," "swarms of flies," "buzzed the Name of God"
Metaphor: Peasants compared to "swarms of flies"
Simile: "Like swarms of flies"
Alliteration: "Steady rain," "May the poison purify"
Repetition: "May" repeated in peasants' prayers
Personification: "Diabolic tail" of scorpion
Irony: Rationalist father using superstitious cures
Juxtaposition: Father's skepticism vs. desperate actions
Enjambment: Lines flow continuously without breaks
Realism: Authentic depiction of Indian village scene
Important Lines and Quotations

"Ten hours of steady rain had driven him to crawl beneath a sack of rice."
"Parting with his poison - flash of diabolic tail in the dark room"
"The peasants came like swarms of flies and buzzed the name of God"

"May the poison purify your flesh of desire, and your spirit of ambition"

"My mother only said Thank God the scorpion picked on me and spared my children"
Detailed Line-by-Line Analysis
Lines 1-4: Introduction - narrator remembers the night, describes ten hours of rain that drove scorpion to shelter
Lines 5-8: The scorpion stings the mother and escapes into darkness; described as "parting with his poison"
Lines 9-15: Peasants arrive "like swarms of flies" with lanterns and candles, searching for the scorpion
Lines 16-32: Peasants sit around chanting prayers beginning with "May," offering various superstitious interpretations about karma, sins, suffering, and afterlife
Lines 33-35: Peasants believe scorpion's movement spreads poison in mother's blood
Lines 36-39: Description of father's desperate attempts using both rational and superstitious methods
Lines 40-42: Holy man performs incantations and religious rites
Lines 43-46: Mother's prolonged suffering for twenty hours, described graphically
Lines 47-48: Mother's first words after recovery - thanking God the scorpion stung her instead of her children
In Hindi
(Stanza 1)

Line 1-2
English: I remember the night my mother was stung by a scorpion. / Ten hours of steady rain had driven him to crawl beneath a sack of rice.
Hindi Meaning: मुझे वह रात याद है जब मेरी माँ को बिच्छू ने डंक मारा था। / दस घंटे की लगातार बारिश ने उसे चावल की बोरी के नीचे रेंगने पर मजबूर किया था।
Simple Explanation: कवि उस रात को याद कर रहा है जब उसकी माँ को बिच्छू ने डंक मारा था। लगातार बारिश के कारण बिच्छू घर में आ गया था और चावल की बोरी के नीचे छिप गया था।

Line 3-4
English: Parting with his poison - flash of diabolic tail in the dark room - / he risked the rain again.
Hindi Meaning: अपना ज़हर छोड़कर - अंधेरे कमरे में शैतानी पूँछ की चमक - / वह फिर से बारिश का जोखिम उठाकर चला गया।
Simple Explanation: बिच्छू ने माँ को डंक मारा, अंधेरे कमरे में उसकी पूँछ एक क्षण के लिए चमकी, और फिर वह बारिश में वापस चला गया।

Line 5-7
English: The peasants came like swarms of flies / and buzzed the name of God a hundred times / to paralyse the Evil One.
Hindi Meaning: ग्रामीण मक्खियों के झुंड की तरह आए / और भगवान का नाम सौ बार गुनगुनाया / बुरी आत्मा को पंगु बनाने के लिए।
Simple Explanation: गाँव के लोग बड़ी संख्या में इकट्ठा हुए और ईश्वर का नाम जपने लगे ताकि बिच्छू (बुरी आत्मा के प्रतीक) का प्रभाव कम हो जाए।

Line 8-10
English: With candles and with lanterns / throwing giant scorpion shadows on the mud-baked walls / they searched for him: he was not found.
Hindi Meaning: मोमबत्तियों और लालटेनों के साथ / मिट्टी की दीवारों पर विशाल बिच्छू की छायाएँ फैलाते हुए / उन्होंने उसे खोजा: वह नहीं मिला।
Simple Explanation: लोगों ने मोमबत्तियों और लालटेनों की रोशनी में बिच्छू को ढूँढ़ने की कोशिश की। दीवारों पर मोमबत्तियों की रोशनी से बिच्छू की भयानक छायाएँ पड़ रही थीं, लेकिन बिच्छू नहीं मिला।

Line 11-13
English: They clicked their tongues. / With every movement that the scorpion made his poison moved in Mother’s blood, / they said.
Hindi Meaning: उन्होंने जीभ से चटकारे लिए। / ‘बिच्छू के हर हिलने-डुलने से उसका ज़हर माँ के खून में फैलता है,’ / उन्होंने कहा।
Simple Explanation: ग्रामीण चिंता जताते हुए कहने लगे कि जितना बिच्छू हिलेगा-डुलेगा, उतना ही ज़हर माँ के शरीर में फैलेगा।

Line 14-16
English: May he sit still, they said / May the sins of your previous birth be burned away tonight, / they said.
Hindi Meaning: ‘काश वह स्थिर बैठा रहे,’ उन्होंने कहा। / ‘काश आपके पिछले जन्म के पाप आज रात जल जाएँ,’ / उन्होंने कहा।
Simple Explanation: ग्रामीणों ने प्रार्थना की कि बिच्छू स्थिर रहे ताकि ज़हर न फैले। वे यह भी कह रहे थे कि यह पीड़ा माँ के पिछले जन्म के पापों को धो देगी।

Line 17-19
English: May your suffering decrease the misfortunes of your next birth, / they said. May the sum of all evil balanced in this unreal world / against the sum of good become diminished by your pain.
Hindi Meaning: ‘काश आपका दर्द आपके अगले जन्म के दुर्भाग्य को कम कर दे,’ / उन्होंने कहा। ‘काश इस अवास्तविक दुनिया में सभी बुराइयों का योग / अच्छाई के योग के विरुद्ध आपके दर्द से कम हो जाए।’
Simple Explanation: ग्रामीण धार्मिक विश्वासों के अनुसार कह रहे थे कि माँ का वर्तमान दर्द उनके अगले जन्म के दुःख को कम करेगा और दुनिया की बुराई को कम करने में योगदान देगा।

Line 20-22
English: May the poison purify your flesh of desire, / and your spirit of ambition, / they said, and they sat around on the floor with my mother in the centre,
Hindi Meaning: ‘काश यह ज़हर आपके शरीर को इच्छाओं से / और आपकी आत्मा को महत्वाकांक्षा से शुद्ध कर दे,’ / उन्होंने कहा, और वे फर्श पर मेरी माँ को बीच में रखकर बैठ गए,
Simple Explanation: ग्रामीण मानते थे कि यह दर्द माँ के शरीर और आत्मा को विकारों से मुक्त कर देगा। वे सभी माँ के चारों ओर फर्श पर बैठ गए।

Line 23-24
English: the peace of understanding on each face. / More candles, more lanterns, more neighbours, more insects, and the endless rain.
Hindi Meaning: हर चेहरे पर समझ की शांति थी। / अधिक मोमबत्तियाँ, अधिक लालटेन, अधिक पड़ोसी, अधिक कीड़े, और अनंत बारिश।
Simple Explanation: सभी ग्रामीणों के चेहरों पर एक विशेष प्रकार की शांति थी, जैसे वे इस स्थिति को समझते हों। समय के साथ और अधिक लोग, मोमबत्तियाँ, कीड़े जमा हो गए, और बारिश लगातार जारी थी।
दूसरा छंद (Stanza 2)

Line 25-26
English: My mother twisted through and through, / groaning on a mat.
Hindi Meaning: मेरी माँ बार-बार मरोड़ खाती रहीं, / चटाई पर कराहती हुई।
Simple Explanation: माँ दर्द से तड़प रही थी, बिच्छू के ज़हर के कारण उनका शरीर ऐंठ रहा था और वे चटाई पर लेटकर दर्द से कराह रही थीं।

Line 27-29
English: My father, sceptic, rationalist, / trying every curse and blessing, / powder, mixture, herb and hybrid.
Hindi Meaning: मेरे पिता, संदेहवादी, तर्कवादी, / हर शाप और आशीर्वाद, / पाउडर, मिश्रण, जड़ी-बूटी और संकर का प्रयोग कर रहे थे।
Simple Explanation: कवि के पिता संदेहवादी और तर्कवादी थे, फिर भी वे हर संभव उपचार कर रहे थे - धार्मिक मंत्रों से लेकर औषधियों तक।

Line 30-31
English: He even poured a little paraffin upon the bitten toe / and put a match to it.
Hindi Meaning: उन्होंने डंक मारे हुए पैर के अंगूठे पर थोड़ा केरोसिन भी डाला / और उसे माचिस से जला दिया।
Simple Explanation: पिता ने माँ के डंक वाले अंगूठे पर केरोसिन डालकर उसे जला दिया, संभवतः यह मानते हुए कि गर्मी ज़हर को नष्ट कर देगी।

Line 32-33
English: I watched the flame feeding on my mother. / I watched the holy man perform his rites to tame the poison with an incantation.
Hindi Meaning: मैंने देखा कि आग मेरी माँ को जला रही है। / मैंने देखा कि पंडित अपने मंत्रों से ज़हर को काबू में करने के लिए अनुष्ठान कर रहा है।
Simple Explanation: कवि देख रहा था कि उसकी माँ केरोसिन की आग से जल रही है। साथ ही एक धार्मिक व्यक्ति मंत्रों से ज़हर को नियंत्रित करने का प्रयास कर रहा था।

Line 34
English: After twenty hours it lost its sting.
Hindi Meaning: बीस घंटों के बाद ज़हर ने अपना प्रभाव खो दिया।
Simple Explanation: बीस घंटों के बाद आखिरकार बिच्छू के ज़हर का असर कम हो गया और माँ की हालत बेहतर होने लगी।

Line 35-37
English: My mother only said / Thank God the scorpion picked on me / And spared my children.
Hindi Meaning: मेरी माँ ने केवल इतना कहा, / ‘भगवान का शुक्र है कि बिच्छू ने मुझे चुना / और मेरे बच्चों को बख्श दिया।’
Simple Explanation: इतनी पीड़ा झेलने के बाद भी माँ ने केवल यही कहा कि वह खुश है कि बिच्छू ने उनके बच्चों को नहीं, बल्कि उन्हें डंक मारा।
समग्र अर्थ (Overall Meaning in Hindi)

“Night of the Scorpion” निसिम एज़ेकिएल की एक प्रसिद्ध कविता है जो एक माँ की बिच्छू के डंक से उपजी पीड़ा और उसके प्रति ग्रामीणों और परिवार की प्रतिक्रिया का वर्णन करती है। कविता बारिश की रात में शुरू होती है जब एक बिच्छू घर में प्रवेश करके कवि की माँ को डंक मार देता है।

कविता भारतीय ग्रामीण जीवन, पारंपरिक विश्वास, और आधुनिक तर्कवादी दृष्टिकोण के बीच के अंतर को दर्शाती है। ग्रामीण लोग अंधविश्वासों और धार्मिक उपचारों का सहारा लेते हैं, जबकि कवि के पिता, जो एक तर्कवादी हैं, दवाइयों और अन्य उपचारों का प्रयोग करते हैं।

कविता का सबसे महत्वपूर्ण संदेश माँ के अंतिम शब्दों में निहित है। इतना दर्द सहने के बावजूद, वह केवल इस बात पर आभारी हैं कि बिच्छू ने उनके बच्चों को नहीं, बल्कि उन्हें चुना। यह मातृ-प्रेम की अद्भुत मिसाल है, जहाँ माँ अपने बच्चों के लिए किसी भी दर्द को सहने को तैयार है।
कविता में ग्रामीण संस्कृति, परिवार के संबंध, धार्मिक और अंधविश्वास, आधुनिक और पारंपरिक दृष्टिकोण के बीच का संघर्ष, और सबसे ऊपर मातृत्व की अनंत शक्ति का चित्रण है।

Peasants' Prayers and Beliefs
The peasants' "May" prayers reveal their worldview:
"May the sins of your previous birth be burned away tonight" - Belief in karma and reincarnation
"May your suffering decrease the misfortunes of your next birth" - Suffering as penance
"May the poison purify your flesh of desire" - Physical purification through pain
"May the poison purify your spirit of ambition" - Spiritual cleansing
"May the sum of all evil balanced in this unreal world against the sum of good become diminished by your pain" - Cosmic balance theory
Symbolism

| Symbol | Meaning |

| Scorpion | Nature's indifference; instinctive survival; catalyst for human drama |
| Rain | Monsoon season; cause of scorpion's intrusion; natural cycle |
| Darkness | Uncertainty, fear, unknown |
| Flame/Fire | Dual meaning - holy man's ritual and mother's suffering |
| Sack of Rice | Basic sustenance; rural poverty; shelter |
| Lanterns/Candles | Human attempt to illuminate darkness; search for solutions |
| Peasants as "swarms of flies" | Overwhelming crowd; persistence; perhaps irritation |
| Twenty Hours | Extended suffering; time's passage during crisis |
| Poison | Physical pain and metaphorical purification |
Indian Cultural Elements
Monsoon Season: Ten hours of steady rain typical of Indian monsoons
Village Community: Collective response to individual crisis
Karma and Reincarnation: Hindu/Buddhist concepts of past and future lives
Superstitious Beliefs: Traditional explanations for suffering
Joint Family System: Extended community involvement
Holy Man: Spiritual practitioner performing rites
Rural Setting: Sack of rice, peasants, mud floor mentioned
Religious Pluralism: Mix of Hindu rituals despite poet's Jewish background
Contrast Between Father and Peasants

| Peasants | Father |
| --- | --- |
| Superstitious | Rationalist, skeptic |
| Traditional beliefs | Scientific outlook |
| Passive prayers | Active searching for cure |
| Accept fate | Fights against suffering |
| Spiritual explanations | Practical solutions |
| BUT Father also tries "every curse and blessing" - irony |  |
Poetic Techniques
Single Stanza: Creates continuous narrative flow, mimics the unbroken night of suffering
Free Verse: Natural speech pattern, realistic narration
Enjambment: Lines flow into each other without pause
Concrete Details: Specific imagery (ten hours, twenty hours, sack of rice)
Detached Tone: Narrator observes without heavy emotional commentary
Realistic Dialogue: "Thank God the scorpion picked on me"
Temporal Markers: "Ten hours," "twenty hours" emphasize duration
Central Ironies
Father's Contradiction: Skeptic and rationalist tries superstitious cures
Mother's Response: After intense suffering, thinks of children's safety first
Peasants' Arrival: Come to help but only offer prayers, not practical aid
Search for Scorpion: Intense search but creature never found
Purification Through Poison: Belief that suffering cleanses sins
Unreal World: Peasants call world "unreal" while mother suffers very real pain
Critical Interpretations
Feminist Reading: Mother as archetypal selfless woman sacrificing for children
Post-Colonial Reading: Clash between Western rationalism (father) and Indian tradition (peasants)
Religious Reading: Different responses to suffering - faith vs. reason
Social Reading: Community bonding and support system in rural India
Humanist Reading: Universal mother-child bond transcending culture
Tone and Mood
Tone: Detached, observational, slightly ironic but not mocking
Mood: Tense, concerned, gradually moving toward relief
Narrator's Stance: Non-judgmental observer; neither condemns peasants nor father
Emotional Restraint: Horror of situation conveyed through facts, not emotional outbursts
Final Note: Touch of admiration for mother's selflessness
Language Characteristics
Simple, conversational English
No complex metaphors or obscure references
Indian English syntax at times
Concrete, specific details over abstract ideas
Colloquial expressions: "clicked their tongues"
Mixture of elevated (diabolic) and everyday language
Historical and Literary Context
Post-Independence Indian English poetry
Movement toward indigenous themes in English
Realistic depiction replacing romantic/exotic India
Part of modern Indian poetry establishment
Influenced by British modernism but distinctly Indian in content
Contemporary of A.K. Ramanujan, Kamala Das, R. Parthasarathy
Why This Poem Is Famous
Authentic depiction of Indian rural life
Universal theme of motherly love
Balanced presentation of superstition and rationalism
Accessible language and clear narrative
Memorable ending line
Represents modern Indian sensibility
Frequently anthologized in Indian curricula
Combines local and universal elements

Text of the Poem

Driving from my parent's
home to Cochin last Friday
morning, I saw my mother,
beside me,
doze, open mouthed, her face
ashen like that
of a corpse and realized with pain
that she was as old as she
looked but soon
put that thought away, and
looked out at Young
Trees sprinting, the merry children spilling
out of their homes, but after the airport's
security check, standing a few yards
away, I looked again at her, wan, pale
as a late winter's moon and felt that old
familiar ache, my childhood's fear,
of losing her, but all I said was, see you soon,
Amma, all I did was smile and smile and
smile......

Complete Poem Text Summary

The poet is driving from her parent's home to Cochin airport. She looks at her mother sitting beside her, who has dozed off with her mouth open. The mother's face looks ashen like a corpse, pale as winter's late moon. The poet feels the familiar childhood fear of losing her mother. To distract herself, she looks outside at young trees sprinting and merry children spilling out of their homes. At the airport, after security check, the poet looks at her mother again - she appears wan and pale as winter's late moon. The poet smiles and smiles continuously, saying "see you soon, Amma," while feeling the old familiar childhood ache and fear of separation and loss.

समग्र अर्थ (Overall Meaning in Hindi)

“My Mother at Sixty-six” कमला दास की एक प्रसिद्ध कविता है जो माँ के प्रति पुत्री के प्रेम और उसके बुढ़ापे और मृत्यु के डर से जूझने का मार्मिक चित्रण करती है। कविता में एक युवा महिला अपनी बूढ़ी माँ के साथ कार में यात्रा करते हुए अचानक उसके मृत्यु-सदृश चेहरे को देखकर चौंक जाती है।

कविता का सबसे महत्वपूर्ण पहलू है - वह विरोधाभास जो कवयित्री के अंदर चल रहा है। एक ओर वह अपनी माँ के प्रति गहरा प्रेम और चिंता रखती है, दूसरी ओर वह अपने डर और दर्द को व्यक्त नहीं करती। हवाई अड्डे पर विदाई के समय, अपनी माँ से “जल्द मिलेंगे” कहने और मुस्कुराते रहने के अलावा वह कुछ नहीं कर पाती, जबकि उसके अंदर माँ को हमेशा के लिए खोने का डर सालता रहता है।

कविता में जीवन और मृत्यु, युवावस्था और बुढ़ापे के बीच का विरोधाभास भी दिखाया गया है। कार से दिखाई देने वाले दौड़ते पेड़ और खुश बच्चे जीवन और युवावस्था का प्रतीक हैं, जबकि माँ का “लाश जैसा” चेहरा और “सर्दी के अंत के चाँद” जैसी उपमाएँ मृत्यु और बुढ़ापे की ओर इशारा करती हैं।

कविता की भाषा सरल है, लेकिन भावनाएँ गहरी और जटिल हैं। अंतिम पंक्तियों में दोहराए गए “मुस्कुराती रही” शब्द कवयित्री के अव्यक्त दर्द और दमित भावनाओं की ओर इशारा करते हैं। कविता का खुला अंत पाठकों को सोचने पर मजबूर करता है कि क्या कवयित्री अपनी माँ से फिर कभी मिल पाएगी या नहीं।

# Chapter 18: Arun Kolatkar - The Bus
Author Facts
Arun Balkrishna Kolatkar
Birth: November 1, 1932, Kolhapur, Maharashtra, India
Death: September 25, 2004, Mumbai, India
Full Name: Arun Balkrishna Kolatkar
Nationality: Indian
Languages: Wrote in both English and Marathi
Education: J.J. School of Art, Mumbai (studied painting)
Occupation: Poet, graphic designer, advertising professional
Artistic Background: Originally trained as a painter and sculptor
Work: Worked in advertising agencies in Mumbai as a graphic designer
Literary Recognition: One of the most significant bilingual Indian poets
Awards and Recognition
Commonwealth Poetry Prize (1977) - for "Jejuri"
Considered for Neustadt International Prize for Literature
Posthumous recognition and critical acclaim
Influenced generation of Indian poets in both English and Marathi
Major Works by Arun Kolatkar
English Poetry:
Jejuri (1976) - Most famous work, pilgrimage poems
Kala Ghoda Poems (2004) - Published posthumously
Sarpa Satra (2004) - Long poem, published posthumously
Marathi Poetry:
Arun Kolatkarchi Kavita - Collection of Marathi poems
Bhijki Vahi - Marathi poetry collection
Numerous Marathi poems considered groundbreaking
Poem Publication Facts
Publication Year: 1976
Collection: "Jejuri" (1976)
Form: Free Verse
Type: Narrative/Descriptive poem
Total Lines: 23 lines
Stanzas: 5 stanzas of varying lengths (4, 3, 6, 6, 4 lines)
Rhyme Scheme: No fixed rhyme scheme
Meter: No regular meter
Setting: Bus journey to Jejuri, a pilgrimage town in Maharashtra
Style: Modernist, minimalist, ironic
Language: Simple, concrete English
About Jejuri
Jejuri is a pilgrimage town in Pune district, Maharashtra
Famous for Khandoba temple (Hindu deity)
Located approximately 48 km southeast of Pune
Known for yellow-painted walls and religious significance
Pilgrims visit for religious merit and blessings
The collection "Jejuri" contains 31 poems about pilgrimage experience
Text of the Poem

the tarpaulin flaps are buttoned down
on the windows of the state transport bus.
all the way up to jejuri.

a cold wind keeps whipping
and slapping a corner of tarpaulin at your elbow.

you look down to the roaring road.
you search for the signs of daybreak in what little light spills out of bus.

your own divided face in the pair of glasses
on an oldman\`s nose
is all the countryside you get to see.

you seem to move continually forward.
toward a destination
just beyond the castemark beyond his eyebrows.

outside, the sun has risen quitely
it aims through an eyelet in the tarpaulin.
and shoots at the oldman\`s glasses.

a sawed off sunbeam comes to rest gently against the driver\`s right temple.
the bus seems to change direction.

at the end of bumpy ride with your own face on the either side
when you get off the bus.

you dont step inside the old man\`s head.
Line-by-Line Paraphrase
Lines 1-3: Setting the Scene

"the tarpaulin flaps are buttoned down / on the windows of the state transport bus. / all the way up to jejuri."
The windows of the government bus have canvas or plastic covers fastened shut instead of glass. This journey continues for the entire distance to Jejuri (a pilgrimage town in Maharashtra).
Lines 4-5: The Uncomfortable Ride

"a cold wind keeps whipping / and slapping a corner of tarpaulin at your elbow."
The harsh wind repeatedly hits and beats against the loose edge of the canvas covering near where the passenger sits, creating physical discomfort.
Lines 6-8: Limited View

"you look down to the roaring road. / you search for the signs of daybreak in what little light spills out of bus."
The passenger looks down at the noisy highway below and tries to find hints of morning light coming through the small gaps in the bus's makeshift covering.
Lines 9-11: Reflection as Landscape

"your own divided face in the pair of glasses / on an oldman's nose / is all the countryside you get to see."
The only view of the outside world comes through seeing the passenger's own reflection split or doubled in an elderly fellow passenger's spectacles. This reflection becomes the substitute for seeing the actual landscape.
Lines 12-14: Movement Toward Mystery

"you seem to move continually forward. / toward a destination / just beyond the castemark beyond his eyebrows."
The passenger feels the sense of moving ahead toward a goal that lies somewhere beyond the old man's religious caste mark on his forehead. The destination seems both physical and spiritual.
Lines 15-17: Sunrise Intervention

"outside, the sun has risen quitely / it aims through an eyelet in the tarpaulin. / and shoots at the oldman's glasses."
Dawn has broken peacefully outside, and now sunlight targets the old man's glasses like a weapon firing through a small hole in the canvas covering.
Lines 18-19: Dramatic Change

"a sawed off sunbeam comes to rest gently against the driver's right temple. / the bus seems to change direction."
A fragment of sunlight settles softly against the bus driver's head, and after this moment, the bus appears to alter its course. The "sawed off sunbeam" suggests something truncated or incomplete.
Lines 20-22: Journey's End

"at the end of bumpy ride with your own face on the either side / when you get off the bus."
After the uncomfortable journey, during which the passenger could only see reflections of themselves, the trip finally concludes and the passenger disembarks.
Line 23: Final Choice

"you dont step inside the old man's head."
The passenger chooses not to enter into the old man's way of thinking or worldview. This suggests a rejection of traditional religious or cultural perspectives represented by the elderly fellow traveler.

The poem explores themes of modern skepticism versus traditional faith, the discomfort of physical and spiritual journeys, and the choice between following established paths or forging one's own way. The bus serves as both a literal vehicle and a metaphor for the journey between old and new India, with the passenger ultimately choosing independence over conformity to traditional religious practices.

समग्र अर्थ (Overall Meaning in Hindi)

अरुण कोलटकर की “The Bus” कविता उनके प्रसिद्ध काव्य संग्रह “जेजुरी” का हिस्सा है, जिसमें महाराष्ट्र के जेजुरी तीर्थस्थल की यात्रा का वर्णन है। यह कविता एक सामान्य बस यात्रा का वर्णन करते हुए गहरे दार्शनिक विचारों को प्रस्तुत करती है।

कविता में यात्री एक राज्य परिवहन की बस में सफर कर रहा है जिसकी खिड़कियों पर तिरपाल के पर्दे लगे हुए हैं। बस के अंदर अंधेरा है, और यात्री बाहर की दुनिया को नहीं देख पाता। उसका संपर्क बाहरी दुनिया से एक बूढ़े आदमी के चश्मे में पड़ने वाले अपने प्रतिबिंब तक सीमित है।

कविता यात्रा के भौतिक अनुभव से परे, अध्यात्मिक और दार्शनिक यात्रा का प्रतीक है। जाति चिह्न और भौंहों के परे के गंतव्य का उल्लेख हिंदू धर्म के जाति व्यवस्था से परे की यात्रा और आध्यात्मिक ज्ञान की प्राप्ति का संकेत हो सकता है।

कविता के अंत में, यात्री बस से उतरता है लेकिन बूढ़े आदमी के दिमाग में प्रवेश नहीं करता। यह दर्शाता है कि हमारी यात्राएँ और अनुभव व्यक्तिगत होते हैं। हम एक ही बस में यात्रा कर सकते हैं, एक ही स्थान पर जा सकते हैं, लेकिन हमारे अनुभव और समझ अलग-अलग होती हैं। प्रत्येक व्यक्ति का अपना दृष्टिकोण और अनुभव होता है जिसे कोई अन्य व्यक्ति पूरी तरह से नहीं समझ सकता।
कोलटकर की यह कविता आधुनिक भारतीय अंग्रेजी कविता का एक महत्वपूर्ण उदाहरण है, जो सामान्य अनुभवों को गहरे दार्शनिक अर्थों से जोड़ती है।

Form: 5 stanzas, uneven lengths

Tone: Detached, ironic, matter-of-fact

Style: Anti-romantic, realistic, modernist
Technique: Concrete imagery, minimal commentary
Main Themes
Anti-Romantic Pilgrimage: Pilgrimage stripped of spiritual glamour
Physical Discomfort: Emphasis on bodily reality over spiritual experience
Ordinariness: Mundane, unglamorous journey
Detachment: Observer's emotional distance
Reality vs. Idealism: Realistic portrayal vs. romanticized expectations
Class and Caste: State transport bus, caste marks, common people
Minimalism: Less is more, concrete details over abstract philosophy
Modern Alienation: Inability to connect deeply with religious experience
The Commonplace: Focus on everyday, overlooked details
Acceptance: Taking things as they are without interpretation

Metaphor: "a town enters the bus" (people as collective town)
Imagery: Tarpaulin flaps, beads of moisture, caste mark, creases

Minimalism: Stripped-down language and description
Concrete Details: Specific, physical observations
Second Person "You": Creates distance, universalizes experience
Enjambment: Lines flow naturally across breaks
Understatement: Deliberate lack of emotion or interpretation

Text of the Poem

I made an assignation with the Night;
    In the abyss was fixed our rendezvous:
In my breast carrying God's deathless light
    I came her dark and dangerous heart to woo.

I left the glory of the illumined Mind
    And the calm rapture of the divinised soul
And travelled through a vastness dim and blind
 To the grey shore where her ignorant waters roll.

I walk by the chill wave through the dull slime
   And still that weary journeying knows no end;
Lost is the lustrous godhead beyond Time,
    There comes no voice of the celestial Friend.

And yet I know my footprints' track shall be
A pathway towards Immortality.

Explanation in Hindi
(First Quatrain)

Line 1-2
English: I made an assignation with the Night; / In the abyss was fixed our rendezvous:
Hindi Meaning: मैंने रात्रि के साथ एक नियत मिलन किया; / अतल गहराई में तय हुआ था हमारा मिलन स्थल:
Simple Explanation: कवि कहते हैं कि उन्होंने रात्रि (अंधकार, अज्ञान) के साथ मिलने का निर्णय लिया। उनका मिलन स्थान एक गहरी खाई या अतल गहराई में तय किया गया था।

Line 3-4
English: In my breast carrying God’s deathless light / I came her dark and dangerous heart to woo.
Hindi Meaning: अपने हृदय में ईश्वर का अमर प्रकाश लिए हुए / मैं उसके अंधकारमय और खतरनाक हृदय को रिझाने आया।
Simple Explanation: कवि अपने भीतर ईश्वरीय अमर ज्योति लेकर आए हैं, और उस रात्रि (अज्ञान) के अंधकारमय और भयावह हृदय को अपनी ओर आकर्षित करने का प्रयास कर रहे हैं।
दूसरा चतुष्क (Second Quatrain)

Line 5-6
English: I left the glory of the illumined Mind / And the calm rapture of the divinised soul
Hindi Meaning: मैंने प्रबुद्ध मन की महिमा को छोड़ दिया / और दिव्य आत्मा के शांत आनंद को त्याग दिया
Simple Explanation: कवि कहते हैं कि उन्होंने ज्ञान से प्रकाशित मन की महिमा और दिव्य आत्मा के शांत आनंद को पीछे छोड़ दिया है, अर्थात उन्होंने उच्च चेतना की अवस्था से नीचे उतरने का निर्णय लिया है।

Line 7-8
English: And travelled through a vastness dim and blind / To the grey shore where her ignorant waters roll.
Hindi Meaning: और यात्रा की एक धुंधले और अंधे विस्तार से होकर / उस धूसर तट तक जहाँ उसके अज्ञान के जल लहराते हैं।
Simple Explanation: कवि एक अंधकारमय और अज्ञानपूर्ण विस्तार से होकर यात्रा करते हैं, और अंततः उस धूसर समुद्र तट तक पहुँचते हैं जहाँ अज्ञान का सागर लहरें उठा रहा है।
तीसरा चतुष्क (Third Quatrain)

Line 9-10
English: I walk by the chill wave through the dull slime / And still that weary journeying knows no end;
Hindi Meaning: मैं ठंडी लहर के किनारे उस सुस्त कीचड़ से होकर चलता हूँ / और अभी भी उस थकाऊ यात्रा का कोई अंत नहीं दिखता;
Simple Explanation: कवि ठंडी लहरों और निष्प्राण कीचड़ से होकर अपनी यात्रा जारी रखते हैं। यह थकाऊ यात्रा अनंत प्रतीत होती है, इसका कोई अंत नज़र नहीं आता।

Line 11-12
English: Lost is the lustrous godhead beyond Time, / There comes no voice of the celestial Friend.
Hindi Meaning: खो गया है वह देदीप्यमान ईश्वरत्व जो समय से परे है, / वहाँ स्वर्गीय मित्र की कोई आवाज़ नहीं आती।
Simple Explanation: कवि अनुभव करते हैं कि समय से परे का वह चमकदार ईश्वरीय तत्व अब खो गया है। उन्हें अपने दिव्य मित्र (ईश्वर) की कोई आवाज़ सुनाई नहीं देती है।
अंतिम युग्म (Final Couplet)

Line 13-14
English: And yet I know my footprints’ track shall be / A pathway towards Immortality.
Hindi Meaning: और फिर भी मुझे पता है कि मेरे पदचिह्नों का मार्ग होगा / अमरता की ओर एक पथ।

Simple Explanation: इस सब के बावजूद, कवि को विश्वास है कि उनके द्वारा बनाया गया यह मार्ग, उनके पदचिह्न, अंततः अमरत्व की ओर ले जाएँगे। अर्थात, यह कठिन यात्रा व्यर्थ नहीं है, बल्कि यह अंततः अमरता तक पहुँचाएगी।
समग्र अर्थ (Overall Meaning in Hindi)

श्री अरविंद की यह कविता “The Pilgrim of the Night” आध्यात्मिक यात्रा का एक गहन और प्रतीकात्मक चित्रण है। शीर्षक स्वयं इस बात का संकेत देता है कि कवि अंधकार (अज्ञान, भौतिकता) के बीच एक तीर्थयात्री की तरह यात्रा कर रहे हैं।

कविता में कवि एक ऐसी यात्रा का वर्णन करते हैं जिसमें वे ज्ञान और प्रकाश की उच्च अवस्था से अज्ञान और अंधकार की निम्न अवस्था में उतरते हैं। श्री अरविंद, जो एक योगी और दार्शनिक थे, इस कविता के माध्यम से आध्यात्मिक साधना के एक महत्वपूर्ण पहलू को प्रस्तुत करते हैं - वह है अंधकार की अनुभूति और उसका सामना करने का साहस।

कवि ईश्वरीय प्रकाश को अपने अंदर लेकर जानबूझकर अज्ञान (रात्रि) की गहराइयों में उतरते हैं, यानी वे दिव्य ज्ञान को अज्ञान के अंधकार में ले जाते हैं। यह श्री अरविंद के “पूर्ण योग” (Integral Yoga) का एक महत्वपूर्ण सिद्धांत है - उनका मानना था कि आध्यात्मिक उन्नति का अर्थ संसार से पलायन नहीं, बल्कि संसार में रहकर उसे दिव्य चेतना से परिवर्तित करना है।

कविता में “रात्रि” अज्ञान, अंधकार, और चेतना के निम्न स्तरों का प्रतीक है। “अतल गहराई” उस अचेतन मन का प्रतिनिधित्व करती है जहाँ अज्ञान का वास है। “ईश्वर का अमर प्रकाश” आत्मज्ञान और दिव्य चेतना का प्रतीक है। “धूसर तट” और “अज्ञान के जल” भौतिक जगत और उसके भ्रमों का प्रतिनिधित्व करते हैं।

कविता के अंत में, कवि आशावादी दृष्टिकोण प्रस्तुत करते हैं। वे विश्वास करते हैं कि यह कठिन यात्रा, यह अंधकार से होकर गुज़रना, अंततः अमरत्व की ओर ले जाएगा। यह श्री अरविंद के दर्शन का सार है - भौतिक और अंधकारमय विश्व का सामना करना और उसे रूपांतरित करना, ताकि पृथ्वी पर ही दिव्य जीवन की स्थापना हो सके।
