Author Facts - Charles Dickens
Charles John Huffam Dickens
Birth: February 7, 1812, Portsmouth, England
Death: June 9, 1870, Gad's Hill Place, Kent, England (aged 58)
Lifespan: 1812–1870
Nationality: English
Occupation: Novelist, journalist, social critic, editor
Literary movement: Victorian literature, Social realism
Pen name: "Boz" (early works)
Famous works: Oliver Twist (1837-39), David Copperfield (1849-50), Great Expectations (1860-61), Bleak House (1852-53), Hard Times (1854)
Notable fact: Father imprisoned for debt; Dickens worked in blacking factory as child
Marriages: Catherine Hogarth (1836-1858, separated)
Children: 10 children
Periodicals founded: Household Words (1850), All the Year Round (1859)
Death cause: Stroke
Burial place: Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey
Publication Details
Full Title: A Tale of Two Cities
Publication Year: 1859
First publication: Serial publication in All the Year Round (April 30 – November 26, 1859)
Book form: Published in 1859 by Chapman & Hall (London)
Number of volumes: 3 volumes in first edition
Number of books: 3 books within the novel
Number of chapters: 45 chapters total (Book 1: 6 chapters, Book 2: 24 chapters, Book 3: 15 chapters)
Original illustrations: By Hablot Knight Browne ("Phiz")
Genre: Historical fiction, historical novel
Language: English
Dedication: To Lord John Russell
Length: Approximately 135,000 words
Format: Weekly serialized installments
Historical Background
French Revolution: 1789-1799
Bastille stormed: July 14, 1789
Reign of Terror: September 5, 1793 – July 28, 1794
Period covered: 1775-1793 (18 years)
Maximilien Robespierre: Key revolutionary leader (1758-1794)
King Louis XVI: Executed January 21, 1793
Marie Antoinette: Executed October 16, 1793
Guillotine: Primary execution method during Terror
Revolutionary Tribunal: Established March 1793
Sans-culottes: Working-class revolutionaries
Jacobins: Radical political group
Committee of Public Safety: Governing body during Terror
Setting Details
Paris, France
Saint Antoine district (working-class area)
Bastille prison
La Force prison
Conciergerie prison
The Defarge wine-shop
Revolutionary Tribunal
Place de la Grève (execution site)
Tellson's Bank (Paris branch)
London, England
Tellson's Bank (main office)
Soho Square (Manette residence)
Temple Bar
Dover Road
Old Bailey (courthouse)
Clerkenwell
Dover
Port town
Royal George Hotel
Time Period
Opens: 1775
Main action: 1780-1792
Final events: 1793
Main Idea

A Tale of Two Cities is set against the backdrop of the French Revolution and contrasts life in Paris and London. The story follows the Manette family and their associates through personal and political upheaval. Dr. Alexandre Manette, imprisoned for 18 years in the Bastille, is reunited with his daughter Lucie. She marries Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat who has renounced his title and moved to England. Sydney Carton, a dissolute English lawyer who loves Lucie hopelessly, forms a friendship with the family. When Darnay returns to Paris to save a servant, he is arrested and condemned to death by revolutionaries seeking revenge against his aristocratic family. In an act of ultimate redemption and sacrifice, Carton switches places with Darnay at the guillotine, giving his life so that Lucie and her family can live happily. The novel explores themes of resurrection, sacrifice, duality, revolution, and revenge.
Character List (with One-Line Descriptions)
Main Characters
Sydney Carton - Dissolute English lawyer; loves Lucie; sacrifices himself for Darnay
Charles Darnay (Charles Evrémonde) - French aristocrat who renounces title; Lucie's husband
Lucie Manette - Dr. Manette's daughter; central figure of love and goodness
Dr. Alexandre Manette - Physician imprisoned 18 years in Bastille; Lucie's father
Monsieur Ernest Defarge - Wine-shop owner; revolutionary leader; former servant to Dr. Manette
Madame Thérèse Defarge - Defarge's wife; relentless revolutionary knitting revenge
Jarvis Lorry - Tellson's Bank employee; family friend to Manettes
Miss Pross - Lucie's devoted servant and companion
Marquis St. Evrémonde (Uncle) - Charles Darnay's cruel uncle; murdered
Marquis St. Evrémonde (Father) - Charles's father; deceased; responsible for Dr. Manette's imprisonment
Supporting Characters
Jerry Cruncher - Porter at Tellson's; "resurrection man" (grave robber)
Young Jerry Cruncher - Jerry's son
Stryver - Ambitious lawyer; Sydney Carton's employer
The Vengeance - Madame Defarge's lieutenant; fellow revolutionary
Jacques Three - Revolutionary; wood-sawyer
Gabelle - Steward of Evrémonde estate; imprisoned
John Barsad (Solomon Pross) - Spy; Miss Pross's brother
Roger Cly - Spy; false witness
Attorney-General - Prosecutor in Darnay's first trial
The Seamstress - Young woman executed with Carton
Foulon - French official killed by mob
Gaspard - Peasant who kills the Marquis
Little Lucie - Daughter of Lucie and Charles Darnay
Jerry Cruncher's Wife - Religious woman; "flopping" (praying)
Book Summaries
Book the First: Recalled to Life
# Chapter 1: The Period

The novel opens with one of the most famous lines in literature: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." This chapter sets the scene in 1775, a time when both England and France were full of contradictions. Kings and queens ruled both nations with absolute power, but underneath the surface of order, chaos was brewing. In England, crime was everywhere and hangings were common entertainment. The country was filled with thieves, and even the roads weren't safe from highway robbers. In France, the common people were starving and suffering terribly while the rich aristocracy lived in incredible luxury, completely ignoring the suffering around them. The chapter hints strongly at the coming French Revolution without naming it directly. Dickens uses the metaphor of woodsmen in the forest, preparing trees that will eventually fall, to represent the revolutionary forces slowly building strength. The chapter sets up the idea that great changes are coming to both nations, and violence is inevitable.
# Chapter 2: The Mail

On a foggy, cold November night, a mail coach carrying passengers and mail struggles slowly up Shooter's Hill just outside London. The fog is so thick and the hill so muddy and steep that the passengers have to get out and walk alongside the horses. Nobody trusts anyone in this dark, fearful time. Robbery and murder on the roads are common, so every traveler views every other person with suspicion. Jerry Cruncher, who works odd jobs for Tellson's Bank, rides up on horseback looking for one particular passenger. He's carrying an urgent message for Mr. Jarvis Lorry, a businessman traveling on the coach. Jerry delivers his mysterious message: "Wait at Dover for Mam'selle." Mr. Lorry, after reading it, sends back an equally cryptic reply: "Recalled to life." The other passengers are curious and nervous about this strange exchange. Jerry rides back to London through the darkness, and the chapter ends with a sense of mystery and foreboding about what "recalled to life" could possibly mean.
# Chapter 3: The Night Shadows

This chapter takes us inside the mind of Mr. Jarvis Lorry as the mail coach continues through the foggy night toward Dover. Mr. Lorry is an elderly gentleman who has worked for Tellson's Bank for many years. As he tries to sleep in the bouncing coach, he thinks about his strange mission. He's going to meet a young woman and take her to Paris to reunite with her father, who has been locked away in prison for eighteen long years. Everyone believed the man was dead, but somehow he has survived and is being "recalled to life." Mr. Lorry keeps imagining what this reunion will be like. He wonders what condition the prisoner will be in after nearly two decades of imprisonment. Will the man still be sane? Will he remember he ever had a daughter? Will he recognize her? These troubling questions keep Mr. Lorry awake as the coach travels through the darkness. He rehearses in his mind how he will break this shocking news to the young woman. The chapter emphasizes that we can never truly know what's going on in another person's mind, just as the passengers in the coach are mysteries to each other on this dark night.
# Chapter 4: The Preparation

Mr. Jarvis Lorry arrives at the Royal George Hotel in Dover and settles in to wait. When Miss Lucie Manette arrives the next day, she turns out to be a beautiful young woman of about seventeen, with golden hair, blue eyes, and a gentle manner. Mr. Lorry must carefully tell her the shocking news about her father. He tries to break it to her gently, telling her that Tellson's Bank has some business regarding her father's estate. Lucie explains that she always believed her father, Doctor Alexandre Manette, died before she was even old enough to remember him. Her mother died when Lucie was just two years old. Mr. Lorry then reveals the stunning truth: her father is actually alive. He has been found in Paris after being imprisoned in the Bastille for eighteen years. Lucie is overwhelmed by this news. She faints from the shock, and a strange red-headed woman appears to help revive her. This woman is Miss Pross, Lucie's devoted servant and companion. Miss Pross is fiercely protective of Lucie, treating her almost like a mother would. Once Lucie recovers, Mr. Lorry explains that they must travel to Paris immediately to bring her father home to England. The chapter ends with preparations being made for the journey across the English Channel.
# Chapter 5: The Wine-Shop

The scene shifts to Paris, France, specifically to a poor neighborhood called Saint Antoine. A wine cask has accidentally broken in the street outside a wine shop, and all the poor, desperate people of the neighborhood rush to scoop up the spilled wine with their hands, cups, or even muddy rags. They drink it desperately, laughing and trying to enjoy this rare treat, but the scene is more tragic than joyful. After the wine is gone, one man writes the word "BLOOD" on a wall using wine as ink, predicting the violence to come. The wine shop is owned by Monsieur Ernest Defarge, a bull-necked, dark-haired man of about thirty. His wife, Madame Defarge, sits at the counter knitting constantly. She is described as having a watchful eye and a steady composure. When Mr. Lorry and Lucie arrive at the wine shop looking for Doctor Manette, Defarge takes them upstairs to a dark garret room. He explains that he was Doctor Manette's former servant, and he has been protecting the doctor since his release from the Bastille. As they climb the stairs, Defarge warns them that the doctor is in a very bad condition. Before entering the room, Defarge shows the doctor to a few men who are addressed as "Jacques," which is a code name used by revolutionaries. The wine shop is clearly a meeting place for those planning revolution.
# Chapter 6: The Shoemaker

In a dark, gloomy garret room, Mr. Lorry and Lucie find Doctor Manette. The sight is heartbreaking. The doctor sits at a workbench making shoes, which is a trade he learned during his long imprisonment. He is thin, pale, and has a long white beard. His voice is weak and barely audible, and he seems completely disconnected from reality. He doesn't remember his real name and only identifies himself as "One Hundred and Five, North Tower," which was his cell number in the Bastille prison. The doctor's mind has been broken by his years of isolation and suffering. When asked what he's making, he can only answer that he's making shoes, which is all he knows now. Mr. Lorry gently tries to question him, but the doctor gives confused, fragmented answers. Then Lucie approaches her father. Although she doesn't say who she is at first, something about her golden hair stirs a deep memory in the doctor. He remembers that his wife had beautiful golden hair, and he kept a piece of it with him in prison. When Lucie finally reveals that she is his daughter, the doctor is both overjoyed and confused. He can hardly believe it's real. Lucie embraces him with love and compassion, promising to take him home and care for him. The doctor breaks down in tears, and the chapter ends with Lucie and Mr. Lorry preparing to take the broken man back to England, hoping that love and care can restore his shattered mind.
Book the Second: The Golden Thread
# Chapter 1: Five Years Later

The scene shifts to 1780, five years after Doctor Manette was rescued from Paris. We're now at Tellson's Bank in London, an old, dark, and cramped building that prides itself on being old-fashioned. The bank is described as ugly and inconvenient, but it refuses to change because its ancient traditions make it respectable. Here we meet Jerry Cruncher, who does odd jobs for the bank. Jerry is a messenger and general errand-runner. He lives in a small apartment with his wife and son, young Jerry. Jerry is rough and bad-tempered, especially toward his wife, whom he accuses of "praying against him." He believes her prayers are ruining his side business, though we don't yet know what that business is. Jerry's main job is to sit outside Tellson's Bank on a stool and wait for messages to deliver. This particular morning, Jerry and his son are called into the bank and told to go to the Old Bailey courthouse, where there's a treason trial happening. Mr. Lorry needs Jerry to be there in case any messages need to be sent.
# Chapter 2: A Sight

Jerry Cruncher and his son arrive at the Old Bailey criminal court, where a large crowd has gathered for a treason trial. The courthouse is dirty and foul-smelling, and the crowd is excited because treason is a capital crime, which means the defendant could be executed. Everyone loves the drama and potential violence of a trial that might end in death. The crowd pushes and shoves to get a better look at the prisoner. Young Jerry asks his father what "quartering" means (a brutal form of execution for traitors), and Jerry explains the horrifying process. We learn that the man on trial is Charles Darnay, accused of being a spy for France. He's charged with traveling between France and England, supposedly passing secrets. If found guilty, he will be executed in a gruesome manner. The atmosphere in the courtroom is ugly and violent, with the crowd already treating Darnay as if he's guilty. The bloodthirsty spectators are disappointed when they learn the trial might take time, as they're eager to see a conviction and execution.
# Chapter 3: A Disappointment

The trial of Charles Darnay begins. He is a young, handsome gentleman of about twenty-five, well-mannered and composed despite his terrible situation. The main evidence against him comes from two witnesses. First, John Barsad testifies that Darnay was involved in suspicious activities. Then Roger Cly, who claims to have been Darnay's servant, says that Darnay had secret papers. In the courtroom gallery sit two people who catch our attention: Doctor Manette and his daughter Lucie. Doctor Manette has recovered somewhat from his ordeal, though he still looks fragile. The Attorney General prosecuting the case makes dramatic speeches about Darnay's supposed treachery. Lucie is called to testify. She admits that she met Darnay on a ship returning from France five years earlier, and that he was kind to her and her father. She also admits that Darnay made multiple trips between France and England, but she insists he never seemed like a spy. Lucie is clearly distressed at having to testify against someone who showed her kindness. The prosecution seems to be building a strong case against Darnay, and execution seems likely.
# Chapter 4: Congratulatory

Just when things look hopeless for Darnay, his defense lawyer's assistant makes a brilliant observation. The assistant, Sydney Carton, is a careless, slovenly man who appears half-drunk. He whispers something to the lead defense attorney, Mr. Stryver. Carton points out that the prosecution's case relies on witness identification of Darnay at a certain place and time. Then Carton removes his wig and stands near Darnay. The resemblance is striking—Carton and Darnay look remarkably similar. This proves that the witnesses could have been mistaken, as they might have seen Carton rather than Darnay. The prosecution's case falls apart, and Darnay is acquitted. After the trial, the courtroom clears, and those who were hoping for an execution are disappointed (hence the chapter title "A Disappointment"). Doctor Manette seems disturbed by Darnay, though we don't yet know why. Lucie is relieved but faints from the stress. Sydney Carton helps her recover, showing unexpected gentleness. Later, Carton, Darnay, and Mr. Stryver go to a tavern to celebrate. However, Carton seems moody and bitter rather than celebratory. His resemblance to Darnay is even more apparent now, but their characters are completely different—Darnay is upright and respectable, while Carton seems dissolute and self-destructive.
# Chapter 5: The Jackal

This chapter reveals the relationship between Sydney Carton and Mr. Stryver, the defense lawyer. Stryver is called "the lion" and Carton "the jackal" because Carton does most of Stryver's legal work, but Stryver gets all the credit and glory. Every night, Carton goes to Stryver's chambers and works until dawn, preparing legal cases while Stryver sleeps or socializes. Carton is brilliant but has no ambition or self-respect. He drinks heavily and wastes his talents. This particular night, after Darnay's trial, Carton works on legal papers while drinking and brooding. Stryver is pushy, ambitious, and full of himself, while Carton is clearly the more intelligent of the two but completely unmotivated. Stryver bosses Carton around and takes advantage of his work. When Stryver goes to bed, Carton continues working and drinking alone. He looks at his own reflection in a mirror and sees the resemblance to Charles Darnay. This depresses him greatly because Darnay represents everything Carton could have been but isn't—successful, respectable, and with a bright future. Carton breaks down in tears, lamenting the waste he's made of his life. He finally falls asleep at dawn, exhausted and drunk. The chapter shows us that Carton is a tragic figure, a man of great potential who has destroyed himself through drink and despair.
# Chapter 6: Hundreds of People

Doctor Manette and Lucie live in a quiet corner house in Soho, London. Thanks to Lucie's love and care over the past five years, Doctor Manette has mostly recovered from his trauma, though he still has occasional relapses. He has resumed his medical practice and is respected in the community. However, Lucie notices that sometimes her father slips back into his old prison mentality, especially when he's under stress. In the house with them lives Miss Pross, Lucie's fiercely protective servant, and this chapter shows us their daily life. Their home becomes a gathering place for friends. One frequent visitor is Mr. Lorry, the kind banker who helped reunite Lucie and her father. Another is Charles Darnay, the Frenchman who was on trial for treason. Darnay visits often and clearly has developed feelings for Lucie. Sydney Carton also visits occasionally, though he behaves strangely and seems uncomfortable. The title "Hundreds of People" comes from Miss Pross's exaggerated claim that hundreds of people come to visit, when in reality it's only a handful. Miss Pross particularly dislikes all the men who visit because she worries they're suitors trying to take Lucie away from her. The chapter establishes that Lucie has become the center of a small circle of people, like the "golden thread" that binds them together. Doctor Manette has a workshop room where he keeps his shoemaking bench, though he rarely uses it anymore. When stressed, however, he sometimes retreats there to make shoes, returning mentally to his prison days.
# Chapter 7: Monseigneur in Town

The scene shifts back to France, where we see the corruption and excess of the French aristocracy. The focus is on a powerful aristocrat known simply as "Monseigneur," who lives in Paris surrounded by incredible luxury. He has dozens of servants for the most trivial tasks—one just to serve his chocolate drink, for instance. Monseigneur represents everything wrong with the French nobility: he's completely selfish, wasteful, and has no concern for the common people who are starving. The chapter describes the elaborate, ridiculous court rituals and the fake, shallow relationships among the aristocrats. After a morning of silly ceremonies, Monseigneur holds a reception where wealthy and powerful people compete for his favor. Among the guests is the Marquis St. Evrémonde, a cruel-looking man about sixty years old, with a face like a mask. He's Charles Darnay's uncle, though we don't learn this immediately. The Marquis leaves the reception and travels in his carriage through the streets of Paris. He drives recklessly fast through the poor neighborhoods, caring nothing for the people in his way. Suddenly, his carriage runs over and kills a small child in the street. The father of the dead child, Gaspard, is devastated. Instead of showing any remorse, the Marquis coldly throws a gold coin at the man to pay for the "inconvenience." He complains that the poor people should get out of the way of their betters. The crowd is horrified and angry. Defarge, the wine shop owner, tries to comfort Gaspard. A coin comes flying back at the Marquis, thrown by someone in the crowd, though we don't see who. The Marquis threatens that he could easily have the coin-thrower killed, showing his absolute contempt for human life. This chapter powerfully illustrates why revolution is brewing in France.
# Chapter 8: Monseigneur in the Country

The Marquis St. Evrémonde continues his journey from Paris to his château (castle) in the countryside. As his carriage travels through rural France, we see the terrible poverty of the peasants. They are starving, living in crumbling buildings, wearing rags, and working hopelessly in barely productive fields. The land has been overtaxed and exploited by the aristocracy. A poor road-mender tells the Marquis that he saw a man hanging underneath his carriage earlier. The Marquis asks if the man is still there, and when told no, shows no further interest, not caring about why someone might need to cling desperately to his carriage. When the Marquis arrives at his château, he asks for his nephew, who hasn't arrived yet. He has supper alone in grand style, served by numerous servants, while all around his estate people are starving. That evening, Charles Darnay arrives. We now learn that Darnay is actually Charles St. Evrémonde, the Marquis's nephew. The two men have dinner together, but there's clearly tension between them. Darnay expresses his disgust with the family's treatment of the common people. He says the family name is hated throughout France, and rightfully so. The Marquis coldly defends the aristocracy's right to do whatever they want to the peasants. He says the common people are like animals and deserve their suffering. Darnay announces that he's renouncing his inheritance and will not continue his family's cruel traditions. He plans to make his own way in England, where he's been living. The Marquis is contemptuous of his nephew's idealism and essentially disowns him. They part in anger. That night, the Marquis goes to sleep in his luxurious bedroom. The next morning, he's found dead in his bed, stabbed through the heart with a knife. Pinned to the body is a note that reads "Drive him fast to his tomb. This, from Jacques"—the name used by revolutionaries. Gaspard, the man whose child was killed, has taken his revenge.
# Chapter 9: The Gorgon's Head

This chapter deals with the aftermath of the Marquis's murder. The "Gorgon's Head" refers to the stone decorations on the château that look like the mythological creature whose gaze turned people to stone. The whole estate seems frozen and cursed. The peasants who work on the estate show no sorrow at the Marquis's death—only fear of punishment. Gaspard has disappeared, and soldiers search everywhere for him. The château servants and local villagers are questioned, but no one will betray Gaspard. The authorities continue searching while Charles Darnay has already returned to England. This chapter is shorter than others and serves as a transition, showing that the murder of one cruel aristocrat is just the beginning of the violence to come.
# Chapter 10: Two Promises

We return to London, where Charles Darnay has been working honestly as a French tutor and translator. He visits Doctor Manette's home frequently, and it's clear he's in love with Lucie. One day, Darnay asks to speak privately with Doctor Manette. He tells the doctor that he loves Lucie and wishes to marry her, but first he wants Doctor Manette's permission and blessing. Darnay also says that if Lucie accepts him, he needs to tell Doctor Manette his real name and the story of his family in France. This seems to trouble the doctor greatly, as he has bad associations with French aristocrats (though we don't yet know the full story). However, the doctor gives his permission for Darnay to propose, on one condition: Darnay must not reveal his real name and family history until the morning of the wedding, if there is to be one. Darnay agrees. Doctor Manette makes Darnay promise this, and Darnay makes the doctor promise not to hold his family background against him. After Darnay leaves, Doctor Manette becomes very disturbed and agitated. His face turns pale, and he seems to have a flashback to his time in prison. That night, the doctor retreats to his workshop room and begins making shoes again, a sign that he's relapsed into his traumatized state. Lucie and Miss Pross hear the sound of hammering from his workshop late into the night, and they're worried about his condition.
# Chapter 11: A Companion Picture

Sydney Carton also visits the Manette household, though less frequently than Darnay. One evening, Carton comes to see Lucie when he knows her father is out with Darnay. He's been drinking, as usual, and seems even more miserable than normal. He tells Lucie that he knows he's a waste of a man and that his life is worthless. Lucie tries to comfort him kindly, saying she's sure he can improve himself. Carton says it's too late for him—he's too far gone. Then he tells Lucie that he loves her, but he knows he's not worthy of her and will never ask her to marry him. He says that even though he's wasted his life, knowing her has made him dream of being better. He asks her to remember that there's a man who would give his life to keep her and those she loves safe. Lucie is moved to tears by his confession and his obvious pain. Carton makes her promise to keep this conversation secret and to remember his words. Then he leaves. The chapter title "A Companion Picture" refers to how this scene mirrors the previous chapter—two men declaring their feelings to or about Lucie, but in very different ways. Darnay offers hope and a future, while Carton offers only devotion from a distance, knowing he can never truly be with her.
# Chapter 12: The Fellow of Delicacy

Mr. Stryver, the boastful lawyer, decides he wants to marry Lucie Manette. He sees her as a pretty, pleasant wife who would make him look good in society. Stryver is completely full of himself and assumes Lucie will be honored to marry him. Before proposing, he mentions his plans to Mr. Lorry at Tellson's Bank. Mr. Lorry is horrified because he knows Lucie doesn't care for Stryver at all. Very tactfully, Mr. Lorry suggests that Stryver should let him "feel out" the situation first before making a formal proposal, to avoid an embarrassing rejection. Stryver is shocked that anyone might reject him, but he agrees. Mr. Lorry goes to the Manette house and confirms that Lucie would definitely refuse Stryver. When Mr. Lorry reports this back, Stryver's ego is bruised, but he quickly convinces himself that he's actually the one rejecting Lucie, not the other way around. He decides she wouldn't have been good enough for him anyway. This somewhat humorous chapter shows Stryver's ridiculous vanity and also demonstrates Mr. Lorry's protective care for Lucie and her father.

chapters.title: Chapter 13: The Fellow of No Delicacy

content.value: # Chapter 13: The Fellow of No Delicacy

In contrast to Stryver ("fellow of delicacy"), this chapter focuses on Sydney Carton ("fellow of no delicacy"). Carton continues to visit the Manette household occasionally, though he's often in bad condition from drinking. He makes no effort to hide his wasted state. However, Lucie treats him with kindness and compassion, remembering his confession of love and his promise to do anything for her. Carton sometimes seems to improve slightly when he's around Lucie, as if her goodness inspires him to be better, at least temporarily. Doctor Manette has fully recovered from his relapse after Darnay's conversation with him. The household settles into a peaceful routine. This shorter chapter emphasizes the difference between Stryver's false "delicacy" (which is really just vanity and self-interest) and Carton's honest lack of it—he knows he's a wreck and doesn't pretend otherwise, but his feelings for Lucie are genuine.
# Chapter 14: The Honest Tradesman

We return to Jerry Cruncher and learn more about his mysterious "night work." The chapter begins with Jerry sitting on his stool outside Tellson's Bank as usual. His son, young Jerry, watches his father work and tries to imitate him. Jerry is bad-tempered and complains constantly about his wife's praying, which he's sure is hurting his business. One day, Jerry and young Jerry follow a funeral procession through London. The funeral is for Roger Cly, one of the witnesses who testified against Charles Darnay in his treason trial. The crowd at the funeral is rowdy and unruly, turning it into a chaotic, almost riot-like event. After the funeral, Jerry sends young Jerry home and tells him to go to bed. But young Jerry is curious about what his father does at night, so he stays awake and watches. He sees his father leave the house late at night carrying tools, along with two other men. Young Jerry secretly follows them to the cemetery where Roger Cly was buried. There, he watches in horror as his father and the other men dig up the fresh grave. Jerry is a "Resurrection Man"—a grave robber who digs up corpses and sells them to medical schools for anatomy lessons. This illegal and gruesome trade explains Jerry's mysterious night work and why he doesn't want his wife praying against his business. Young Jerry runs home in terror after seeing his father digging up the grave. The next morning, Jerry accuses his wife of praying against his business again because the grave robbing apparently didn't go well (though we don't learn the details). Young Jerry, despite his initial horror, tells his father he wants to become a Resurrection Man too when he grows up, much to his mother's dismay. This darkly comic chapter adds another layer to the novel's themes about death and resurrection.
# Chapter 15: Knitting

The scene shifts back to Paris and Defarge's wine shop in the poor Saint Antoine neighborhood. It's been years since we last saw this place. Monsieur Defarge is still running the wine shop, and his wife, Madame Defarge, still sits knitting constantly. But we now learn that her knitting has a secret purpose: she's knitting a register of names—people marked for death when the revolution comes. Each symbol in her knitting represents a person condemned by the revolutionaries. The wine shop is a secret meeting place for revolutionaries who call each other "Jacques." One day, a stranger enters the shop—John Barsad, who is actually an English spy. He pretends to be sympathetic to the revolution and tries to gather information. He mentions that Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat living in England, has married Lucie Manette, the daughter of Doctor Manette who was once imprisoned in the Bastille. Madame Defarge's face shows intense interest at this news, though she remains seemingly calm. After Barsad leaves, Madame Defarge adds new names to her knitting register. A road-mender (the same one from earlier who saw the man under the Marquis's carriage) comes to the wine shop and is brought to meet the revolutionary leaders. He tells them that Gaspard, who killed the Marquis, was captured and executed—hanged above the village fountain where everyone had to see his body rotting for days. The revolutionaries are told that this is what will happen to any who oppose the aristocracy. But instead of being frightened, the revolutionaries grow more determined and angry. Defarge and his wife take the road-mender to Versailles to show him the king's palace and the outrageous luxury of the aristocracy, which further fuels revolutionary feeling.
# Chapter 16: Still Knitting

Madame Defarge continues her knitting as the revolution grows closer. More and more people are added to her register. She is cold, calculating, and absolutely committed to revenge against the aristocracy. We learn that Madame Defarge has a personal vendetta, though the details aren't yet revealed. Her husband, Monsieur Defarge, sometimes shows moments of compassion or hesitation, but Madame Defarge is completely ruthless. She argues that the suffering of the common people has been so great for so long that no mercy can be shown to the oppressors. One day, John Barsad the spy returns to the wine shop. He brings news about the Manettes and Darnay in England, trying to get information from the Defarges. Madame Defarge reveals nothing but mentally adds more names to her deadly register. This chapter builds tension as we see the revolution approaching and understand that Madame Defarge's knitting represents death sentences for many people, possibly including characters we care about. The chapter ends with an ominous feeling that the storm of revolution is about to break.
# Chapter 17: One Night

Back in England, Lucie and Charles Darnay have been happily married for several years. It's now 1789, and they have a young daughter, also named Lucie (nicknamed "little Lucie"). They also had a son who died young, which was a source of great sorrow. Doctor Manette lives with them and has been well for years, with no relapses. The family is peaceful and content. One night, Lucie and her father sit by the window while Darnay works in another room. Lucie tells her father about a strange feeling she sometimes has—she hears echoing footsteps approaching, as if something threatening is coming toward them from far away. Doctor Manette comforts her, but the reader knows that these "echoing footsteps" represent the approaching revolution in France, which will soon disrupt their peaceful life. This is one of the novel's most beautifully written chapters, using Lucie's premonition to foreshadow the coming trouble.
# Chapter 18: Nine Days

This chapter reveals what happened on the morning of Lucie and Darnay's wedding, years earlier. As promised, Darnay privately told Doctor Manette his real name and the story of his aristocratic family in France. We don't hear what Darnay said, but Doctor Manette was clearly shocked and disturbed by the revelation. Despite this, the wedding went ahead, and Doctor Manette seemed fine during the ceremony. However, after the couple left for their honeymoon, Doctor Manette suffered a complete relapse. He reverted to his traumatized prison state and spent nine days obsessively making shoes, just as he did in the Bastille. He didn't recognize Miss Pross or Mr. Lorry, who stayed with him and cared for him during this terrible episode. He only answered to his prison cell number and seemed completely lost in the past. After nine days, the fit gradually passed, and Doctor Manette returned to normal, with no memory of the episode. Mr. Lorry gently talks with Doctor Manette about what happened (without revealing that he witnessed it). Doctor Manette explains that the relapse was triggered by something that reminded him forcefully of his past trauma. He doesn't expect it to happen again. Mr. Lorry asks if they should get rid of the shoemaking tools and bench, which seem to be a trigger for these relapses. At first, Doctor Manette is reluctant—the tools were his only comfort during years of suffering. But eventually, he agrees. Mr. Lorry and Miss Pross secretly destroy the shoemaking bench and bury the tools. This chapter shows how traumatic Doctor Manette's imprisonment was and hints that Darnay's family connection somehow relates to that trauma.
# Chapter 19: An Opinion

This is the conclusion to the previous chapter, describing how Doctor Manette has fully recovered and life has returned to normal. Mr. Lorry discusses with Doctor Manette whether he might relapse again, and the doctor assures him that the worst is over. The chapter is short and serves as a transition back to the present time, where the family has been living peacefully for years.
# Chapter 20: A Plea

Sydney Carton continues to visit the Darnay household occasionally. He has not improved his life or stopped drinking, but he's kept his promise to Lucie—he's always there if she needs him, watching over her family from a distance. One evening, Charles Darnay talks with Carton and says he wishes they could be friends. Carton says he's not worth having as a friend. Darnay generously says that Carton saved his life during the treason trial and that he'll always be grateful. He tells Carton that he's always welcome in their home. Carton asks Darnay to promise that he'll always be allowed to visit, no matter how dissolute and worthless he seems. Darnay, not fully understanding why this matters so much to Carton, promises. This chapter shows Carton still loving Lucie from afar and maintaining his connection to her family, preparing us for his later sacrifice.
# Chapter 21: Echoing Footsteps

The "echoing footsteps" that Lucie heard years earlier have finally arrived. It's July 1789, and the French Revolution begins. In Paris, the common people have finally risen up against their oppressors. The chapter describes the storming of the Bastille, the famous prison fortress that symbolized royal tyranny. Defarge leads a group of revolutionaries to the prison. The mob attacks with incredible fury, driven by generations of suffering and anger. They break down the gates and free the prisoners. Defarge has a specific purpose—he rushes to the cell that was once occupied by Doctor Manette, "One Hundred and Five, North Tower." He searches the cell frantically, looking for something, and tears apart the walls and floor. His wife, Madame Defarge, stands beside him, cold and determined as always. They find what they're looking for—a hidden document written by Doctor Manette during his imprisonment. Defarge takes it. Outside, the revolution spreads like wildfire through Paris. The aristocrats are being killed in the streets, and the old order is being violently torn down. Back in England, Lucie continues her peaceful life with her husband and child, not yet knowing how the revolution will affect her family. Mr. Lorry tells them about the chaos in France, and they're concerned but feel safe in England. However, the echoing footsteps have finally reached them, and their lives are about to change forever.
# Chapter 22: The Sea Still Rises

The violence in France continues to escalate. The sea of revolution rises higher and higher. A week after the storming of the Bastille, more violence erupts. Foulon, a cruel aristocrat who once said that starving people could eat grass, is captured by the revolutionaries. The mob drags him through the streets and murders him brutally, stuffing his mouth with grass. His son-in-law is also captured and killed. The wine shop in Saint Antoine becomes an even more important center for revolutionary activity. Madame Defarge watches everything with her cold, steady gaze, still knitting, adding more names to her register. The road-mender who witnessed the Marquis's cruelty is now living in Paris and participating in the revolution. He dances in the streets with other revolutionaries, celebrating their victories. The Defarges and their fellow revolutionaries grow more powerful and more bloodthirsty. Three years pass (it's now 1792), and the revolution has become the Reign of Terror. Thousands of aristocrats and suspected enemies of the revolution are being executed by guillotine. The revolutionaries are now as cruel as the aristocrats they overthrew. Anyone can be denounced and executed on the slightest suspicion. France has descended into chaos and violence.
# Chapter 23: Fire Rises

This chapter takes us back to the Marquis's château in the countryside. After the Marquis was murdered years ago, the estate fell into neglect. Charles Darnay never returned to claim his inheritance, and the peasants continued to suffer under the management of Gabelle, the tax collector who tried to be somewhat kind but was still part of the oppressive system. Now, with revolution spreading across France, the peasants finally take their revenge. They march to the château with torches and fury. They set fire to the great house, burning it to the ground. The flames light up the countryside, and the fire spreads to other aristocratic estates. Gabelle, the tax collector, is captured and imprisoned by the revolutionaries, accused of working for the aristocracy. The chapter describes the violence spreading across rural France like wildfire, with châteaux burning throughout the countryside. This represents the complete destruction of the old aristocratic order. The revolutionaries show no mercy, killing anyone associated with the nobility.

chapters.title: Chapter 24: Drawn to the Loadstone Rock

content.value: # Chapter 24: Drawn to the Loadstone Rock

Three more years pass, and it's now August 1792. The revolution has grown even more violent and extreme. Charles Darnay is living peacefully in England with Lucie, their daughter, and Doctor Manette, trying to stay far from the chaos in France. However, Darnay receives a desperate letter from Gabelle, the tax collector who was imprisoned at the château. Gabelle is in prison in France, awaiting execution. He writes to Darnay (using his French name, Evrémonde) begging for help. He says he's been imprisoned because he worked for the Evrémonde family, and only Darnay can save him by coming to France and testifying that Gabelle was actually trying to help the peasants, not oppress them. Darnay is torn about what to do. He knows France is incredibly dangerous for any former aristocrat. However, he feels guilty about Gabelle's imprisonment—after all, Gabelle is suffering because of Darnay's family name. Darnay also believes that because he renounced his aristocratic title and privileges, and has never hurt anyone, the revolutionaries will treat him fairly. He decides to go to France secretly to help Gabelle. He doesn't tell Lucie or Doctor Manette about his plans because he doesn't want to worry them. He tells them he has business in France but will return quickly. He writes letters to Lucie and her father explaining everything, to be delivered after he's gone. Darnay travels to Paris, but the journey is difficult and dangerous. Every town and village has revolutionary checkpoints, and traveling aristocrats are being arrested everywhere. Darnay is repeatedly stopped, questioned, and threatened. His honest answers about his identity (using his real name, Evrémonde) cause alarm everywhere he goes. By the time he reaches Paris, he's been traveling for days under guard. When he finally arrives, he's immediately arrested as an emigrant aristocrat—an enemy of the Republic. The revolutionary tribunal sends him to prison to await trial. Darnay realizes too late that he's made a terrible mistake. He's trapped in revolutionary France with little hope of escape.
Book the Third: The Track of a Storm
# Chapter 1: In Secret

Charles Darnay is imprisoned in La Force prison in Paris. The prison is overcrowded with aristocrats and suspected enemies of the revolution, all awaiting trial and likely execution. Darnay is shocked by the conditions and the number of prisoners. He's placed in a cell and told he's being held "in secret," meaning in solitary confinement without communication with the outside world. The other prisoners, despite their terrible situation, try to maintain dignity and even some cheerfulness. They share what little they have and try to support each other. Darnay learns that trials are happening quickly, and most prisoners are being sent to the guillotine within days of their arrest. That night, Darnay hears the terrible sound of a grindstone being used to sharpen weapons outside the prison. A mob has gathered, and they're preparing to massacre prisoners. This actually happened in the September Massacres of 1792, when revolutionary mobs killed over a thousand prisoners. Darnay fears for his life, but the massacre doesn't reach his section of the prison. He survives, but the experience is traumatic. Days turn into weeks, and Darnay remains imprisoned with no trial date set. He's not allowed any contact with anyone outside the prison. He doesn't know if his letters ever reached Lucie or Doctor Manette, and he has no idea if they know what's happened to him. The chapter ends with Darnay facing an uncertain fate in revolutionary Paris.
# Chapter 2: The Grindstone

Mr. Lorry has been sent by Tellson's Bank to Paris to protect the bank's French business interests. The bank has many French aristocratic customers, and their property and accounts need to be managed during the revolution. Mr. Lorry is staying at the Paris branch of Tellson's Bank, which has become a gathering place for aristocrats and others in danger. One day, to his shock, Lucie and Doctor Manette arrive at the bank. Lucie has received Darnay's letter and immediately traveled to France with her father to try to save her husband. Little Lucie and Miss Pross have come too. Mr. Lorry is horrified that Lucie has come to such a dangerous place, but there's nothing to be done about it now. He finds them a safe place to stay near the bank. That evening, the terrible sound of the grindstone fills the streets. A bloodthirsty mob is outside the bank, sharpening their weapons and preparing for violence. Doctor Manette sees the mob and makes a bold decision. He goes outside and addresses the crowd, identifying himself as a former prisoner of the Bastille who was imprisoned by aristocrats for eighteen years. The revolutionaries immediately respect him—former Bastille prisoners are honored as heroes of the revolution. Doctor Manette tells them his daughter's husband has been arrested, and he needs to help him. The crowd allows Doctor Manette to pass, and he goes to try to use his influence to free Darnay or at least get him a fair trial. The chapter shows how Doctor Manette's suffering has given him special status among the revolutionaries, which may be Darnay's only hope.
# Chapter 3: The Shadow

Lucie, Miss Pross, little Lucie, and Mr. Lorry wait anxiously for news. They've found lodgings in a building near the prison where Darnay is held. Doctor Manette is working tirelessly, using his influence with the revolutionaries to help his son-in-law. Days pass with no clear news. Lucie is terribly worried but tries to stay strong for her child. One day, Lucie discovers a spot on a street corner where, at a certain time of day, Darnay can see her from his prison window. She goes there every afternoon and stands where he can see her, just to let him know she's there and hasn't abandoned him. She does this every day, no matter the weather, hoping to give him strength and comfort. One day, a strange man approaches Lucie on the street. He seems to recognize her and watches her with interest. This man is known as "The Vengeance," a friend of Madame Defarge. Later, Madame Defarge herself appears, along with The Vengeance. Madame Defarge wants to see what Lucie looks like. She studies Lucie carefully with her cold, calculating eyes, as if memorizing her features. Lucie feels chilled by Madame Defarge's presence and recognizes that this woman is dangerous. However, she doesn't understand the full extent of Madame Defarge's hatred for her family. The chapter creates an atmosphere of growing danger and shows that Lucie's family may be in even more trouble than they realize.
# Chapter 4: Calm in Storm

Fifteen months pass. Darnay remains in prison all this time without a trial. Doctor Manette continues working to help him, and his efforts have at least kept Darnay alive when many other prisoners have been executed. During this time, Paris remains in chaos. The Reign of Terror continues, and the guillotine claims victims every day. King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette have been executed. The revolution has grown increasingly extreme and violent. Despite the horror all around them, Lucie and her family have settled into a strange sort of routine. Lucie continues her daily vigil, standing where Darnay can see her from his prison window. Doctor Manette uses his status as a former Bastille prisoner to protect his family and work for Darnay's release. Mr. Lorry continues managing Tellson's Bank business. They wait and hope, but the situation seems hopeless. Finally, after fifteen months, Darnay is granted a trial date. Doctor Manette is hopeful because he's been working within the revolutionary system and has made connections with influential revolutionaries. He believes his testimony will save Darnay.
# Chapter 5: The Wood-Sawyer

While waiting for Darnay's trial, Lucie continues her daily routine of standing where he can see her. Near her spot, there's a wood-sawyer who has set up his business. This man is a revolutionary who frequently makes jokes about cutting off aristocratic heads, comparing it to his sawing of wood. His dark humor disturbs Lucie, but she endures it to be near her husband. The wood-sawyer recognizes Lucie from seeing her every day and calls her "the wife of Evrémonde" to others, which is dangerous because the Evrémonde name is hated by revolutionaries. Lucie fears that she and her daughter may also be in danger because of their connection to Darnay. One day, the wood-sawyer tells Lucie that there will be a "show" the next day—meaning executions by guillotine. This casual attitude toward death shows how desensitized people have become to violence. The revolution has corrupted ordinary people, turning them into bloodthirsty spectators of execution. Lucie is horrified but continues her vigil for her husband's sake.
# Chapter 6: Triumph

The day of Darnay's trial arrives. The courtroom is packed with hostile spectators who come to watch trials as entertainment. The revolutionaries want to see aristocrats condemned. Darnay is brought from prison to face the tribunal. The charges against him are that he's an emigrant aristocrat, an Evrémonde, and therefore an enemy of the Republic. Doctor Manette testifies on Darnay's behalf. He tells the court that Darnay renounced his aristocratic title and inheritance years ago because he disagreed with his family's cruel treatment of the people. He says Darnay has lived honestly in England and has never harmed anyone. Doctor Manette's testimony is powerful, and his status as a respected former Bastille prisoner carries great weight. Several witnesses support Darnay's character. Even Defarge, when questioned, admits that Darnay was kind to Doctor Manette. The tribunal deliberates and then announces its verdict: Darnay is acquitted! The courtroom erupts in celebration—not because they love Darnay, but because they love Doctor Manette and are honoring his wish. Darnay is released and reunited with his family. They celebrate tearfully, grateful beyond words. That night, Darnay is finally free to be with Lucie, their daughter, and Doctor Manette. They hold each other and cry with relief and joy. For the first time in fifteen months, Darnay can sleep in his own bed with his wife. The family feels blessed and relieved. However, their triumph is short-lived.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: A Knock at the Door

content.value: # Chapter 7: A Knock at the Door

Only hours after Darnay's release, there's a loud knock at the door. Four rough armed men have come to arrest Darnay again. The family is devastated—they just got him back! The men say that Darnay has been denounced again by new accusers, and he must return to prison immediately. According to revolutionary law, anyone can denounce anyone, and the accused must be arrested and tried. There's no protection against false accusations. Lucie begs to know who has accused her husband this time. The soldiers reveal that the denouncers are Ernest Defarge, his wife Madame Defarge, and one other person whose identity will be revealed at the trial. Darnay is taken away again, back to prison. The family is heartbroken. Doctor Manette, who believed his influence had saved his son-in-law, is shocked and confused. He doesn't understand why the Defarges, who seemed to support him, would denounce Darnay. Lucie is desperate and terrified. This second arrest is even worse than the first because it comes just when they thought they were safe. The chapter ends with Darnay once again imprisoned, and his family facing a new nightmare.
# Chapter 8: A Hand at Cards

Sydney Carton has arrived in Paris. He came because he made a promise to Lucie years ago that he would do anything to help her. Somehow, he learned about the family's trouble and traveled to France. Carton has been observing the situation carefully, and he has a plan forming in his mind. One evening, Carton is at a tavern when he spots someone he recognizes: John Barsad, the English spy who testified at Darnay's trial in England years ago and who has been working in Paris. Carton follows Barsad and confronts him. Through clever questioning and threats, Carton reveals that he knows Barsad's secrets. Barsad has been playing a dangerous game, working as a spy for multiple sides. Carton also reveals that he knows Barsad is actually Solomon Pross, the long-lost brother of Miss Pross, Lucie's devoted servant. Miss Pross appears and confirms this—she's shocked to see her brother after so many years. Solomon/Barsad abandoned his sister years ago and has been living under assumed names. Carton blackmails Barsad, threatening to expose him to the revolutionaries as a spy (which would mean certain death). Carton says he'll keep Barsad's secret on one condition: Barsad must help him with something when the time comes. Barsad reluctantly agrees because he has no choice. Carton doesn't reveal his full plan yet, but he's clearly preparing something. The chapter shows Carton taking action and using his intelligence to set up a way to help Darnay. The title "A Hand at Cards" refers to Carton skillfully playing his cards in this dangerous game.
# Chapter 9: The Game Made

Carton continues his preparations. He meets with Mr. Lorry and tells him that Darnay's situation is extremely dangerous. This new trial is likely to end in conviction and execution. Carton says there's still hope, but Mr. Lorry must help by having traveling papers ready for the family to escape France immediately if needed. Carton also makes Mr. Lorry promise to follow his instructions exactly when the time comes, even if they seem strange. Mr. Lorry agrees, though he doesn't understand what Carton is planning. Carton has secured Barsad's cooperation because Barsad works as a spy in the prisons and has access to prisoners. Carton makes arrangements for the upcoming trial, though he keeps his specific plan secret. He's preparing for the worst outcome while hoping for the best. The chapter is tense with anticipation as we see Carton methodically setting up his plan.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: The Substance of the Shadow

content.value: # Chapter 10: The Substance of the Shadow

Darnay's second trial begins. The courtroom is even more hostile than before. The mood in Paris has grown darker, and the guillotine claims more victims every day. Darnay faces the tribunal again. The Defarges are present to testify against him. Madame Defarge's cold eyes show no mercy. First, Defarge testifies. He explains that when the Bastille was stormed, he went to Doctor Manette's old cell and searched it. He found a document hidden in the wall—a letter written by Doctor Manette during his imprisonment. Defarge produces this letter and reads it aloud to the court. The letter tells Doctor Manette's terrible story. Years ago, in 1757, Doctor Manette was a young, respected physician in Paris. One night, two aristocratic brothers, the Marquis St. Evrémonde and his brother (Darnay's father and uncle), came to Doctor Manette's home. They forced him at gunpoint to come with them to a house in the countryside. There, Doctor Manette found a young peasant woman who was dying, and her younger brother who was already dead from a sword wound. The woman was barely conscious, screaming in pain and fever. The Marquis's brother had raped her, and when her brother tried to defend her, he was stabbed. The boy died in front of Doctor Manette. The woman told Doctor Manette the whole story before she died: she and her husband were peasants on the Evrémonde estate. The aristocratic brothers took a liking to her and forced her husband to work nearly to death. When her husband died from exhaustion, one of the brothers raped her. Her brother sought revenge for the family's honor, so he was killed. As the woman died, she cursed the entire Evrémonde family and all their descendants. Doctor Manette was horrified by this crime but was afraid to report it because the Evrémondes were so powerful. He did try to contact the authorities discretely, writing to the minister about the crime without naming names directly. However, the Evrémondes discovered this. They used their influence to have Doctor Manette arrested on false charges and thrown into the Bastille. Doctor Manette was imprisoned for eighteen years to keep him silent about the Evrémonde brothers' crimes. He wrote this letter while in prison, documenting the truth and cursing the entire Evrémonde family for destroying his life. The letter ends with Doctor Manette condemning the Evrémondes and all their descendants to face justice for their terrible crimes. When Defarge finishes reading the letter, the courtroom erupts in fury. The revolutionaries are enraged by this story of aristocratic cruelty. They now understand that Charles Darnay is the nephew of the men who committed these crimes and had Doctor Manette imprisoned. Even though Darnay himself is innocent and wasn't even born when these events happened, the revolutionaries believe he must pay for his family's sins. Then Madame Defarge reveals her connection to the story: she is the younger sister of the woman who was raped and killed by the Evrémondes. She was just a young girl when her family was destroyed. Her sister, brother, father (who died of grief), and another brother all died because of the Evrémonde family. She has waited her entire life for revenge. This is why she's been knitting a register of names—she's been marking every member of the Evrémonde family and everyone connected to them for death. The tribunal condemns Charles Darnay to death. He is to be executed within twenty-four hours. The sentence is pronounced because of his family's crimes, even though Darnay renounced his family and tried to live a better life. The revolutionaries believe that aristocratic blood is guilty blood, no matter what. Doctor Manette is devastated. He realizes that his own written testimony has condemned his son-in-law to death. The letter he wrote to document the truth has now destroyed his daughter's husband. It's a terrible irony—Doctor Manette's words have sealed Darnay's fate.
# Chapter 11: Dusk

After the trial, Lucie approaches her father. Doctor Manette is in shock, realizing what he's done. Lucie tries to comfort him, telling him he's not to blame—he couldn't have known when he wrote that letter that his daughter would one day marry an Evrémonde. Doctor Manette is overwhelmed with guilt and grief. Lucie herself is devastated but tries to remain strong. She goes to the prison, hoping to see Darnay one last time before his execution the next day. She's allowed to stand in a certain spot where Darnay can see her from his cell window, just as she did during his long imprisonment. She stays there for hours as evening falls, standing in the growing darkness so her husband knows she hasn't abandoned him. Other family members of condemned prisoners are also there, all desperate to be near their loved ones one last time. The chapter is heartbreaking, showing Lucie's devotion and the family's despair.
# Chapter 12: Darkness

Sydney Carton has been moving through Paris, observing and preparing. He goes to Defarge's wine shop and overhears a conversation between Madame Defarge, The Vengeance, and other revolutionaries. Madame Defarge reveals her complete plan: she's not satisfied with just executing Charles Darnay. She wants revenge on the entire family. She plans to denounce Lucie and little Lucie as well, and even Doctor Manette if necessary. She argues that the wives and children of aristocrats must also be eliminated so that the family line is completely destroyed. The Vengeance and others support her plan. Madame Defarge is consumed by hatred and will not rest until everyone connected to the Evrémonde name is dead. Carton hears all of this and realizes that even if Darnay is executed, Lucie and her child will still be in mortal danger. He returns to Mr. Lorry and tells him that the family must escape Paris immediately after Darnay's execution. They need to leave within hours or they'll all be arrested and killed. Carton gives detailed instructions about having the carriage ready and the travel papers prepared. He tells Mr. Lorry to have everyone ready to leave at a moment's notice. Mr. Lorry is confused but agrees to follow Carton's instructions. Carton goes to a chemist and purchases some drugs—a powerful sedative. He's preparing to execute his plan, though he still hasn't revealed what it is. The chapter ends with darkness falling over Paris, both literally and metaphorically. The situation seems completely hopeless.
# Chapter 13: Fifty-Two

The next morning is the day of Darnay's scheduled execution. Fifty-two people are scheduled to die by guillotine that day, and Darnay is on the list. In his prison cell, Darnay tries to prepare himself for death. He thinks of Lucie and his daughter and tries to find peace with his fate. He knows that his wife and child are provided for financially, at least, and he hopes they'll survive and remember him with love. Suddenly, the door to his cell opens, and Sydney Carton enters. Darnay is surprised to see him. Carton quickly explains that he's come to save him. Before Darnay can react, Carton instructs him to exchange clothes with him. Darnay is confused and resists, but Carton is insistent and forceful. Carton has bribed Barsad to let him into the prison and to look the other way during the exchange. Carton makes Darnay write a letter dictated by him. The letter explains what Carton is doing and why. As Darnay writes, Carton secretly drugs him with the sedative he bought. Within moments, Darnay becomes unconscious. Carton quickly switches their clothes—putting his own clothes on the unconscious Darnay and dressing himself in Darnay's garments. The two men look so similar that with the clothing exchange, they're nearly indistinguishable. Barsad returns and carries the unconscious "Sydney Carton" out of the prison, supposedly because he's too drunk. The prison guards let them pass. In reality, Barsad is carrying Charles Darnay to safety. Meanwhile, the real Sydney Carton remains in the cell, now dressed as Charles Darnay. He will go to the guillotine in Darnay's place. Carton is calm and at peace. For the first time in his wasted life, he's doing something truly meaningful and noble. He's keeping the promise he made to Lucie years ago—that he would give his life to keep her and those she loves safe. The chapter title "Fifty-Two" refers to the number of people scheduled to die that day, and Carton has now made himself one of them.
# Chapter 14: The Knitting Done

While Carton is preparing to sacrifice himself, Madame Defarge prepares to denounce Lucie and her child. She tells The Vengeance and others that she's going to Lucie's lodgings to catch them and accuse them of mourning an enemy of the Republic (which is now considered treason). She plans to have them arrested and executed. Madame Defarge goes to the apartment where Lucie has been staying. However, Lucie, Doctor Manette, little Lucie, and Mr. Lorry have already left, following Carton's instructions. The only person still there is Miss Pross, who has stayed behind to make it look like the apartment is still occupied, giving the family extra time to escape. When Madame Defarge bursts into the apartment demanding to know where everyone is, she finds only Miss Pross. Miss Pross, though terrified, refuses to let Madame Defarge past. She doesn't speak French well, and Madame Defarge doesn't speak English, so they can barely communicate. But Miss Pross understands that this woman wants to harm Lucie, and she won't allow it. The two women face each other—Miss Pross with her fierce devotion to Lucie, and Madame Defarge with her cold hatred and her pistol. They struggle violently. In the fight, Madame Defarge's gun goes off, and Madame Defarge is killed by her own weapon. Miss Pross is unharmed physically, though the sound of the gunshot so close to her head has deafened her permanently. She leaves quickly and meets Jerry Cruncher, who has been helping with the escape preparations. They rush to join Mr. Lorry and the others. Madame Defarge's death means that the main threat to Lucie's family is gone. The knitting is done—Madame Defarge will never add another name to her register of death. Miss Pross's courage has saved the family.

chapters.title: Chapter 15: The Footsteps Die Out Forever

content.value: # Chapter 15: The Footsteps Die Out Forever

This is the final chapter, and it describes the conclusion of Sydney Carton's sacrifice. Carton is taken from the prison with the other condemned prisoners. There are fifty-two people scheduled to die by guillotine that day. As Carton waits in the cart taking them to the execution site, he notices a young seamstress who was also condemned. She recognizes that Carton isn't actually Charles Darnay but someone who has taken his place. She sees the nobility in what he's doing and is comforted by his presence. She asks if she can hold his hand as they go to their deaths, and Carton agrees. He provides her with courage and peace in her final moments. As the cart moves through the streets of Paris toward the guillotine, Carton is calm and serene. He's at peace with his choice. He knows that his death has meaning—he's saving Charles Darnay, giving Lucie back her husband, and allowing their child to grow up with her father. For a man whose life seemed wasted and meaningless, this final act gives everything purpose. Meanwhile, the family has escaped Paris. The unconscious Darnay was carried out of the city with forged papers identifying him as Sydney Carton. Lucie, her daughter, Doctor Manette, and Mr. Lorry are all safely away. When Darnay wakes up, he'll discover what Carton has done for him and his family. At the guillotine, the executions proceed. One by one, the condemned are beheaded. The crowd watches as they always do, treating it as entertainment. When Carton's turn comes, he goes to his death with courage and dignity. The young seamstress goes before him, and he comforts her until the end. Then Carton approaches the guillotine. In his final moments, Carton has prophetic thoughts about the future. Though the novel doesn't explicitly state he speaks these words aloud, Dickens tells us what Carton is thinking: He envisions a better future where this terrible violence ends and France finds peace again. He sees the revolutionaries who are now committing atrocities eventually dying by the same guillotine they're using on others. He imagines Lucie and Darnay living happily in England, having a son whom they'll name Sydney in his honor. He sees this future son becoming a respected man who honors Carton's memory. He envisions himself remembered with love by the family he saved. Carton's final thought is this: "It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done; it is a far, far better rest that I go to than I have ever known." With these words echoing in his mind, Sydney Carton dies on the guillotine.

His sacrifice is complete. Through his death, Carton has achieved the redemption he sought throughout the novel. The wastrel who saw no value in his own life has given it meaning through the ultimate act of love and selflessness. He has saved not just Charles Darnay, but preserved a family and ensured that love triumphs over hatred.

The chapter—and the novel—ends with Carton's prophetic vision fulfilled in spirit: his death becomes the foundation for new life and hope. His final words become some of the most famous in English literature, expressing the Christian ideal of sacrificial love and the possibility of redemption even for those who seem beyond saving. In dying, Sydney Carton finally lives up to his highest potential, transforming from a man who wasted his talents into someone whose sacrifice echoes through generations.

The title "The Footsteps Die Out Forever" refers both literally to Carton's final walk to the guillotine and metaphorically to the end of his tortured existence, replaced by eternal peace and remembrance.
Short Hindi Summary
पुस्तक प्रथम: जीवन में वापसी
प्रारंभिक परिचय

उपन्यास 1775 में शुरू होता है, जब इंग्लैंड और फ्रांस दोनों ही देशों में विरोधाभास भरा समय था। प्रसिद्ध पंक्ति से शुरुआत होती है: "यह सबसे अच्छा समय था, यह सबसे बुरा समय था।" फ्रांस में आम लोग भुखमरी से जूझ रहे थे जबकि अमीर कुलीन वर्ग विलासिता में जी रहा था। क्रांति की आहट सुनाई देने लगी थी।
डॉक्टर मैनेट की मुक्ति

एक कोहरे भरी रात में, जार्विस लॉरी नामक बैंकर को एक रहस्यमय संदेश मिलता है: "जीवन में वापस बुलाया गया।" वह डोवर में मिस लूसी मैनेट से मिलते हैं, एक सुंदर सत्रह वर्षीय युवती। लॉरी उसे बताते हैं कि उसके पिता, डॉक्टर अलेक्जेंड्रे मैनेट, जिन्हें वह मृत समझती थी, वास्तव में अठारह वर्षों तक बास्तील जेल में कैद रहने के बाद जीवित पाए गए हैं।

लूसी और लॉरी पेरिस जाते हैं, जहां वे डिफार्ज की शराब की दुकान पहुंचते हैं। डिफार्ज, जो डॉक्टर मैनेट का पूर्व नौकर था, उन्हें एक अंधेरे कमरे में ले जाता है। वहां डॉक्टर मैनेट जूते बनाते हुए मिलते हैं - एक व्यवसाय जो उन्होंने कारावास में सीखा था। उनका दिमाग टूट चुका है, वे केवल अपनी सेल संख्या "105, उत्तर टॉवर" से खुद को पहचानते हैं।

जब लूसी अपने पिता के पास जाती है, तो उनके सुनहरे बाल उनमें एक धुंधली याद जगाते हैं। धीरे-धीरे उन्हें एहसास होता है कि यह उनकी बेटी है। भावुक मिलन के बाद, लूसी और लॉरी टूटे हुए डॉक्टर को इंग्लैंड वापस ले जाते हैं।
पुस्तक द्वितीय: सुनहरा धागा
लंदन में, टेल्सन बैंक में जेरी क्रंचर काम करता है। डॉक्टर मैनेट ने लूसी के प्यार और देखभाल से काफी हद तक ठीक हो गए हैं, हालांकि तनाव में वे कभी-कभी फिर से जूते बनाने लगते हैं।
चार्ल्स डार्ने का मुकदमा

ओल्ड बेली अदालत में चार्ल्स डार्ने पर देशद्रोह का मुकदमा चलता है। उन पर फ्रांस के लिए जासूसी करने का आरोप है। लूसी और डॉक्टर मैनेट अदालत में मौजूद हैं। जब सब कुछ निराशाजनक लगता है, तब वकील का सहायक सिडनी कार्टन एक शानदार अवलोकन करता है - वह और डार्ने एक जैसे दिखते हैं! यह साबित करता है कि गवाहों ने गलती से पहचाना होगा। डार्ने बरी हो जाता है।
कार्टन और डार्ने

सिडनी कार्टन एक प्रतिभाशाली लेकिन आत्म-विनाशकारी व्यक्ति है जो वकील स्ट्राइवर के लिए काम करता है। वह शराब पीता है और अपनी प्रतिभा बर्बाद करता है। डार्ने को देखकर वह उदास हो जाता है क्योंकि डार्ने वह सब कुछ है जो कार्टन हो सकता था लेकिन नहीं बन पाया।
लूसी का घर
डॉक्टर मैनेट और लूसी सोहो में रहते हैं। मिस प्रॉस, लूसी की समर्पित सेविका, उनके साथ रहती है। चार्ल्स डार्ने और सिडनी कार्टन दोनों अक्सर आते हैं, और दोनों को लूसी से प्यार है।
एक दिन, कार्टन लूसी से कहता है कि वह उससे प्यार करता है लेकिन जानता है कि वह उसके लायक नहीं है। वह वादा करता है कि वह और उसके प्रियजनों को सुरक्षित रखने के लिए अपनी जान दे देगा।
फ्रांस में क्रूरता

फ्रांस में, मार्क्विस सेंट एव्रेमोंडे (डार्ने का चाचा) एक क्रूर कुलीन है। उसकी गाड़ी एक बच्चे को कुचल देती है। पिता गैसपार्ड तबाह हो जाता है, लेकिन मार्क्विस बेरहमी से एक सोने का सिक्का फेंक देता है। उस रात, गैसपार्ड मार्क्विस को मार देता है।
चार्ल्स डार्ने (जिसका असली नाम चार्ल्स सेंट एव्रेमोंडे है) अपने चाचे से मिलने आता है। वह अपने परिवार के क्रूर व्यवहार से घृणा करता है और अपनी विरासत त्याग देता है।
विवाह

डार्ने, डॉक्टर मैनेट से लूसी से शादी करने की अनुमति मांगता है। डॉक्टर सहमत हो जाते हैं लेकिन शर्त रखते हैं कि डार्ने शादी की सुबह तक अपना असली नाम न बताए। शादी के बाद, डॉक्टर मैनेट नौ दिनों तक फिर से जूते बनाने लगते हैं - उनका दिमाग फिर से टूट गया है।
लूसी और डार्ने खुशी से रहते हैं और उनकी एक बेटी होती है।
क्रांति की शुरुआत

1789 में, फ्रांसीसी क्रांति शुरू होती है। बास्तील जेल पर हमला होता है। डिफार्ज डॉक्टर मैनेट की पुरानी सेल में जाता है और दीवार में छिपा एक पत्र ढूंढता है। हिंसा पूरे फ्रांस में फैल जाती है, और मैडम डिफार्ज अपनी बुनाई में मौत के लिए नाम जोड़ती रहती है।
फ्रांस के लिए जाल

1792 में, डार्ने को गैबेल नामक कर संग्रहकर्ता से एक पत्र मिलता है जो फ्रांस में जेल में है और मदद मांग रहा है। डार्ने, अपनी जिम्मेदारी महसूस करते हुए, गुप्त रूप से फ्रांस जाने का फैसला करता है। लेकिन पहुंचते ही उसे एक प्रवासी कुलीन के रूप में गिरफ्तार कर लिया जाता है और ला फोर्स जेल में डाल दिया जाता है।
पुस्तक तृतीय: तूफान का मार्ग
जेल में

डार्ने पंद्रह महीने तक बिना मुकदमे के जेल में रहता है। लूसी, डॉक्टर मैनेट और मिस प्रॉस पेरिस पहुंचते हैं। डॉक्टर मैनेट, एक पूर्व बास्तील कैदी के रूप में, क्रांतिकारियों में सम्मानित हैं। वे अपने प्रभाव का उपयोग डार्ने की मदद करने के लिए करते हैं।
लूसी हर दिन उस स्थान पर खड़ी होती है जहां से डार्ने जेल की खिड़की से उसे देख सकता है। मैडम डिफार्ज लूसी को देखने आती है और उसे ध्यान से याद करती है।
पहला मुकदमा - बरी
आखिरकार डार्ने का मुकदमा होता है। डॉक्टर मैनेट गवाही देते हैं कि डार्ने ने अपनी कुलीन उपाधि त्याग दी थी और ईमानदारी से जीवन जिया था। डार्ने बरी हो जाता है और परिवार राहत की सांस लेता है।
दूसरी गिरफ्तारी
लेकिन कुछ घंटों बाद ही, डार्ने को फिर से गिरफ्तार कर लिया जाता है। इस बार डिफार्ज दंपत्ति ने उस पर आरोप लगाया है।
कार्टन की योजना
सिडनी कार्टन पेरिस पहुंचता है। वह जॉन बारसाड को ढूंढता है, जो एक जासूस है और जेलों में काम करता है। कार्टन उसे ब्लैकमेल करता है और उससे मदद का वादा करवाता है।
डॉक्टर मैनेट का पत्र
डार्ने के दूसरे मुकदमे में, डिफार्ज वह पत्र पढ़ता है जो डॉक्टर मैनेट ने जेल में लिखा था। पत्र में एक भयानक कहानी है:

1757 में, दो एव्रेमोंडे भाई (डार्ने के पिता और चाचा) ने एक युवा किसान महिला के साथ बलात्कार किया। जब उसके भाई ने उसका बचाव करने की कोशिश की, तो उसे तलवार से मार दिया गया। डॉक्टर मैनेट को घटनास्थल पर बुलाया गया, लेकिन जब उन्होंने चुपचाप अधिकारियों से संपर्क करने की कोशिश की, तो एव्रेमोंडे भाइयों ने उन्हें अठारह साल के लिए बास्तील में बंद करवा दिया।
मैडम डिफार्ज प्रकट करती है कि वह उस मारी गई महिला की छोटी बहन है। उसका पूरा परिवार एव्रेमोंडे परिवार के कारण नष्ट हो गया था। वह पूरे जीवन बदला लेने की प्रतीक्षा कर रही थी।
डार्ने को मौत की सजा सुनाई जाती है। डॉक्टर मैनेट तबाह हो जाते हैं - उनके अपने शब्दों ने उनके दामाद को मौत की सजा दिला दी है।
कार्टन का बलिदान
कार्टन की योजना पूरी हो चुकी है। मैडम डिफार्ज लूसी और उसकी बेटी को भी मारने की योजना बना रही है, इसलिए परिवार को तुरंत भागना होगा।

कार्टन बारसाड की मदद से जेल में प्रवेश करता है। वह डार्ने को बेहोश कर देता है और उसके साथ कपड़े बदल लेता है। बारसाड बेहोश डार्ने को बाहर ले जाता है, जबकि कार्टन जेल में रहता है, डार्ने के कपड़े पहनकर।
मैडम डिफार्ज लूसी के घर जाती है, लेकिन वहां केवल मिस प्रॉस है। दोनों महिलाओं के बीच संघर्ष होता है, और मैडम डिफार्ज अपनी ही बंदूक से मारी जाती है। परिवार सुरक्षित रूप से पेरिस से भाग जाता है।
अंतिम बलिदान

अगले दिन, कार्टन को अन्य कैदियों के साथ गिलोटिन ले जाया जाता है। एक युवा सीमस्ट्रेस उसके साथ है, जो उसकी बहादुरी से सांत्वना पाती है। कार्टन शांत और शांतिपूर्ण है। वह जानता है कि उसकी मृत्यु का अर्थ है - वह डार्ने को बचा रहा है, लूसी को उसका पति वापस दे रहा है, और उनकी बेटी को पिता के साथ बड़ा होने का मौका दे रहा है।
जैसे ही वह गिलोटिन की ओर बढ़ता है, कार्टन भविष्य की कल्पना करता है। वह देखता है कि लूसी और डार्ने खुशी से इंग्लैंड में रह रहे हैं, एक बेटा है जिसका नाम सिडनी है, जो उसकी याद में रखा गया है।
उसके अंतिम विचार हैं: "यह एक बहुत, बहुत बेहतर काम है जो मैं करता हूं, जितना मैंने कभी किया है; यह एक बहुत, बहुत बेहतर आराम है जिसमें मैं जाता हूं, जितना मैंने कभी जाना है।"

सिडनी कार्टन की मृत्यु हो जाती है, लेकिन उसका बलिदान पूर्ण है। एक बर्बाद जीवन जीने वाले व्यक्ति ने अंततः प्रेम और निस्वार्थता के सर्वोच्च कार्य के माध्यम से अपने जीवन को अर्थ दिया। मरकर, सिडनी कार्टन अंततः अपनी सर्वोच्च क्षमता तक पहुंच गया, एक ऐसे व्यक्ति से जो अपनी प्रतिभा बर्बाद कर रहा था, किसी ऐसे व्यक्ति में बदल गया जिसका बलिदान पीढ़ियों तक गूंजता है।
Major Themes
Resurrection and Rebirth - Dr. Manette recalled to life, Carton's spiritual rebirth through sacrifice
Sacrifice and Redemption - Carton's ultimate sacrifice redeems his wasted life
Duality and Doubles - Two cities, Carton/Darnay resemblance, opposing forces
Social Injustice and Revolution - Causes and consequences of French Revolution
Revenge vs. Mercy - Madame Defarge's vendetta vs. Lucie's compassion
Fate and Destiny - Echoing footsteps, knitting as recording fate
Love and Loyalty - Multiple forms of love drive characters' actions
Imprisonment and Freedom - Physical and psychological imprisonment
