# Chapter 28: Malgudi Days
Author Facts
R.K. Narayan (1906-2001)
Full name: Rasipuram Krishnaswami Iyer Narayanaswami
Born: October 10, 1906, in Madras (now Chennai), India
Died: May 13, 2001, in Chennai, India (aged 94)
Education: Bachelor’s degree from Maharaja College of Mysore
Family: Married Rajam in 1933, who died of typhoid in 1939; they had one daughter, Hema
Notable awards: Padma Bhushan (1964), Padma Vibhushan (2000), AC Benson Medal from the Royal Society of Literature (1980)
Nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature multiple times
First Indian writer to receive widespread recognition in the West
Career: Initially worked as a journalist before becoming a full-time writer

Notable works: “Swami and Friends” (1935), “The Bachelor of Arts” (1937), “The English Teacher” (1945), “The Financial Expert” (1952), “The Guide” (1958), “The Man-Eater of Malgudi” (1961), “The Vendor of Sweets” (1967)
Literary style: Simple language, gentle humor, irony, and focus on ordinary middle-class life
Close friendship with Graham Greene, who helped get his first novel published
The fictional town of Malgudi serves as the setting for most of his works
Publication Details
“Malgudi Days” first published in 1943 by Indian Thought Publications
Expanded edition published in 1982 by Viking Press, including stories from “An Astrologer’s Day and Other Stories” (1947) and “Lawley Road and Other Stories” (1956)
Subsequently translated into numerous languages
Some stories originally appeared in The Hindu newspaper
The 1982 edition contains 32 stories
Illustrated by Narayan’s younger brother R.K. Laxman, a famous cartoonist
Adapted into a television series by Kannada director Shankar Nag in 1986
Genre: Short story collection
Setting: The fictional South Indian town of Malgudi
Genre Classification
Form: Short story collection
Characteristics: Realistic fiction, slice-of-life narratives, gentle social satire
Style: Simple, direct prose with subtle humor and irony
Tradition: Follows the tradition of regional realism while incorporating Indian sensibilities
Innovation: Creation of a fictional yet believable small-town Indian setting (Malgudi)
Purpose: To depict ordinary life in post-colonial small-town India
Approach: Character-centered, focusing on human foibles, aspirations, and struggles
Main Idea

“Malgudi Days” presents a kaleidoscopic view of life in a fictional South Indian town through interconnected short stories that capture the everyday experiences, struggles, aspirations, and peculiarities of its diverse inhabitants. Through these seemingly simple tales, Narayan explores universal themes of human nature while providing an authentic portrayal of mid-20th century small-town Indian life during and after colonial rule.
Summary

“Malgudi Days” is a collection of short stories set in the fictional town of Malgudi, a microcosm of traditional Indian society undergoing gradual modernization. Each story focuses on different characters from various walks of life—astrologers, beggars, businessmen, schoolchildren, teachers, and artists—capturing their dreams, disappointments, and daily routines.

The stories are characterized by Narayan’s gentle humor, keen observation of human behavior, and compassionate portrayal of ordinary people. They often follow a simple pattern: a character faces a problem or situation, attempts to resolve it (sometimes through deception or self-deception), and reaches either a resolution or a moment of self-realization. The conflicts are rarely dramatic but reveal deeper aspects of human nature and social dynamics.

Throughout the collection, Malgudi emerges as a character itself—a town with its own rhythms, landmarks, and social hierarchies. It serves as a backdrop that is both distinctly Indian and universally relatable, allowing Narayan to explore tensions between tradition and modernity, reality and imagination, individual desires and social expectations.

Though the stories were written during and after India’s struggle for independence, explicit political themes are largely absent. Instead, Narayan focuses on how ordinary people navigate their daily lives, portraying a society in transition with sympathy and understated humor.
Story Summaries
1\. An Astrologer's Day

A man works as an astrologer even though he knows nothing about stars or predictions. He got this job after running away from his village for unknown reasons. People believe his predictions because of his practice and clever guessing. One day, a customer bets money that the astrologer cannot tell him anything true. The astrologer resists until he recognizes the man as Guru Nayak. He then reveals that the man was once stabbed and left for dead in a well. The impressed customer pays (though not the full amount) and the astrologer warns him never to return to this area. That night, the astrologer confesses to his wife that he was the one who tried to kill this man years ago.
2\. The Missing Mail

Thanappa is a postman who talks to everyone on his delivery route. He has known Ramanujam since before his daughter was born, and now she is getting married. After the last marriage proposal fails, Thanappa suggests a groom from a faraway town. The wedding must happen on May 20th or it will be delayed three years due to the groom's training schedule. After the wedding is successfully completed, Thanappa reveals he had received a postcard on May 20th about the death of Ramanujam's relative. He hid the letter to avoid disrupting the wedding, even though this could cost him his job. Ramanujam says he will not file a complaint against him.
3\. The Doctor's Word

Dr. Raman is a physician known for his blunt honesty and is only called for serious life-and-death situations. He believes pleasant lies cannot save lives. Suddenly his best friend Gopal falls terribly ill. After examining him, the doctor privately thinks Gopal has only 1 in 1000 chances of surviving, and his condition will worsen if he exerts himself. Gopal begs the doctor to tell him if he will make it, as he needs to sign his will immediately if not. Dr. Raman cannot bear to tell his friend the truth, but also cannot let him strain himself. He tells Gopal he will be fine. The next morning, Gopal's health has miraculously recovered, leaving the doctor puzzled for the rest of his life.
4\. Gateman's Gift

Govind Singh worked as a gatekeeper and security guard for 25 years. He only spoke to the General Manager twice and came to see him as god-like. After retiring, he takes up making miniature clay models and dioramas. Each time he collects his pension, he gives his clay work to the company accountant, always asking what the GM thought of the last one. The accountant always says the GM liked it. One day, a registered letter from the GM arrives. Singh is too afraid to open it, thinking it contains something horrible. He even goes to an X-ray technician to see inside without opening it. He acts like a madman around town until the accountant opens the letter for him. The GM had thanked him, sent a large check, and hoped to see more work. Strangely, Singh gives up his clay hobby, saying it is no work for a sane man.
5\. The Blind Dog

A stray dog befriends a blind beggar. When the old woman caring for the blind man dies, he puts a leash on the dog and uses him to beg while walking the streets. The blind man discovers he makes much more money this way and becomes greedy. He constantly kicks and beats the dog to keep working. When market sellers learn the blind man is so rich he's lending money, they cut the leash with scissors and the dog runs away. After a few weeks of not seeing them, the sellers see them again - but now the dog's leash is a metal chain. The blind man says his dog came back to him one night on his own. The sellers pity the loyal dog.
6\. Fellow-Feeling

Rajam Iyer, a Tamil Brahmin, is traveling on an express train. Another passenger gets on and starts verbally abusing a third passenger. Rajam gets involved and the bully complains that Brahmins are secretly eating meat and driving prices up. The argument escalates until they stand to fight. Rajam stops short of the first blow and bluffs, threatening to rearrange the bully's face so his mouth is under his left ear. As he is about to strike again, the bully sees they are at a station stop and leaps out the window, claiming this is his stop. Rajam lies to other passengers saying the bully got back on in a different compartment, but they don't believe him.
7\. The Tiger's Claw

The Talkative Man tells a story to some children after hunters bring a dead tiger into town. He claims that when he was a fertilizer salesman, he stayed overnight in a tiny village train station. He left the door cracked because it was too hot. A tiger barged in and woke him in the middle of the night. He barricaded himself behind furniture so the tiger could only reach in one paw. He used his knife to cut off three toes before the tiger retreated. Back in town, the children ask to see the tiger's paw - sure enough, three toes are missing. However, the hunters explain that tribesmen like to take tiger cubs and cut off three toes as good luck charms, suggesting the story may not be true.
8\. Iswaran

Iswaran failed his intermediate college exams nine years in a row. After taking the exams a tenth time, the day scores are reported arrives. Instead of checking his scores, Iswaran goes to the cinema. When other boys come celebrating their success, Iswaran becomes self-loathing and is sure he failed again. He decides to drown himself in the river and writes a suicide note, leaving it in his jacket on the shore. But wanting to know for sure, he checks his score. He not only passed but got second-class honors! In his excitement, he leaps into the river to celebrate. His body and suicide note are discovered the next day, making it look like suicide.
9\. Such Perfection

A sculptor finishes a statue of the god Nataraja after five years of labor. Everyone says it is so perfect that if people saw it, the glory of the god would consume them. The priest asks the sculptor to break off the statue's little toe so it will be safe to view, but the sculptor refuses. The priest then refuses to consecrate it in the temple. The sculptor turns his house into a temple to have it consecrated there. The god then comes to life and creates natural disasters - earthquakes, floods, and storms that kill many people. People beg the sculptor to mar the statue's perfection, but he won't. He runs to the overflowed lake to drown himself as an offering, but on the way, a tree falls on his house. He returns to find the statue unharmed except for a severed little toe. The now-imperfect statue is consecrated at the temple, and the sculptor gives up his trade forever.
10\. Father's Help

Swami oversleeps on Monday and convinces his mother to let him stay home from school. His father insists he go with his "headache," so Swami lies and says his teacher Samuel beats children severely for being late or any small offense. His father writes a letter for Swami to deliver to the headmaster that will surely get Samuel fired, maybe even imprisoned. At school, Swami provokes Samuel to do something deserving of dismissal, but Samuel only canes his hands lightly, which Swami doesn't even react to. When he tries to deliver the letter, the headmaster is on leave all week. The assistant headmaster could accept it, but it's Samuel himself! Swami runs home without delivering the letter. His father thinks he was lying about the headmaster being on leave and says he deserves Samuel as his teacher.
11\. The Snake-Song

The Talkative Man leaves a concert looking tortured while others enjoyed it. He says taste has declined and tells his story. He studied the bamboo flute with a master musician. One night, a beggar interrupts his practice and asks for food. The Talkative Man refuses the beggar even the right to come in and listen. The beggar curses him, saying this was his last day of music. Later that night, a massive cobra comes and listens to him play. It gets agitated when he stops or plays anything other than the snake-song. After playing the same song all night to keep the snake calm, he throws himself down and begs the snake to spare him. When he looks up, it is gone. The Talkative Man says he gave up his flute, but if he could find the beggar and ask forgiveness, he would take up his flute again.
12\. Engine Trouble

The Talkative Man wins a road engine (steam-powered tractor) at a carnival. Not knowing how to drive or power it, he simply leaves it in the park. The city starts fining him for the parking space at more than double his home rent. He arranges to move it, but it crashes into a wall instead, and he must pay for damages. A swami comes to town performing stunts like eating glass and burying himself alive. The swami asks for a road engine for his assistant to run over his chest, but the magistrate refuses. After a massive earthquake, the road engine lodges in a well owned by the same man whose wall was destroyed. The man thanks the Talkative Man because the city was going to fine him for dirty water if the well wasn't sealed. Of course, you can't see the engine in the well anymore as it's now sealed with concrete.
13\. Forty-Five a Month

Shanta, a primary school student, is eager to go home early because her father Venkat Rao promised to take her to the cinema. At home, she gets dressed and waits for him. When he doesn't come, she tries to find his office but gets lost. Meanwhile, Venkat Rao feels guilty that he works until after his daughter goes to bed seven days a week. That afternoon, he asks his boss for personal leave or else he resigns. His boss tells him nothing is more urgent than work. Fed up with being bought for forty rupees a month, Venkat Rao writes a resignation letter. His boss then tells him he got a raise to forty-five rupees a month, so he tears up his letter. When he finally gets home, his daughter is already asleep. He tells his wife he can't take Shanta out at all since he got a raise - meaning he'll work even more now.
14\. Out of Business

Rama Rao loses his gramophone business when the only factory in the region closes down. He looks for local jobs with no success. The family lays off servants and rents out their house to live in a smaller place. With no job prospects, Rama Rao enters a magazine crossword contest where everyone who gets every answer right wins 4000 rupees. After seeing how badly he lost, he lies down on train tracks to die. After waiting too long, he finds a crowd at the station and hears that a derailment has delayed all trains three more hours. Recognizing his good fortune at being saved, he goes home. His wife tells him the renters want to buy their house. He is excited to sell for 4500 rupees and will use some of the money to go to Madras and get a job there.
15\. Attila

After the neighborhood experiences break-ins, a family buys a dog for security and names him Attila after the "Scourge of Europe." He is friendly with everyone and doesn't stop thieves from taking garden flowers, so the family keeps him inside at night. One night, a thief named Ranga breaks in to steal jewels. Attila is so excited to meet this new friend that he follows Ranga into the open street. The family assumes the dog was stolen too, but they see Attila run after him. Ranga gets scared and runs but trips over the dog, spilling the stolen jewels. The police arrest Ranga, and Attila is praised for being a master detective, even though he was just being friendly.
16\. The Axe

An astrologer predicted Velan would live in a three-story house. Velan came from the poorest family in his village. At age 18, his father slapped his face in public and he left home. After days of walking and begging, he got a job as a gardener for an old man. The plot was large and they built a three-story mansion on it, but Velan lived in his hut on the grounds. He gripped a young margosa tree's stem and told it to grow big and worthy of the house or he would pluck it out. It grew magnificently, and his master's great-grandchildren played under it with hundreds of birds in its branches. After his master dies, the house trades hands among family until it looks haunted and only Velan lives there. Years later, a man arrives saying the plot has been bought and will be cleared for small housing. One morning, Velan wakes to the sound of men chopping down the margosa tree with axes. He begs them to stop until he has gathered his belongings and gone out of earshot.
17\. Lawley Road

After India's independence, there is a surge of patriotism. The municipality renames streets from English to Indian names. There is a statue of Sir Frederick Lawley in town, and when the street bearing his name is changed, the municipality votes to remove the statue. People research Lawley and believe he was a British tyrant. When the city cannot find anyone to remove it within budget, the Talkative Man takes it for himself and lodges it halfway inside his house with great difficulty. When he writes in the news about getting the statue, historical societies across India are outraged. There were two Sir Lawleys, and this statue celebrated a kind man who founded Malgudi and even died saving Indians. The public protests the removal. An election is coming, and if the statue isn't returned, the whole council will be voted out. The Chairman of Malgudi buys the Talkative Man's house with his private fund to solve the problem.
18\. Trail of the Green Blazer

Ranga is a small-time pickpocket in Malgudi who makes a living by blending into busy marketplaces and stealing from unsuspecting people. One day, he spots a well-dressed man wearing a green blazer. Ranga carefully follows him, pretending to be an ordinary passerby. When the man stops to buy something, Ranga slips his hand into the pocket and grabs a wallet. But the man suddenly realizes what is happening and grabs Ranga's wrist. In the chaos, a crowd gathers. Ranga tries to wriggle free by pretending innocence, but guilt is written on his face. The story highlights how greed and human weakness can cause a moment's miscalculation to undo years of stealth and careful work.
19\. The Martyr's Corner

Ramu is a poor man in Malgudi who earns a living by selling snacks in the busy market square. His tiny makeshift stall consists of only a few items but attracts steady customers every evening. For Ramu, this modest trade is his entire world and only means of survival. One day, a political rally and protest break out near his corner. The situation turns violent and the crowd clashes with police. In the chaos, Ramu's stall is overturned and destroyed. His livelihood is wiped out in a single moment. Later, the very spot where he once worked becomes known as "Martyr's Corner," a symbolic site for political memory. Ironically, while the world sees it as a place of patriotic sacrifice, for Ramu it is a painful reminder of his personal tragedy and ruined life.
20\. Wife's Holiday

A man feels restless after his wife goes to her parents' house for a short visit. At first, he looks forward to his freedom, believing he can relax without her watchful eye. He spends time enjoying food outside, meeting friends, and indulging in little pleasures. However, he soon realizes her absence creates a deep void. The house feels empty and joyless, and he begins to miss her constant care and companionship. His routine becomes chaotic with no one to cook, manage the household, or share conversations. What started as excitement for a "holiday" quickly turns into loneliness and regret. The story captures the emotional bond in marriage where partners often fail to appreciate each other until they are apart - the very things we take for granted are what we miss most when gone.
21\. A Shadow

Sambu, a young boy, longs to see his deceased father on the cinema screen. His father had acted in a film before his death, and now it is being shown in town. While Sambu is excited, his mother is horrified and reluctant, as watching the film would reopen her grief. Despite her resistance, Sambu eagerly attends the show and is deeply moved to see his father alive again - singing, walking, and talking. For him, the film brings back cherished memories and he feels his father has returned. However, the mother finds the experience unbearable, breaking down when a scene reminds her of their personal life. For her, the film is a painful shadow of loss. The story portrays how memories of the dead affect people differently - Sambu's innocence and longing versus his mother's sorrow.
22\. A Willing Slave

Ayah, a devoted servant, works tirelessly in a household, giving complete loyalty and affection to her employers and their children. She treats the children as if they were her own, serving them with love, care, and patience. Over time, her identity becomes tied entirely to her role in the family, leaving her with no life of her own. However, when the children grow up, she becomes unnecessary. The family that once relied on her slowly detaches, leaving her with nothing to cling to. Even when she realizes she is no longer wanted, Ayah remains loyal, unable to separate her existence from the family's needs. The story highlights the thankless sacrifices of domestic workers who dedicate their lives selflessly yet are left without recognition or security in old age. It reflects on love, loyalty, and the cruel irony of devotion that binds someone to servitude until they lose themselves completely.
23\. Leela's Friend

Sidda, a poor man, finds work as a servant in a wealthy family's household. He quickly forms a deep bond with their young daughter Leela, who adores him. Sidda spends hours playing with her, telling imaginative stories, and caring for her with patience and kindness. To Leela, Sidda is not just a servant but a trusted friend and companion. However, when a gold chain goes missing, suspicion falls on Sidda simply because of his lower status. The police arrest him and the family, without proof, assumes his guilt. Later, the chain is found elsewhere, proving Sidda's innocence. Yet by then, his reputation and dignity are destroyed. Leela, too young to understand the injustice, simply longs for her friend's return. The story exposes harsh realities of class discrimination and blind prejudices faced by the poor, even when they show love and loyalty.
24\. Mother and Son

This story explores the relationship between an overprotective mother and her grown-up son, caught between his own desires and his mother's controlling nature. The mother, widowed and insecure, constantly interferes in her son's decisions, believing she knows what is best. She dictates everything from his marriage choices to his career. The son, though dutiful, feels suffocated by her dominance and longs for independence. At the same time, he is bound by guilt and responsibility, unable to rebel openly. This constant struggle creates tension in the household, with both mother and son locked in emotional dependence. The story presents the irony of parental love that transforms into possessiveness, depriving children of freedom while keeping parents anxious and unfulfilled. It highlights the universal theme of individuality versus duty within families, showing how excessive control can erode both affection and peace.
25\. Naga

This story revolves around a snake charmer and his beloved pet cobra Naga, who is not just an animal but his livelihood. The man earns a living by showing tricks with Naga, moving from place to place performing in front of crowds. He treats the snake with affection, feeding and caring for it like a family member. However, times change and fewer people are interested in watching such shows. The man's earnings decline sharply, leaving him struggling to survive. Despite his hardships, he refuses to part with Naga as their bond is deeper than money. Finally, faced with starvation, he reluctantly considers letting the snake go, but his heart cannot bear the separation. The story reflects themes of poverty, love for animals, and the struggle of traditional professions against modernization. It shows how survival can clash with sentiment, leaving the poor torn between livelihood and emotional attachment.
26\. Selvi

Selvi is a talented young woman with a mesmerizing voice who rises to fame as a singer. She comes from a humble background but is discovered by Mohan, a theater owner, who quickly becomes both her manager and husband. Under his strict control, Selvi's life changes drastically. Mohan exploits her talent, using her for wealth and status, while Selvi remains obedient, living entirely under his shadow. Despite her fame and success, she is unhappy as she has no freedom over her own choices or career. Her art becomes more of a business than an expression of passion. As time passes, Selvi begins to realize she is trapped in an unequal marriage where love has been replaced by control and manipulation. The story highlights the exploitation of women and artists, showing how talent can be commodified when power and authority overshadow personal happiness and dignity.
27\. Second Opinion

A young man is focused on his studies when his mother asks him to marry a family friend's daughter. He finds this request irritating and rejects her efforts. However, he discovers that his mother has actually been very ill for a long time and reassesses the reason for her wanting him to get married. Feeling guilty that she might be dying, he tells her he will consider her request to make her happy. But after getting a second medical opinion, he learns that she is not dying at all. He grows distraught about his hasty decision to consider marriage, realizing he agreed under false assumptions. The story portrays the anxiety and confusion that comes from conflicting medical advice and how guilt can make people make decisions they don't truly want.
28\. Cat Within

A shopkeeper is troubled by what he believes is a demonic cat in his store that won't leave. He calls an exorcist to help get rid of it. Instead of just removing the cat, the exorcist makes the shopkeeper confess all the wrong things he has done - cheating customers, being dishonest, and other sins. After the shopkeeper admits his wrongdoings and feels genuine remorse, the cat mysteriously leaves. The story is both humorous and symbolic, showing that the cat represented the shopkeeper's guilty conscience. It illustrates how human imagination and superstition often magnify small issues into larger troubles, and how inner guilt can manifest as external problems. Only by confronting and admitting his wrongs can the shopkeeper find peace.
29\. The Edge

Ranga is a knife-grinder who lives a simple life sharpening knives and scissors in Malgudi. Though his profession is humble and outdated, he takes pride in his work. However, times are changing and fewer people require his services, leaving him struggling for survival. Ranga's dreams for his daughter - to study and have a better life - clash with his wife's traditional desire for her to marry early. The story also shows constant quarreling between Ranga and his wife who is always scolding their daughters. Desperate for money, Ranga becomes involved in a risky scheme hoping to secure his family's future. He ends up sleeping in a field and being arrested. When he realizes he's about to be forcibly sterilized, he flees in terror. The story highlights dignity in labor, struggles of the working class, and how desperate circumstances can lead people into dangerous situations.
30\. God and the Cobbler

A foreign hippie and an Indian cobbler meet in Malgudi and have a philosophical conversation. The hippie, having renounced wealth and modern life, wanders freely, while the cobbler toils daily in poverty. Each man idealizes the other - the hippie admires the cobbler's simplicity, mistaking it for spiritual bliss, while the cobbler sees the foreigner as almost divine given his strange lifestyle. Their conversation reveals mutual misunderstandings about life, religion, and happiness. At one point, the hippie suggests that flowers falling on the cobbler all day are divine blessings, but the cobbler bluntly asks, "Can I eat this flower?" - showing the stark difference between romanticized poverty and real suffering. The story uses irony to contrast perspectives: the hippie escapes life's burdens by choice, while the cobbler is trapped by circumstances.
31\. Hungry Child

A man named Raman takes care of a lost child at a fair. As he looks after the boy, Raman reflects on his own unhappiness at not being married or having children of his own. He feels happy experiencing what it's like to care for a child, even temporarily. The boy's parents eventually reunite with him and scold the child. Raman is left alone again with his unfulfilled dreams of having a family. The story captures the loneliness of being unmarried and childless, and how even a brief moment of caring for a child can awaken deep longings. It shows the contrast between Raman's gentle care and the parents' harsh scolding, highlighting different approaches to children.
32\. Emden

An elderly man named Raman recalls his past as a powerful and corrupt government official during World War II. The story reflects the wartime atmosphere when fear of air raids spread across Indian towns. People of Malgudi lived in constant anxiety, imagining dangers that may never arrive. They recalled the name "Emden," the notorious German warship known for bombarding cities, using it as a symbol of terror. While trying to destroy old papers from his corrupt past, the old man ends up being compelled to revisit an old street. A dog takes his walking cane, leaving him stranded there. As he looks around, he realizes everyone from his past is gone - dead or moved away. He's left alone with memories of his corrupt past and the emptiness of old age. The story blends the psychology of wartime fear with personal reflection on a life of corruption and loneliness.
Summaries in Hindi
1\. An Astrologer's Day

एक व्यक्ति ज्योतिषी का काम करता है, हालांकि उसे सितारों या भविष्यवाणियों के बारे में कुछ नहीं पता। एक दिन एक ग्राहक शर्त लगाता है कि ज्योतिषी उसके बारे में कुछ सच नहीं बता सकता। ज्योतिषी उस व्यक्ति को गुरु नायक के रूप में पहचान लेता है और बताता है कि उसे कभी छुरा घोंपकर कुएं में फेंका गया था। ग्राहक प्रभावित होकर पैसे देता है। उस रात, ज्योतिषी अपनी पत्नी से स्वीकार करता है कि वही व्यक्ति था जिसने साल पहले इस आदमी को मारने की कोशिश की थी।
2\. The Missing Mail

थनप्पा एक डाकिया है जो अपने मार्ग पर सभी से बात करता है। रामानुजम की बेटी की शादी 20 मई को होनी चाहिए वरना तीन साल के लिए टलेगी। शादी सफलतापूर्वक पूरी होने के बाद, थनप्पा बताता है कि उसे 20 मई को रामानुजम के रिश्तेदार की मृत्यु के बारे में एक पोस्टकार्ड मिला था। उसने शादी में बाधा न डालने के लिए पत्र छिपा दिया, भले ही इससे उसकी नौकरी जा सकती थी। रामानुजम कहता है कि वह उसके खिलाफ शिकायत नहीं करेगा।
3\. The Doctor's Word

डॉक्टर रमन अपनी कड़वी ईमानदारी के लिए जाने जाते हैं। अचानक उनका सबसे अच्छा दोस्त गोपाल बुरी तरह बीमार पड़ जाता है। डॉक्टर सोचते हैं कि गोपाल के बचने की केवल 1000 में से 1 संभावना है। गोपाल डॉक्टर से विनती करता है कि वह सच बताए क्योंकि उसे अपनी वसीयत पर हस्ताक्षर करने हैं। डॉक्टर अपने दोस्त को सच नहीं बता पाते और कहते हैं कि वह ठीक हो जाएगा। अगली सुबह, गोपाल का स्वास्थ्य चमत्कारिक रूप से ठीक हो जाता है, जिससे डॉक्टर जीवन भर हैरान रहते हैं।
4\. Gateman's Gift

गोविंद सिंह 25 साल तक गेटकीपर और सुरक्षा गार्ड के रूप में काम करता है। वह जनरल मैनेजर को भगवान की तरह देखने लगता है। सेवानिवृत्त होने के बाद, वह मिट्टी के लघु मॉडल बनाता है। हर बार पेंशन लेते समय, वह अकाउंटेंट को अपना काम देता है, हमेशा पूछता है कि जीएम को पिछला मॉडल कैसा लगा। एक दिन, जीएम का एक पंजीकृत पत्र आता है। सिंह इसे खोलने से बहुत डरता है और यहां तक कि एक्स-रे तकनीशियन के पास जाता है। अकाउंटेंट पत्र खोलता है - जीएम ने उसे धन्यवाद दिया, एक बड़ा चेक भेजा, और अधिक काम देखने की उम्मीद जताई। अजीब बात यह है कि सिंह अपना मिट्टी का शौक छोड़ देता है, कहता है कि यह पागलों का काम है।
5\. The Blind Dog

एक आवारा कुत्ता एक अंधे भिखारी से दोस्ती करता है। जब अंधे की देखभाल करने वाली बूढ़ी महिला मर जाती है, तो वह कुत्ते को पट्टे से बांध लेता है और भीख मांगने के लिए उसका उपयोग करता है। वह पाता है कि इस तरह से वह बहुत अधिक पैसा कमाता है और लालची हो जाता है। वह कुत्ते को लगातार लात मारता और पीटता है। जब बाजार के विक्रेताओं को पता चलता है कि अंधा इतना अमीर है कि पैसे उधार दे रहा है, तो वे पट्टे को कैंची से काट देते हैं और कुत्ता भाग जाता है। कुछ हफ्तों बाद, विक्रेता उन्हें फिर से देखते हैं - लेकिन अब कुत्ते का पट्टा धातु की जंजीर है। अंधा कहता है कि उसका कुत्ता एक रात अपने आप वापस आ गया। विक्रेता वफादार कुत्ते पर तरस खाते हैं।
6\. Fellow-Feeling

राजम अय्यर, एक तमिल ब्राह्मण, एक्सप्रेस ट्रेन में यात्रा कर रहे हैं। एक अन्य यात्री तीसरे यात्री को गाली देना शुरू कर देता है। राजम शामिल हो जाते हैं और गुंडा शिकायत करता है कि ब्राह्मण चुपके से मांस खा रहे हैं। बहस बढ़ जाती है। राजम पहला वार रोकते हैं और धमकी देते हैं कि वे गुंडे का चेहरा इस तरह से फिर से व्यवस्थित कर देंगे कि उसका मुंह उसके बाएं कान के नीचे होगा। जैसे ही वह फिर से मारने वाले होते हैं, गुंडा देखता है कि वे एक स्टेशन स्टॉप पर हैं और खिड़की से बाहर कूद जाता है।
7\. The Tiger's Claw

बातूनी आदमी बच्चों को एक कहानी सुनाता है। वह दावा करता है कि जब वह एक उर्वरक विक्रेता था, तो उसने एक छोटे से गांव के रेलवे स्टेशन पर रात बिताई। एक बाघ अंदर घुस आया और उसे आधी रात में जगा दिया। उसने खुद को फर्नीचर के पीछे बैरिकेड कर लिया ताकि बाघ केवल एक पंजा पहुंचा सके। उसने अपने चाकू से तीन पैर की उंगलियां काट दीं। शहर में वापस, बच्चे बाघ का पंजा देखने के लिए कहते हैं - वास्तव में, तीन पैर की उंगलियां गायब हैं। हालांकि, शिकारी बताते हैं कि आदिवासी लोग शुभकामना के रूप में बाघ के शावकों को लेना और तीन पैर की उंगलियां काटना पसंद करते हैं।
8\. Iswaran

ईश्वरन लगातार नौ वर्षों तक अपनी इंटरमीडिएट कॉलेज परीक्षाओं में फेल हो जाता है। दसवीं बार परीक्षा देने के बाद, जिस दिन स्कोर की रिपोर्ट आती है, ईश्वरन अपने स्कोर की जांच करने के बजाय सिनेमा देखने चला जाता है। जब अन्य लड़के अपनी सफलता का जश्न मनाते हुए आते हैं, तो ईश्वरन को यकीन हो जाता है कि वह फिर से फेल हो गया। वह खुद को नदी में डुबोने का फैसला करता है और एक आत्महत्या का नोट लिखता है। लेकिन जानना चाहते हुए, वह अपना स्कोर चेक करता है। वह न केवल पास हुआ बल्कि सेकंड-क्लास ऑनर्स मिले! अपने उत्साह में, वह जश्न मनाने के लिए नदी में कूद जाता है। उसका शरीर और आत्महत्या का नोट अगले दिन खोजा जाता है, जो आत्महत्या जैसा लगता है।
9\. Such Perfection

एक मूर्तिकार पांच साल के श्रम के बाद भगवान नटराज की एक मूर्ति पूरी करता है। सभी कहते हैं कि यह इतना सही है कि अगर लोग इसे देखें, तो भगवान की महिमा उन्हें नष्ट कर देगी। पुजारी मूर्तिकार से मूर्ति की छोटी उंगली तोड़ने के लिए कहता है, लेकिन मूर्तिकार मना कर देता है। पुजारी फिर इसे मंदिर में प्रतिष्ठित करने से इनकार कर देता है। मूर्तिकार अपने घर को मंदिर में बदल देता है। फिर भगवान जीवित हो जाते हैं और प्राकृतिक आपदाएं उत्पन्न करते हैं - भूकंप, बाढ़ और तूफान जो कई लोगों को मारते हैं। लोग मूर्तिकार से मूर्ति की पूर्णता को खराब करने की भीख मांगते हैं, लेकिन वह नहीं करता। एक पेड़ उसके घर पर गिर जाता है। वह लौटता है और मूर्ति को एक कटी हुई छोटी उंगली को छोड़कर अक्षत पाता है। अब अपूर्ण मूर्ति मंदिर में प्रतिष्ठित है, और मूर्तिकार हमेशा के लिए अपना व्यापार छोड़ देता है।
10\. Father's Help

स्वामी सोमवार को देर से उठता है और अपनी मां को उसे घर पर रहने देने के लिए राजी करता है। उसके पिता जोर देते हैं कि वह जाए, तो स्वामी झूठ बोलता है कि उसका शिक्षक सैमुअल बच्चों को बुरी तरह पीटता है। उसके पिता स्वामी को प्रधानाचार्य को देने के लिए एक पत्र लिखते हैं जो निश्चित रूप से सैमुअल को नौकरी से निकलवा देगा। स्कूल में, स्वामी सैमुअल को कुछ करने के लिए उकसाता है, लेकिन सैमुअल केवल उसके हाथों को हल्के से बेंत मारता है। जब वह पत्र देने की कोशिश करता है, तो प्रधानाचार्य पूरे सप्ताह छुट्टी पर हैं। सहायक प्रधानाचार्य स्वयं सैमुअल हैं! स्वामी बिना पत्र दिए घर भाग जाता है।
11\. The Snake-Song

बातूनी आदमी एक संगीत कार्यक्रम से यातना भोगते हुए निकलता है। वह कहता है कि स्वाद में गिरावट आई है और अपनी कहानी बताता है। उसने एक मास्टर संगीतकार के साथ बांस की बांसुरी का अध्ययन किया। एक रात, एक भिखारी उसके अभ्यास को बाधित करता है और भोजन मांगता है। बातूनी आदमी भिखारी को अंदर आने और सुनने का अधिकार भी देने से इनकार कर देता है। भिखारी उसे शाप देता है, कहता है कि यह संगीत का उसका आखिरी दिन था। उस रात बाद में, एक विशाल कोबरा आता है और उसे बजाते हुए सुनता है। जब वह रुकता है या सांप-गीत के अलावा कुछ भी बजाता है तो यह उत्तेजित हो जाता है। पूरी रात एक ही गीत बजाने के बाद, वह खुद को नीचे फेंक देता है और सांप से उसे बख्शने की भीख मांगता है। जब वह ऊपर देखता है, तो यह चला गया है। बातूनी आदमी कहता है कि उसने अपनी बांसुरी छोड़ दी, लेकिन अगर वह भिखारी को ढूंढ सके और माफी मांग सके, तो वह फिर से अपनी बांसुरी उठाएगा।
12\. Engine Trouble

बातूनी आदमी एक कार्निवल में एक रोड इंजन (भाप-संचालित ट्रैक्टर) जीतता है। इसे चलाना नहीं जानते हुए, वह बस इसे पार्क में छोड़ देता है। शहर उसे पार्किंग स्थान के लिए उसके घर के किराए से दोगुने से अधिक जुर्माना लगाना शुरू कर देता है। वह इसे स्थानांतरित करने की व्यवस्था करता है, लेकिन यह एक दीवार से टकरा जाता है, और उसे नुकसान के लिए भुगतान करना होगा। एक स्वामी शहर में आता है और करतब करता है जैसे कांच खाना और खुद को जिंदा दफनाना। भूकंप के बाद, रोड इंजन उसी आदमी के कुएं में फंस जाता है जिसकी दीवार नष्ट हो गई थी। आदमी बातूनी आदमी को धन्यवाद देता है क्योंकि शहर उसे गंदे पानी के लिए जुर्माना लगाने वाला था अगर कुआं सील नहीं किया गया था।
13\. Forty-Five a Month

शांता, एक प्राथमिक विद्यालय की छात्रा, जल्दी घर जाने के लिए उत्सुक है क्योंकि उसके पिता वेंकट राव ने उसे सिनेमा ले जाने का वादा किया था। घर पर, वह कपड़े पहनती है और उसका इंतजार करती है। इस बीच, वेंकट राव दोषी महसूस करता है कि वह सप्ताह में सात दिन अपनी बेटी के सोने के बाद तक काम करता है। उस दोपहर, वह अपने बॉस से व्यक्तिगत छुट्टी मांगता है या फिर इस्तीफा देता है। उसका बॉस उसे कहता है कि काम से अधिक जरूरी कुछ नहीं है। चालीस रुपये महीने में खरीदे जाने से तंग आकर, वेंकट राव एक इस्तीफा पत्र लिखता है। उसका बॉस फिर उसे बताता है कि उसे पैंतालीस रुपये महीने की बढ़ोतरी मिल गई है, इसलिए वह अपना पत्र फाड़ देता है। जब वह आखिरकार घर पहुंचता है, तो उसकी बेटी पहले से ही सो रही है। वह अपनी पत्नी से कहता है कि वह शांता को बाहर नहीं ले जा सकता क्योंकि उसे बढ़ोतरी मिली है - मतलब वह अब और भी अधिक काम करेगा।
14\. Out of Business

16\. The Axe

रमन नामक एक बुजुर्ग व्यक्ति द्वितीय विश्व युद्ध के दौरान एक शक्तिशाली और भ्रष्ट सरकारी अधिकारी के रूप में अपने अतीत को याद करता है। कहानी युद्धकालीन वातावरण को दर्शाती है जब हवाई हमलों का डर भारतीय शहरों में फैला। मालगुडी के लोग लगातार चिंता में रहते थे, खतरों की कल्पना करते थे जो कभी नहीं आ सकते। उन्होंने "एम्डेन" नाम को याद किया, कुख्यात जर्मन युद्धपोत जो शहरों पर बमबारी के लिए जाना जाता था, इसे आतंक के प्रतीक के रूप में उपयोग करते हुए। अपने भ्रष्ट अतीत से पुराने कागजात को नष्ट करने की कोशिश करते हुए, बूढ़ा आदमी एक पुरानी सड़क पर जाने के लिए मजबूर हो जाता है। एक कुत्ता उसकी चलने की छड़ी ले जाता है, उसे वहां फंसा छोड़ देता है। जैसे ही वह चारों ओर देखता है, उसे एहसास होता है कि उसके अतीत के सभी लोग चले गए हैं - मृत या दूर चले गए। वह अपने भ्रष्ट अतीत और बुढ़ापे के खालीपन की यादों के साथ अकेला रह गया है।

# Chapter 29: Macbeth
Shakespeare Facts
Full name: William Shakespeare
Born: April 23, 1564, in Stratford-upon-Avon, England
Died: April 23, 1616 (age 52), in Stratford-upon-Avon, England
Theater: Co-owner of the Globe Theatre (built in 1599)
Known as: “The Bard of Avon”
Works: 37 plays, 154 sonnets, and 2 narrative poems
Theater company: Lord Chamberlain’s Men (later known as the King’s Men after King James I became patron)
Married: Anne Hathaway in 1582
Children: Susanna, and twins Hamnet and Judith
Play Details
Full title: The Tragedy of Macbeth
Written: 1605-1606
First performed: Likely 1606
First published: First Folio, 1623
Source: Holinshed’s Chronicles (1587)
Setting: Scotland and England, 11th century
Classification: Tragedy
Shortest of Shakespeare’s tragedies: Approximately 2,100 lines
Number of acts: 5
Number of scenes: 28 total (Act 1: 7 scenes, Act 2: 4 scenes, Act 3: 6 scenes, Act 4: 3 scenes, Act 5: 8 scenes)
Language: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) and prose
Historical basis: Based loosely on the historical King Macbeth of Scotland (ruled 1040-1057)
Character List
Major Characters
Macbeth: Thane of Glamis, later Thane of Cawdor and King of Scotland
Lady Macbeth: Macbeth’s wife and partner in crime
Banquo: Macbeth’s friend and fellow general; later murdered on Macbeth’s orders
Fleance: Banquo’s son who escapes murder
Duncan: King of Scotland (murdered by Macbeth)
Malcolm: Duncan’s elder son, heir to the throne, later King of Scotland
Donalbain: Duncan’s younger son who flees to Ireland
Macduff: Thane of Fife, loyal to Duncan, later kills Macbeth
Lady Macduff: Macduff’s wife (murdered along with her children)
Supporting Characters
Three Witches (Weird Sisters): Prophesize Macbeth’s rise and fall
Hecate: Goddess of witchcraft who appears briefly to scold the witches
Ross: Scottish nobleman and cousin to Macduff
Lennox: Scottish nobleman
Angus: Scottish nobleman
Menteith: Scottish nobleman
Caithness: Scottish nobleman
Siward: Earl of Northumberland, general of English forces
Young Siward: Son of Siward (killed by Macbeth)
Seyton: Macbeth’s servant and armor-bearer
Porter: Gatekeeper at Macbeth’s castle
Doctor: Observes Lady Macbeth’s sleepwalking
Gentlewoman: Lady Macbeth’s attendant
Captain: Wounded soldier who reports on battle at the beginning
Murderers: Hired by Macbeth to kill Banquo and Macduff’s family
Act-wise Plot Points
Act 1: The Prophecy and the Plot
Scene 1: A desert place
The three witches meet amid thunder and lightning, establishing the play's ominous atmosphere.
They plan to encounter Macbeth after the battle concludes, showing their supernatural foreknowledge.
The witches speak in paradoxes and riddling language that will characterize their prophecies.
Establishes the supernatural element with the prophetic line: "Fair is foul, and foul is fair."
Their familiar spirits call them away, and they vanish into the fog and filthy air.
This opening scene introduces the theme of appearance versus reality that pervades the play.
Scene 2: A camp near Forres
King Duncan receives reports of the battle against the rebel forces led by Macdonwald.
A wounded Captain describes Macbeth's extraordinary bravery and savage fighting prowess against Macdonwald.
The Captain recounts how Macbeth "unseamed" Macdonwald "from the nave to th' chops" and fixed his head upon the battlements.
Duncan praises Macbeth as "O valiant cousin, worthy gentleman" for his loyalty and courage.
Ross arrives with additional news that the Thane of Cawdor has treacherously betrayed Duncan by aiding the Norwegian forces.
Duncan expresses shock at Cawdor's betrayal, saying "There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face."
Duncan immediately orders Cawdor's execution for treason.
As reward for Macbeth's valor, Duncan transfers Cawdor's title and lands to Macbeth.
This scene establishes Macbeth's initial nobility and Duncan's generous, trusting nature.
Scene 3: A heath
The witches meet on the heath, sharing tales of their malicious supernatural activities.
One witch describes tormenting a sailor's wife and cursing her husband's ship.
The witches encounter Macbeth and Banquo as they return victorious from battle.
Macbeth's first words eerily echo the witches: "So foul and fair a day I have not seen."
The witches deliver their prophecies: Macbeth will be Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and king hereafter.
Banquo receives a paradoxical prophecy: he will be "lesser than Macbeth, and greater," not king himself but father to future kings.
Macbeth demands the witches explain how he can be Cawdor when the current Thane lives, but they vanish mysteriously.
Banquo questions whether they've eaten "the insane root that takes the reason prisoner."
Ross and Angus arrive to announce Macbeth's new title as Thane of Cawdor, confirming the prophecy's first part.
Macbeth is shocked that the prophecy has already begun to come true.
In an aside, Macbeth immediately begins to contemplate murdering Duncan to fulfill the final prophecy.
He experiences his first moment of internal conflict, recognizing his "horrible imaginings."
Banquo warns that "instruments of darkness tell us truths" to betray us in deeper consequence.
Scene 4: Forres, the palace
Duncan inquires whether the traitorous Cawdor has been executed yet.
Malcolm reports that Cawdor died confessing his treasons and repenting deeply.
Duncan reflects ironically that he had absolute trust in Cawdor, foreshadowing his trust in Macbeth.
Duncan warmly praises Macbeth and Banquo for their service, expressing his deep gratitude.
Duncan announces he will visit Macbeth's castle at Inverness, honoring him with the royal presence.
In a crucial political move, Duncan publicly names his son Malcolm as Prince of Cumberland and heir to the throne.
This formal designation of Malcolm as successor places a concrete obstacle in Macbeth's path to the crown.
Macbeth realizes in an aside that Malcolm is now "a step on which I must fall down, or else o'erleap."
He recognizes his "black and deep desires" and asks the stars to hide their fires from his dark intentions.
Macbeth departs to prepare for Duncan's visit, his mind already working on treacherous plans.
Scene 5: Inverness, Macbeth's castle
Lady Macbeth reads aloud a letter from Macbeth describing his encounter with the witches and their prophecies.
She immediately grasps the significance and possibility of becoming queen.
Lady Macbeth fears that Macbeth's nature is "too full o' th' milk of human kindness" to seize the crown by murder.
She worries he desires greatness but lacks the ruthless "illness" (evil) necessary to achieve it.
A messenger arrives with news that Duncan will arrive that very night.
Lady Macbeth sees this as the perfect opportunity and invokes dark spirits in her famous "unsex me here" soliloquy.
She calls on spirits to "stop up th' access and passage to remorse" and fill her with "direst cruelty."
She asks darkness itself to hide the "keen knife" from seeing the wound it makes.
Macbeth arrives, and Lady Macbeth immediately begins persuading him that Duncan "must be provided for."
She instructs him to "look like th' innocent flower, but be the serpent under't."
Lady Macbeth takes psychological command, telling Macbeth to leave the planning to her.
Scene 6: Before Macbeth's castle
Duncan and his sons arrive at Inverness with Banquo and other thanes.
Duncan comments on how pleasant and sweet the air is around the castle, heavy with dramatic irony.
Banquo notes that martlets (birds) nest there, saying the location proves the air is "delicate."
Lady Macbeth emerges to greet Duncan with elaborate courtesy and false hospitality.
She pledges their service and devotion to Duncan, calling his visit an honor.
Duncan praises her as "our honored hostess" and graciously thanks her.
He asks to be taken to Macbeth, whom he says he loves and will continue to favor.
The scene's pleasantness contrasts sharply with the murder being planned within.
Scene 7: Macbeth's castle
While Duncan dines, Macbeth leaves to contemplate the planned assassination in solitude.
In a lengthy soliloquy, Macbeth weighs all the reasons against killing Duncan.
He fears divine justice and earthly consequences: "we but teach bloody instructions, which return to plague th' inventor."
He lists Duncan's virtues: his kinsman, his subject, and his host, each role forbidding the murder.
He acknowledges Duncan is such a good king that his virtues "will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued."
Macbeth admits his only motivation is "vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself."
He resolves to abandon the plot and tells Lady Macbeth they will "proceed no further in this business."
Lady Macbeth responds with scorn, questioning his manhood and calling him a coward.
She accuses him of being "green and pale" in his commitment, like a drunkard after a binge.
In a shocking statement, she says she would dash out her own nursing infant's brains rather than break such an oath.
Lady Macbeth outlines her murder plan: they'll get the chamberlains drunk and blame them for the deed.
She convinces Macbeth by assuring him they cannot fail if they show courage.
Macbeth, persuaded, praises her "undaunted mettle" and agrees to proceed, resolved to "bend up each corporal agent to this terrible feat."
Act 2: The Murder and Its Immediate Aftermath
Scene 1: Court of Macbeth's castle
After midnight, Banquo and his son Fleance walk in the castle courtyard, unable to sleep.
Banquo gives Fleance his sword, showing his unease and the late hour.
He mentions the heavy darkness and his desire to suppress "cursed thoughts that nature gives way to in repose."
Banquo reveals he dreamed of the three weird sisters, suggesting the prophecies haunt him.
Macbeth encounters them and lies, saying he hasn't thought of the witches.
Macbeth suggests they should discuss the prophecies later; Banquo agrees, provided he maintains his honor.
After Banquo and Fleance leave, Macbeth dismisses his servant and is left alone.
Macbeth experiences a terrifying hallucination of a dagger floating in the air, pointing toward Duncan's chamber.
In the famous "dagger" soliloquy, he questions: "Is this a dagger which I see before me, the handle toward my hand?"
He tries to grasp it but cannot, then sees it covered in blood and "dudgeon" (drops).
He realizes his "heat-oppressèd brain" is creating false visions driven by his guilty purpose.
A bell rings—Lady Macbeth's signal—and Macbeth proceeds to Duncan's chamber with the words "Hear it not, Duncan, for it is a knell that summons thee to heaven or to hell."
Scene 2: Duncan's chamber
Lady Macbeth waits tensely, having drugged the chamberlains' wine with drugs and drink.
She reveals she would have killed Duncan herself, except he resembled her father as he slept.
Macbeth enters, his hands bloody, saying "I have done the deed."
He is immediately consumed with psychological torment and paranoia.
Macbeth describes hearing Duncan's sons Malcolm and Donalbain wake and pray in an adjacent chamber.
He reveals his deep spiritual disturbance: when they said "God bless us," he could not say "Amen."
He heard a voice cry "Macbeth does murder sleep"—predicting he will "sleep no more."
Lady Macbeth grows frustrated with his weakness, calling his thoughts "brainsickly."
Macbeth realizes he still carries the bloody daggers, which were meant to be left with the drugged guards.
He refuses to return to the chamber, saying he's afraid to "think what I have done."
Lady Macbeth takes the daggers herself, chiding him: "Infirm of purpose! Give me the daggers."
She plants the daggers on the guards and smears them with Duncan's blood.
Loud knocking begins at the castle gate, startling them both.
Macbeth wishes Duncan could be awakened by the knocking, revealing immediate remorse.
Lady Macbeth hurries him away to wash and change, worried they'll be discovered.
Scene 3: Porter's gate
The drunken Porter staggers to answer the persistent knocking, providing comic relief.
He imagines himself as porter of Hell's gate, admitting various sinners.
He jokes about equivocators, traitors, and those who commit sins, ironically foreshadowing Macbeth's fate.
The Porter finally admits Macduff and Lennox, apologizing for the delay.
Macduff asks if the king has awakened; Macbeth enters and directs him to Duncan's chamber.
Lennox describes the strange, violent weather during the night: winds, screams, prophesying of dire events.
Macbeth agrees it was a "rough night," with heavy irony.
Macduff enters Duncan's chamber and immediately discovers the murdered king.
Macduff emerges crying "horror, horror, horror!" and rings the alarm bell.
He announces "murder and treason" and calls everyone to witness the destruction.
Lady Macbeth enters, feigning ignorance; Macduff tells her the horror is too terrible to speak to a woman.
Banquo, Malcolm, and Donalbain arrive to learn of Duncan's death.
Macbeth delivers a rehearsed speech about Duncan's body being a "breach in nature."
Lennox reports that the chamberlains had blood on them and their daggers were found unwiped.
Macbeth announces he killed the guards in a fury of love for Duncan, claiming righteous rage.
Lady Macbeth conveniently faints, perhaps genuinely overcome or creating a diversion.
Malcolm and Donalbain speak privately, realizing they're in danger as Duncan's heirs.
The brothers decide to flee: Malcolm to England, Donalbain to Ireland, reasoning that separating makes them harder targets.
They recognize "there's daggers in men's smiles" and that those closest have most to gain.
Scene 4: Outside Macbeth's castle
Ross and an Old Man discuss the unnatural events that occurred during the night of Duncan's murder.
The Old Man, despite his seventy years, has never seen such terrible darkness and strange occurrences.
Ross reports Duncan's horses broke loose and ate each other, acting against their nature.
An owl killed a falcon, another reversal of natural order symbolizing the chaos unleashed.
Macduff arrives with news that Malcolm and Donalbain have fled, making them prime suspects.
The suspicion falls on Duncan's sons, who are now believed to have bribed the servants to commit murder.
Macduff reports that Macbeth has been chosen as the new king and will go to Scone for his coronation.
Ross plans to attend the coronation at Scone.
Macduff notably declines to attend, saying he will return home to Fife instead, hinting at his suspicions.
The Old Man gives a blessing, hoping "good" will triumph over "evil," marking the moral struggle of the play.
Act 3: The Paranoid King
Scene 1: Forres, palace
Banquo, now at court under King Macbeth, soliloquizes that he suspects Macbeth "play'dst most foully" for the crown.
He recalls the witches prophesied his descendants would be kings and hopes it might come true.
Macbeth, now king, enters with Lady Macbeth, Lennox, Ross, and other lords.
Macbeth questions Banquo about his plans, learning he'll ride that afternoon and return for a feast.
Macbeth specifically asks if Fleance will accompany Banquo, confirming both will be together.
After the court disperses, Macbeth reveals his deep fear of Banquo in a soliloquy.
He describes Banquo as having a "royalty of nature" and wisdom that makes him dangerous.
Macbeth resents that he murdered Duncan only to place Banquo's descendants on the throne.
He has "filed" (defiled) his mind and given his "eternal jewel" (soul) to the devil for Banquo's issue.
Macbeth summons two murderers whom he has previously manipulated, convincing them Banquo is their enemy.
He persuades them by blaming Banquo for their past misfortunes and questioning their manhood.
Macbeth hires them to kill both Banquo and Fleance, emphasizing it must happen that night away from the palace.
He stresses that Fleance's death is as important as Banquo's, fearing the prophecy.
Scene 2: Palace
Lady Macbeth, now queen, expresses her dissatisfaction despite achieving her goal.
She observes that they have gained everything but are not content: "Nought's had, all's spent, where our desire is got without content."
Macbeth enters, equally miserable, saying "'Tis safer to be that which we destroy than by destruction dwell in doubtful joy."
Lady Macbeth tries to cheer him, telling him to be bright and jovial at the feast.
She advises him to stop brooding: "What's done is done," hoping to move forward.
Macbeth counters that the snake (their enemies) is only "scotched, not killed," still capable of reviving.
He envies Duncan, who lies in peaceful death beyond treasons and anxieties.
Macbeth hints cryptically at his plan against Banquo but doesn't share specific details with Lady Macbeth.
He tells her "Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck, till thou applaud the deed."
He invokes night to conceal the "bloody and invisible hand" that will tear apart the bond keeping him in fear.
This scene marks a shift: Macbeth now acts independently, and their partnership begins to dissolve.
Scene 3: Park near the palace
The two murderers wait with a mysterious Third Murderer who joins them, possibly sent by Macbeth for assurance.
They discuss who sent the third man and confirm their instructions.
As twilight falls, Banquo and Fleance approach on horseback with a torch.
The murderers attack, first extinguishing the light.
Banquo, realizing the betrayal, shouts to Fleance: "O, treachery! Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly!"
Banquo is brutally killed, but in the darkness and confusion, Fleance manages to escape.
The murderers panic at Fleance's escape, realizing they've only accomplished half their mission.
They decide to report to Macbeth what has happened, knowing he'll be displeased.
Scene 4: Banquet hall
Macbeth hosts a state banquet with Lady Macbeth, Ross, Lennox, and Scottish lords.
Macbeth plays the gracious host, welcoming everyone and encouraging them to sit according to their rank.
The First Murderer appears at the door; Macbeth goes to speak with him privately.
The murderer reports Banquo's death but reveals Fleance's escape.
Macbeth is deeply disturbed, saying he would otherwise be "perfect, whole as the marble, founded as the rock."
Now he feels "cabined, cribbed, confined, bound in to saucy doubts and fears."
Macbeth returns to the banquet; Lady Macbeth reminds him to be a good host.
As Macbeth prepares to sit, he sees Banquo's ghost sitting in his designated place.
Macbeth reacts with horror, addressing the ghost: "Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake thy gory locks at me."
The lords are confused and alarmed; Lady Macbeth tries to excuse his behavior as an old affliction.
The ghost disappears; Macbeth regains composure and apologizes.
When he mentions Banquo's name, the ghost reappears, and Macbeth again loses control.
He shouts at the ghost with desperate bravado, challenging it to speak or point at him.
Lady Macbeth, seeing the banquet ruined, hastily dismisses the guests without ceremony.
Alone with his wife, Macbeth notes that Macduff's absence from the feast is suspicious.
He resolves to visit the witches again, saying "I am in blood stepped in so far that should I wade no more, returning were as tedious as go o'er."
Macbeth reveals his descent into pure tyranny: "We are yet but young in deed," suggesting more violence to come.
Scene 5: The heath
Hecate, the goddess of witchcraft, appears and scolds the three witches angrily.
She berates them for dealing with Macbeth without consulting her as their mistress.
Hecate criticizes Macbeth as "a wayward son, spiteful and wrathful, who loves for his own ends, not for you."
She reveals her plan to summon Macbeth to a pit of Acheron in the morning.
Hecate will create powerful, artificial spirits and visions to give Macbeth false confidence.
She plans to make him overconfident, leading him to spurn fate and death itself.
Her goal is Macbeth's destruction through his own security and overconfidence.
Hecate declares "security is mortals' chiefest enemy," identifying his fatal flaw.
Scene 6: Somewhere in Scotland
Lennox speaks with another Scottish Lord, discussing recent suspicious events.
Lennox uses heavy irony to suggest Macbeth's guilt without stating it directly.
He sarcastically notes how "monstrous" it was for Malcolm and Donalbain to kill their father.
He comments on how conveniently Macbeth killed the guards who "couldn't" have committed the murder.
Lennox ironically pities that Fleance fled, since Banquo walking out late "clearly" got him killed.
The Lord reports that Macduff has gone to England to join Malcolm at the English court.
Malcolm has been received by the pious King Edward, who will support his cause.
The Lord reveals that Macduff refused Macbeth's summons, angering the tyrant.
They discuss hopes that Macduff will convince England to send military aid against Macbeth.
Both express their fervent hope for Scotland's liberation from Macbeth's increasingly tyrannical rule.
They pray for a quick end to Scotland's suffering under the illegitimate king.
Act 4: The Second Prophecy and the Tide Turns
Scene 1: A cavern with a cauldron
The three witches gather around a bubbling cauldron, preparing a powerful potion.
They chant their famous spell: "Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn, and cauldron bubble."
The witches add grotesque ingredients: poisoned entrails, eye of newt, toe of frog, wool of bat, tongue of dog.
They include body parts of various creatures and humans: finger of birth-strangled babe, liver of blaspheming Jew.
Hecate arrives briefly, praising their work and adding her own contribution to the charm.
Macbeth arrives demanding answers, threatening to curse the witches if they don't comply.
The witches offer to let him hear answers from their masters rather than from them.
They summon three apparitions with increasingly deceptive prophecies for Macbeth.
First Apparition (an armed head): Warns "Macbeth! Macbeth! Macbeth! Beware Macduff, beware the Thane of Fife."
Second Apparition (a bloody child): Declares "Be bloody, bold, and resolute. Laugh to scorn the power of man, for none of woman born shall harm Macbeth."
Macbeth interprets this as invincibility since everyone is born of woman, but resolves to kill Macduff anyway for safety.
Third Apparition (a crowned child holding a tree): Proclaims "Macbeth shall never vanquished be until Great Birnam Wood to high Dunsinane Hill shall come against him."
Macbeth rejoices, believing forests cannot move, thus ensuring his safety.
Despite the apparitions' assurances, Macbeth demands to know if Banquo's descendants will reign.
The witches warn him not to seek this knowledge, but Macbeth insists.
They show him a procession of eight kings, all resembling Banquo, with Banquo's ghost following, holding a mirror showing more kings.
Macbeth is horrified and furious at this vision confirming the prophecy about Banquo's line.
The witches vanish suddenly to music and dance, leaving Macbeth alone.
Lennox enters, reporting that Macduff has fled to England to join the opposition.
Macbeth, enraged and paranoid, immediately resolves to act on his impulses without reflection.
He decides to massacre Macduff's entire family at Fife: "The castle of Macduff I will surprise, seize upon Fife, give to th' edge o' th' sword his wife, his babes."
This marks Macbeth's complete descent into tyranny, now targeting innocents.
Scene 2: Macduff's castle at Fife
Lady Macduff angrily complains to Ross about her husband abandoning them.
She questions Macduff's love and wisdom, calling his flight to England traitorous cowardice.
Ross defends Macduff, saying his wisdom drove him to flee, but cannot fully explain.
Ross departs after warning that "cruel are the times" and things are uncertain.
Lady Macduff speaks with her young son in a touching scene showing their innocence.
Her son demonstrates wit and wisdom beyond his years, asking about traitors and his father.
The boy insists his father is not dead, and they engage in playful, poignant banter.
A Messenger suddenly arrives, warning Lady Macduff of immediate danger.
He urges her to flee with her children, saying "I doubt some danger does approach you nearly."
Lady Macduff protests she has done no wrong, but the Messenger insists earthly justice doesn't protect her.
Before she can escape, murderers enter asking for Macduff.
When told he's a traitor, the young son bravely defends his father: "Thou liest, thou shag-haired villain!"
The murderers stab the boy, who dies crying to his mother to flee.
Lady Macduff runs screaming "Murder!" with the assassins pursuing her.
She and all her children are killed off-stage, representing Macbeth's ultimate descent into evil.
Scene 3: England, before the King's palace
Malcolm and Macduff meet in England outside King Edward's palace.
Malcolm, suspicious of Macduff's sudden arrival, tests his loyalty through an elaborate deception.
He suggests Macduff might be Macbeth's agent, sent to betray him.
Malcolm proceeds to describe himself as even more evil than Macbeth.
He claims to be lustful, greedy, and lacking all the "king-becoming graces."
Malcolm declares he would "Pour the sweet milk of concord into hell" and cause universal chaos.
Macduff initially tries to excuse Malcolm's vices, desperate for any alternative to Macbeth.
When Malcolm claims he has no good qualities whatsoever, Macduff finally breaks.
Macduff laments Scotland's fate, calling Malcolm "not fit to govern" or even live.
He declares he'll leave Scotland to suffer under Macbeth's tyranny if Malcolm would be worse.
This passionate rejection of tyranny proves Macduff's genuine loyalty to Scotland.
Malcolm immediately reveals the truth: he has none of these vices and has never been with a woman.
He explains the test was necessary because Macbeth has tried to trick him before.
Malcolm reveals that ten thousand English soldiers under Siward are ready to invade Scotland.
A doctor briefly appears, describing King Edward's miraculous healing powers, contrasting good kingship with Macbeth's evil.
Ross arrives from Scotland with dire news of the country's suffering under Macbeth's tyranny.
Ross hesitates to tell Macduff personal news, revealing Macduff's family was "well at peace" (dead) when he left.
Macduff immediately senses tragedy; Ross finally reveals that his wife, children, and servants were all savagely murdered.
Macduff is stunned into silence, struggling to process the horror: "All my pretty ones? Did you say all?"
Malcolm urges him to channel grief into revenge: "Dispute it like a man."
Macduff responds with raw emotion: "I shall do so, but I must also feel it as a man."
He blames himself for their deaths, believing Macbeth killed them because of his absence.
Macduff vows revenge, praying heaven will bring Macbeth face-to-face with him.
Malcolm declares they'll march on Scotland immediately, channeling grief into military action.
Act 5: The Fall of Macbeth
Scene 1: Dunsinane, a room in the castle
A Doctor and Gentlewoman secretly observe Lady Macbeth's disturbing behavior.
The Gentlewoman reports Lady Macbeth has been sleepwalking regularly since Macbeth went to war.
She describes how Lady Macbeth writes during these episodes, then seals the paper.
Lady Macbeth enters in her nightgown, carrying a candle, her eyes open but asleep.
The Gentlewoman reveals Lady Macbeth now insists on having light by her constantly, fearing darkness.
Lady Macbeth performs a hand-washing gesture, rubbing her hands obsessively.
She speaks the famous line: "Out, damned spot! Out, I say!"
Lady Macbeth unconsciously reenacts the night of Duncan's murder in fragmented speeches.
She references the one o'clock bell and their signal, revealing intimate knowledge of the crime.
She speaks of blood: "Yet who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?"
She mentions Lady Macduff: "The Thane of Fife had a wife. Where is she now?"
She obsesses over the smell: "Here's the smell of blood still. All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand."
The Doctor recognizes these are confessions of terrible deeds beyond his ability to cure.
He declares: "More needs she the divine than the physician," recognizing spiritual rather than physical illness.
The Doctor realizes the danger of this knowledge and advises the Gentlewoman to watch Lady Macbeth carefully.
He fears Lady Macbeth might harm herself in her tormented state.
The scene reveals how guilt has completely destroyed Lady Macbeth's earlier steely resolve.
Scene 2: Country near Dunsinane
Scottish nobles including Menteith, Caithness, Angus, and Lennox march with soldiers.
They discuss joining the English forces led by Malcolm, Siward, and Macduff.
Menteith reports the English army is led by Malcolm, "born in right," and good men motivated by revenge.
They plan to meet the English forces near Birnam Wood.
Angus reports that Macbeth is fortifying Dunsinane Castle and preparing for siege.
They discuss Macbeth's mental state: some say he's mad, others that he's in "valiant fury."
Caithness describes Macbeth as feeling his title "hang loose about him, like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief."
They recognize Macbeth's tyrannical crimes have alienated all loyalty.
The nobles commit to purging Scotland's sickness and restoring health under Malcolm's legitimate rule.
They march toward Birnam Wood to join Malcolm's liberating army.
Scene 3: Dunsinane, a room in the castle
Macbeth appears increasingly paranoid, receiving reports of desertions and enemy movements.
He dismisses reports of the approaching army, clinging to the witches' prophecies.
Macbeth repeatedly declares his security: "Till Birnam Wood remove to Dunsinane, I cannot taint with fear."
He boasts that he cannot be harmed by anyone "of woman born."
A Servant enters with news that ten thousand English soldiers approach.
Macbeth alternates between rage at the servant and false bravado about his invincibility.
He calls for his armor despite Seyton telling him it's not needed yet.
Macbeth expresses his weariness with life: "I have lived long enough. My way of life is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf."
He realizes he lacks what should come with old age: "honor, love, obedience, troops of friends."
Instead he receives only "curses, not loud but deep, mouth-honor, breath, which the poor heart would fain deny, and dare not."
The Doctor reports on Lady Macbeth's condition; Macbeth dismisses it impatiently.
Macbeth demands the Doctor cure her, revealing his inability to understand psychological illness.
He asks for medicine to cure Scotland itself: "cast the water of my land, find her disease."
Macbeth oscillates between putting on armor and taking it off, showing his agitated mental state.
He expresses contempt for physical medicine, then in an aside wishes he could flee Dunsinane but knows he's trapped.
Despite his bravado, Macbeth shows signs of desperation and awareness of his isolation.
Scene 4: Country near Birnam Wood
Malcolm, Siward, Young Siward, Macduff, Menteith, Caithness, Angus, and Lennox lead their combined forces.
Malcolm orders every soldier to cut down a branch from Birnam Wood.
Each soldier must carry a bough before him to conceal their numbers from Macbeth's scouts.
This camouflage strategy will make their actual troop strength uncertain to the enemy.
Siward reports they've learned Macbeth confidently remains in Dunsinane, preparing for siege.
Malcolm reveals that some of Macbeth's men serve him only because they must, not from loyalty.
Macduff urges them to stop talking and start fighting, eager for revenge.
Siward counsels patience, saying they'll know the true situation only after battle.
Malcolm expresses hope and optimism, but acknowledges that war's outcome is always uncertain.
They march forward carrying their branches, the moving forest beginning its approach to Dunsinane.
The prophecy begins its fulfillment, though Macbeth doesn't yet know it.
Scene 5: Dunsinane, within the castle
Macbeth confidently boasts that his castle's strength will withstand any siege.
He claims the enemy could stay outside until famine and disease destroy them.
He wishes they could meet in open battle where he could "beard them to our face."
A cry of women is heard from within the castle.
Seyton goes to investigate the source of the disturbance.
Macbeth reflects that he has "almost forgot the taste of fears."
He says there was a time when a night-shriek would have chilled him, but now nothing affects him.
He has "supped full with horrors" and become numb to terror and death.
Seyton returns and reports: "The Queen, my lord, is dead."
Macbeth receives the news with eerie calm and responds with his famous nihilistic soliloquy.
"Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" speech reveals his complete despair about life's meaninglessness.
He describes life as "a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing."
He sees life as "a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage and then is heard no more."
This speech shows Macbeth's spiritual death—he feels nothing even at his wife's demise.
A Messenger enters with impossible news: Birnam Wood appears to be moving toward Dunsinane.
The Messenger trembles as he reports what he saw: the forest began to move.
Macbeth initially threatens to hang the messenger if he's lying, offering torture if the report is false.
Macbeth suddenly realizes the witches' equivocation: "the fiend that lies like truth."
He understands he's been deceived by prophecies that were technically true but misleading.
Despite recognizing his doom, Macbeth resolves to fight: "At least we'll die with harness on our back."
He orders the alarm bell rung and prepares to sally forth from the castle.
Macbeth chooses to fight rather than surrender, preferring death in combat to submission.
Scene 6: Before Dunsinane Castle
Malcolm, Siward, Macduff, and the army arrive at Dunsinane and throw down their branches.
The camouflage is no longer needed now that they've reached the castle.
Malcolm gives strategic orders: worthy Siward and his son will lead the first battalion.
Macduff and Malcolm will follow with the main force and additional support.
Siward assesses the situation, noting that Macbeth's forces are indeed staying within the castle.
Malcolm reports that some of Macbeth's soldiers have defected to their side.
Those remaining with Macbeth are pressed men who serve him unwillingly.
Siward orders trumpets blown and the army to make their presence known.
They prepare for the final assault, ready to restore Scotland to rightful rule.
The scene is brief but marks the beginning of the final battle.
Scene 7: The battlefield
Macbeth emerges from the castle onto the battlefield, refusing to hide or flee.
He compares himself to a bear tied to a stake in bear-baiting, forced to fight.
Young Siward confronts Macbeth, challenging him and asking his name.
When Macbeth identifies himself, Young Siward calls him "abhorred tyrant" and a devil.
Macbeth boasts that he should fear his name more than any name in hell.
Young Siward declares he's not afraid and attacks.
They fight; Macbeth kills Young Siward easily.
Macbeth stands over the body, reaffirming his confidence: "Thou wast born of woman."
He declares that swords, smiles, and weapons wielded by men born of women cannot hurt him.
Macbeth exits, leaving Young Siward's corpse on the battlefield.
Macduff enters from another direction, searching desperately for Macbeth.
Macduff refuses to fight Macbeth's hired soldiers, wanting only the king himself.
He shouts for Macbeth, calling him out: "Tyrant, show thy face!"
Macduff vows that if Macbeth is killed by anyone else, the ghosts of his wife and children will haunt him forever.
He seeks personal vengeance, needing to face Macbeth man-to-man.
Siward enters and reports that the castle has been easily taken.
Malcolm's forces have met little resistance; many of Macbeth's men have switched sides.
The battle is nearly won, with the outcome no longer in doubt.
They prepare for the final confrontation with Macbeth himself.
Scene 8: Another part of the battlefield
Macbeth enters alone, still defiant but increasingly desperate.
He refuses to "play the Roman fool" and die by suicide on his own sword.
He declares that while there are living men around him, his wounds look better on them than himself.
Macduff finally finds Macbeth and calls out: "Turn, hellhound, turn!"
Macbeth recognizes Macduff and reveals he has been avoiding him specifically.
He confesses: "My soul is too much charged with blood of thine already."
Macbeth refers to the murder of Macduff's family, showing some remnant of conscience.
Macduff refuses to talk and demands they fight with swords instead of words.
Macbeth warns Macduff that his labor will be in vain.
He boasts of his charmed life, revealing the prophecy: he cannot be killed by "one of woman born."
Macduff responds with the devastating revelation: "Macduff was from his mother's womb untimely ripped."
He reveals he was born by Caesarean section, not through natural birth.
Macbeth is horrified, cursing the witches who deceived him with double meanings.
He realizes the "juggling fiends" spoke in equivocations: true in one sense but false in another.
Macbeth's confidence completely collapses as he understands both prophecies have been fulfilled through wordplay.
He initially refuses to fight, declaring he won't yield to Macduff.
Macduff commands him to surrender and threatens he'll be displayed like a monster in a show.
The threat of public humiliation—being exhibited alive as a captive tyrant—spurs Macbeth.
Macbeth regains his warrior spirit and refuses to kiss the ground before Malcolm or be mocked by the crowd.
He declares he'll try his last chance: "Lay on, Macduff, and damned be him that first cries 'Hold, enough!'"
They fight offstage in single combat, with Macbeth finally meeting his destined opponent.
Malcolm, Siward, Ross, and other nobles enter the castle, which has been fully captured.
Siward asks about casualties; Ross reports few losses among their forces.
Siward inquires about his son; Ross sorrowfully reports Young Siward died bravely in combat.
Ross tries to soften the news by praising the young man's honorable death.
Siward asks if his son's wounds were on the front of his body (honorable) or back (cowardly).
Learning his son died facing the enemy, Siward accepts the death stoically as a soldier's fate.
He refuses to grieve excessively: "He's worth no more. They say he parted well and paid his score."
Malcolm praises Siward's restraint and dignity in loss.
Macduff enters carrying Macbeth's severed head on a pole.
Macduff hails Malcolm: "Hail, King! For so thou art. Behold where stands th' usurper's cursed head."
He announces that Scotland is free and invites everyone to witness Malcolm's coronation.
The assembled nobles join in proclaiming Malcolm as King of Scotland.
Malcolm's first speech as king thanks those who supported him in the fight.
He announces he will create new earls, making Scotland's first earls in the English fashion.
Malcolm promises to recall all exiles who fled from Macbeth's tyranny.
He vows to bring to justice all of Macbeth's cruel ministers and agents.
Malcolm reveals that Lady Macbeth died by her own hand, confirming her suicide.
He promises to perform all necessary tasks to restore Scotland "in measure, time, and place."
Malcolm invites everyone to his coronation at Scone, where Scottish kings are traditionally crowned.
The play ends with order restored, legitimate kingship returned, and the promise of Scotland's healing.
Malcolm's final words emphasize restoration and the end of tyrannical rule.
The prophecies have all been fulfilled, though in ways Macbeth never anticipated or understood.
